#6401. The Best Cast-Iron Skillets for a Lifetime of Cooking (2026)

For some people there isn’t much of a debate around who makes the best cast-iron skillet. There is a die-hard fan base loyal to the affordable US-made Lodge cast-iron pan that will not hear of any other suggestions.

There are others (cast-iron nerds and collectors) who swear by the superior quality of their vintage pan from Griswold or Wagner that they found at a scrap yard, de-rusted in a bucket with a DIY electrolysis setup, and seasoned with a proprietary oil blend in the furnaces of their bespoke restoration workshop.

To these two camps of people I say: “I don’t want to fight you, and I already know why you feel the way you feel. Please do not send me any angry emails.”

If you’ve been loyal to your own cast-iron pan for years—or decades—I don’t expect to change your mind. My goal is merely to provide recommendations for cast-iron cookware based on side-by-side testing and the input collectively provided by members of our staff. Agree with me and my team or don’t; either way, I’m happy if people are passionate about cooking with cast iron because I too enjoy it a great deal.

Cast-iron frying pans were the original nonstick pans, before ceramic nonstick and PTFE rolled around, and unlike modern nonstick coatings, a cast-iron pan’s surface actually gets more nonstick over time rather than degrading week by week. This is because, through continued cooking, thin layers of oil polymerize to the surface of the pan, creating a glassy nonstick surface that improves with continued use. They are also strong enough to handle metal utensils. The same can’t be said for that Instagram-famous nonstick pan (you know the one).

Yes, there are ways you can damage this seasoning layer, but these pans are far more resilient than lots of people think, and they aren’t actually all that difficult to care for. Talk to cast-iron enthusiasts and they’ll tell you the best way to season a cast-iron skillet is to just keep cooking with it.

And cook with it you can. Cast-iron pans are amazing for fried eggs, skillet hashes, cornbread, and sautéed greens. At a high heat, they do an incredible job searing strip steaks, London broil, and chicken thighs, giving you a burnished crispy exterior.

Bottom line, cast-iron cooking is an absolute joy, and every kitchen tool kit should include some cast iron alongside its stainless-steel and carbon steel pans and enameled Dutch oven.

New in this update: A review of Made In's new cast-iron pan as well as more long-term testing information for our winner.

Size(s): 10.5" (4.5 lb.), 12" (6 lb.), 13.5" (7.5 lb.)Pre-seasoned: Yes

What I loved: Because they’re much more expensive than the Lodges folks got used to, many feel a certain type of way about the new era of smooth, vintage-style cast-iron pans that includes this Lancaster. But when you have the opportunity to test a bunch of these pans side by side, you really get a sense of their differences (however small), and you’d be surprised by the things you notice. It was in this apples-to-apples testing that this pan, manufactured by a small company based in Southeastern Pennsylvania, really set itself apart.

The Lancaster is the lightest cast-iron pan I’ve tested, weighing in at 4 lb. for the No. 8 (10"-diameter) pan. Most cast-iron pans of a similar size are around 5 lb. or more—a seemingly small difference in number that makes a surprisingly big difference in hand. When laid out next to a dozen pans in the Test Kitchen, multiple testers singled out this pan as being the most comfortable to hold and maneuver.

It has thinner walls than a typical cast-iron skillet, which allows it to heat up faster. In testing, it came to temp over one minute faster than pans with thicker walls. We were concerned this would mean a reduction in the level of heat retention you’d want to crisp up the edges of some skillet cornbread, but we didn’t find that to be a problem at all. The cooking surface also demonstrated relatively even heat for a cast-iron pan (you really can’t expect too much from cast iron, though; cold spots are sort of inevitable with the material).

The pan comes pre-seasoned, but as is the case with most smooth cast-iron pans, this seasoning layer isn’t nearly as robust as what you’d find on a conventional Lodge or Victoria pan. The polished surface does aid in the pan’s nonstick properties, though, so we found the pan was exceptionally nonstick right out of the box.

Other testing sites have criticized this style of smooth cast-iron pan for getting stained after cooking, but to that we say: This is the process of seasoning developing on the pan. That staining is a feature, not a bug.

An earlier design of this pan didn’t include a helper handle, a feature we missed but forgave because the pan was already so easy to wield. However, Lancaster recently updated the design to include one—all the better in our book. Check out my full review of the Lancaster No. 8 here.

What I’d leave: The main drawback here is the cost. This pan will set you back $175, a steep price for cookware with a reputation for being budget-friendly. I’ll just say this: People happily pay comparable prices for nonstick ceramic cookware that lasts only a year or two at best. This pan, provided you don’t drop it in an industrial crucible, will last a lifetime.

In the long run: I have more patience than a lot of people when it comes to taking care of pans. So I will concede that the out of the box seasoning isn’t that robust. Some tasks, like searing off meat, can strip the seasoning slightly at first. With the Lancaster, I’ve found that this doesn’t impact the pans overall nonstick-ness. It does, however, mean you have to keep an eye out for rust until it gets a couple uses under its belt.

Below you’ll see two Lancaster pans. The left is four years old and the right is fresh from the box (you can tell because the earlier generation of pans didn’t have the helper handle). These are the pans after searing off two chicken thighs. You can see how the pan on the left has a robust, established seasoning, while the one on the right has some gray patches where the chicken skin pulled off some of that seasoning. From experience (I am the owner of the pan on the left), I can say that all you really need to do is keep cooking with it to get that seasoning back, but if you want to do a whole round of seasoning in the oven yourself, it certainly won’t hurt. Honestly, had I just sautéed some onions in the rendered schmaltz after cooking the chicken, those spots would be taken care of.

For comparison, I seared some chicken thighs in both pans. The factory seasoning might get patchy after the first use. Don’t let that scare you, just keep cooking with it. If you’re really worried about rust, just wipe down the surface of the pan with a tiny bit of neutral oil, buff off the excess, and put it over the heat for a few minutes.

Some people complain about the cosmetic changes to these smooth pans when breaking them in To reiterate: It does not impact the performance of the pan. If it bothers you, I encourage you to think about how it’s a record of use and proof that it’s growing and developing alongside you. Or, if you’re just an unsentimental aesthete, perhaps read up on the concept of wabi-sabi. I personally think that my pan is the most beautiful piece of cookware I own!

If you want a high-quality pan that’s not only a pleasure to cook with, but can serve as a family heirloom for generations to come, consider this one. If you’re just looking for a workhorse that won’t break the bank, go for the budget option below.

Size(s): 4.8" (1.1 lb.), 6.5" (2 lb.), 8" (3.1 lb.), 10" (5.5 lb.), 12" (7.5 lb.)Pre-seasoned: Yes

What I loved: Again, I apologize for snubbing Lodge, as even in our office we have a number of staunch brand loyalists. But in my testing, the Victoria edged out the fan favorite on two separate metrics. Victoria pans are pre-seasoned with flaxseed oil and arrive glossy and exceptionally nonstick. Having a more thorough pre-seasoning is more important on cast-iron pans, as they are prone to sticking early on. We found the Victoria pan’s factory seasoning slicker than Lodge’s, which made frying potatoes and eggs ever so slightly easier. Do all cast-iron seasonings improve with continued use over time? Yes. But we know that some people want as much of a head start as they can get, and this pan offers you the best one.

The other way the Victoria bested the Lodge is in its form factor. The pour spouts on the Victoria are nice and wide, making it easy to pour off oil or other pan juices, and testers found the handle shape slightly more comfortable than the Lodge.

I’ll be honest, though, these differences are pretty small, and if you feel drawn to the Lodge name, I recommend it as well.

What I’d leave: Given it’s bargain pricing, there isn’t much to dislike here. I will note this pan is significantly heavier than the Lancaster pan—a full pound and a half for the same diameter skillet. Heavier skillets are cheaper and easier to produce, so it’s a trade-off you’ll have to accept if you want a less expensive piece of cookware.

1. We had several members of staff handle the pans to get a broad sense of how easy the pans were to maneuver. Then we got to cooking.

2. Using a little bit of oil, we fried eggs sunny-side up and scrambled to see how much (if anything) stuck to the pan.

3. We seared skin-on chicken thighs to get a sense of how evenly heat was distributed around the cooking surface. We also measured how long it took for the pan to reach 375° at medium heat.

4. We washed the pans in hot water, noting any places where seasoning might have worn away.

5. We re-seasoned the pans ourselves in an oven for an hour at 500°.

6. We cooked another round of eggs to observe any changes.

I omitted enameled cast-iron skillets like those made by Le Creuset or Staub because enameled surfaces offer a different experience in terms of both cooking and care. I also chose to exclude any cast-iron griddles or grill pans since they are too different functionally.

Sizing is a bit different from company to company, but I chose to stick with a 10"-diameter skillet—a No. 8 in traditional cast-iron sizing—as it is the most common size available.

I should clarify that cast-iron pans aren’t nonstick in the sense that you can cook an egg in the pan without any oil and slide it around. A really well-seasoned pan that’s a glossy lacquered black from years of use might get close, but the seasoning really just helps food release more easily from the pan—and the more seasoning there is, the less oil you’ll need for food to release.

I evaluated the pans on their out-of-the-box factory seasoning, because having a solid seasoning layer to start with diminishes the amount of time you need to break in a pan. This matters more with cheaper, rough textured cast iron, which is more prone to sticking when it lacks proper seasoning. For polished or vintage-style cast-iron pans (like the Lancaster), factory seasoning is nice, but the smooth surface also aids in preventing sticking, so it isn’t as crucial in the beginning stages of using the pan. That is why, throughout this review you see more emphasis on factory seasoning when discussing budget pans.

Is the pan designed in a way that makes it easy to use?

I counted form and design heavily in how I judged these pans. I wanted the pan to be comfortable and easy to maneuver, so I looked for pans that were lightweight (relatively, we’re talking about iron here) and had handles that were comfortable to grip. If the pan was heavier, I wanted a helper handle for moving it from the cooktop to the oven. I didn’t place an emphasis on whether handle was designed to stay cool, because even a handle billed as “stay cool” will get dangerously hot when cooking for long enough, so I feel it’s better to just make a habit of always using an oven mitt or cloth to grab a cast-iron handle.

Heavy-duty, even-heating, satisfyingly weighty skillets are staples in the BA Test Kitchen because of their versatility. Stainless-steel and carbon steel frying pans get hot quickly, but they don’t always have the heat-retention capabilities of cast iron. And while nonstick pans are nice for scrambled eggs and crispy-skinned fish, many are not oven-safe and should never be exposed to high temperatures, so you can’t sear safely with them.

The Stargazer is a lovely pan. Like the Lancaster, its a vintage-style skillet, so it has a smooth texture that’s easy to clean. The surface develops seasoning well, and the curved lip allows for easy pouring at any angle. Ultimately, it is one of the heavier high-end skillets available on the market, which is why we don’t have it as a winner. However, if weight isn’t a huge concern for you, it is still an excellent pan.

If you know cast-iron pans, you might see the Yeti cast-iron skillet and might find that it looks somewhat familiar. This is because Yeti acquired cult-favorite Butter Pat several years ago. The Yeti skillet is just the Butter Pat by a new name, and apart from the logo, the finish, handle shape, and overall design remain unchanged. This pan has a nice velvety surface that holds on to seasoning very well, while still maintaining a smooth, glossier finish that makes vintage-style pans so desirable. Small gripes: The handle design wasn’t a favorite among testers, and the side walls are a slightly shorter than most other cast-iron pans. It’s also a touch heavier and a couple touches more expensive than our winner. Still, this is an excellent cast-iron pan and makes a great family heirloom.

Lodge Cast-Iron Skillet with Red Mini Silicone Hot Handle Holder, 8"

People who track recommendations like these tend to be shocked that we don’t place the Lodge as our winner or budget pick. It is a fantastic pan, make no mistake. It has a great factory seasoning that’s resilient from the jump, and the 10" costs around twenty bucks—so what gives? When it came down to it, the Victoria pan had a slicker factory seasoning out of the box and a more comfortable handle design.

Another high-end polished cast-iron pan on the list. Smithey pans are gorgeous, so much so that it almost feels wrong cooking with them. However, you should cook with it straight away, as the factory seasoning is a little light on these, and we observed a little bit wearing away after the first couple rounds of cooking prior to us adding an additional layer of seasoning. Senior editor Noah Kaufman has been cooking with the Smithey multiple times a week for a couple years and says that within a few months of regular use and two bouts of seasoning in the oven he no longer worried about stuck eggs or steaks.

Gorgeous as they are, Smithey pans are heavy, though, at 5.8 lb. for the 10" skillet.

This skillet is the second lightest (4.3 lb. at 10") and has a velvety surface that holds on to seasoning a little better than the smooth polished pans. Like the Stargazer, it also has a curved lip instead of a pour spout, but I found that this pan does have a bit of a dribbling problem, which I wasn't crazy about. Still, one member of our team who has now lived with this pan for years loves it and uses it every day.

Lodge Cast-Iron Blacklock Skillet, Triple Seasoned - 10.25"

Lodge released this pan in response to the wave of new and fancy polished pans, and as beautiful (quite beautiful), well-seasoned (three glossy layers), and lightweight as it is (almost even with the Lancaster), our testers found the handle uncomfortable to hold.

Ooni is a pizza oven company, and this pan is really designed for cooking in an oven rather than on the stovetop. It has a detachable handle, which is actually a genius bit of design that makes it easy and comfortable to grab out of a blazing hot pizza oven. But the sides are too shallow for doing more normal cast-iron things like frying chicken or sautéing greens. It is, however, great for cornbread and pizookies.

This is Made In’s official entry into the cast-iron new wave. The pan has a smooth machined surface, nice design touches, like curved sidewalls and a spacious helper handle. The primary handle is nice to hold; however, a longer handle can make a pan feel heavier and add strain on the wrists. This pan is not the lightest, either. I found it difficult to transport the full pan from the stovetop to the oven using only one hand, so consider this a pan for people with meaty forearms. Made In also uses flaxseed oil for the factory seasoning, which is a controversial choice in the cast-iron world. The reason for that controversy is that, while the finish flaxseed oil produces is glossy and attractive, it tends to be brittle. Especially with newer pans, a flaxseed seasoning has a tendency to wear away with regular cooking. After testing, I did notice this pan had some gray (unseasoned) patches after a round of searing meat. Again, not a big deal—just keep cooking with it— but something to keep in mind. All of that being said, I do still think this is a high-quality pan. During the cooking tests, I had absolutely no issues with sticking whatsoever.

This pan is pretty similar to a standard Lodge or Victoria, but with a seasoning that’s not as nonstick out of the box. We did find, however, that it added new layers of seasoning quite well.

The Valor is apparently a favorite in restaurants, but there’s nothing special to it that makes it stand out. If anything, the pour spouts are so small they might as well not be there at all.

We’re all for innovation, which is what Finex sought to do with its octagonal pan and its bulbous handle, but we didn’t really observe any value from the modifications. While the octagonal shape is easier for flipping you could just use a bigger cast-iron pan for anything you want to flip. And its “speed cool” handle was awkward to hold.

Anytime KitchenAid ventures beyond the small appliance space you never quite know what you’re gonna get. In this case, it’s a cast-iron pan that is totally average in every way, except for its minimalist modern design. We think this pan is too expensive for what you’re getting.

“Ooh, a lid!” Was the universal reaction to this cast-iron pan. If you like the idea of having a lid for your pan, then this is your pan. The problem with cast-iron lids, though, is that they don’t benefit from the progressive seasoning development the rest of the pan gets as you cook with it. Lids are only really dealing with evaporative moisture, which makes them even more likely to rust. Smithey, up above, sells glass lids that fit their pans, which, while not as oven-safe, won’t have that rust problem.

This is Victoria’s answer to the high-end polished cast-iron pan. The seasoning is great, but the pan is heavier than the Lancaster, and we didn’t love all the extra design embellishments. The brass insert on the handle had no practical value (it heated up quicker than the surrounding cast iron). Also, all the extra ridges and divots just meant more places for gunk to get stuck in.

Amazon customers really like this pan. It comes with a silicone handle cover and a glass lid, which is nice (glass is a better material for a lid than cast iron). It also has tall 3" sides that make this pan great for frying. Beyond that, though, the pan is heavy and seemed to be barely pre-seasoned.

This is a super polished cast-iron pan with a glossy cooking surface that was nice to work with. However, we noticed quite a few cosmetic issues, like small nicks and rough edges that made it seem like there were some corners cut in the manufacturing process.

Another pan that is just fine. The factory seasoning is minimal, so you’ll have to build that up yourself. There are several better options that are just as affordable from Victoria, Lodge, and others.

This is an affordable pan that looks a lot like a Lodge, but with a lesser factory seasoning.

The seasoning that came on this pan out of the box was pretty bad, and with so many other cheap alternatives that offer much better quality, we don’t see the point in purchasing this pan. It’s also only available in a 15" diameter at the time of writing, which is bigger (and heavier) than most people need.

When you first get your pan, you’ll want to season it. We recommend this even when the pan comes labeled as pre-seasoned. To do this, just lightly rub a bone-dry pan with a thin layer of high-heat neutral vegetable oil and place it upside down in a very hot oven—450°F–500°F should do the trick. Leave for an hour, turn off the heat, let it cool completely in the oven (you should be able to take it out without an oven mitt or towel), rub with a tiny bit more oil, and store. You can season cast iron as many times as you’d like to build up a glossy nonstick surface; when the pan looks dull or dry, it’s time to moisturize.

No, you can’t chuck it in the dishwasher, and you won’t be using your normal hand-wash methods, but a cast-iron skillet really doesn’t require much love. When it’s time to clean up, simply wipe a damp rag across the surface of your pan, then dry it thoroughly. Often, that’ll be enough. But if there are any crusty bits, try pouring coarse salt in there and going at it with a Tawashi scrubber, which has soft bristles that whisk away any detritus. Many will tell you to avoid soap at all costs lest you ruin your careful seasoning, but a little dish soap is fine—just don’t let it sit in hot water. (Read our complete guide to cleaning cast iron.)

For really baked on crumbs, try The Ringer, a handy chain mail scrubber that easily rinses clean between uses. After cleaning your cast iron, be sure to wipe your fry pan very dry—this is key for preventing any rust spots. Then take a teeny bit of neutral cooking oil (like canola or vegetable), smear on a paper towel, and give it a light coating. Take care to get the handle and the bottom as well as the cooking surface, as rust can crop up anywhere. And you’re good to go! It sounds involved, but it really only takes a few minutes. A well-seasoned pan takes virtually no time at all, so dutifully season and you’ll be rewarded.

Tossed your skillet in the sink absentmindedly or left it out in the rain only to find it’s developed a layer of orange rust? Don’t panic—rusting can happen pretty easily if you allow your pan to come into contact with water for an extended period of time (it is made of iron, after all). But that doesn’t mean it’s ruined. A salt scrub will help with most small spots, while a vinegar soak is the cure for more serious cases. (Read more on dealing with pesky cast-iron rust patches.)

If, after all of that, you’re still intimidated by raw cast-iron cookware, you might want to consider an enameled cast-iron skillet. It offers all of the heat retention and distribution of a well-seasoned cast-iron pan, plus it has a porcelain enamel to prevent rusting. Unlike a Le Creuset Dutch oven, enameled cast-iron skillets, like Staub’s, have a dark textured enamel that helps with browning and crisping.

Wilder Davies: I have been Epicurious and Bon Appétit’s resident cookware tester and researcher for over six years. I have cooked with hundreds and hundreds of pans and have asked chefs, materials scientists, and manufacturers far too many questions about things that go clank in the kitchen. I am a big apologist of nonstick alternatives, and strongly believe in a buy-it-for-life ethos when it comes to outfitting your pantry.

#6398. Rewriting History: New Research Reveals Ancient Iron Age King May Have Been a Woman

A ruler whose exile helped trigger Rome’s invasion of Britain may have been a woman, challenging centuries of assumptions about a pivotal figure in British history.

Research led by Dr. Miles Russell at Bournemouth University (BU) challenges the traditional identification of Verica as a male king. Drawing on the ruler’s name and coin imagery, Russell argues that a woman held a central role in the events leading to Rome’s invasion of Britain in AD 43.

Verica ruled the Atrebates, whose lands covered much of modern-day Hampshire and West Sussex. Driven from power around AD 40, the ruler fled to Emperor Claudius in Rome, seeking support. That appeal gave Claudius an opportunity to intervene in Britain and claim a military triumph.

Russell, BU’s Director of Archaeological Fieldwork, argues that Verica’s identity has been filtered through assumptions made by earlier historians. “Verica is assumed to have been male because of the patriarchal mindset of 19th-century classical historians. Verica was not only critical to the special relationship between Britain and Rome in the early first century AD but was indisputably female.”

One clue, he suggests, is the name itself. Its “a” ending also appears in the names of female rulers from the same period, including Cartimandua of the Brigantes (in Yorkshire) and Boudica of the Iceni (in Norfolk). Boudica’s revolt against Roman rule in AD 60 made her the most famous of the three, but Russell considers Verica the more powerful and influential figure.

The title on Verica’s coins has also shaped how the ruler is remembered. “People also assume she was a ‘he’ because of the term ‘rex’ on coins, but ‘rex’ is a non-gender-specific title; both male and female kings were recognized by Rome, Cleopatra of Egypt being the most famous,” Russell said. “The use of the Latin title ‘rex’ on coins shows that Verica ruled with the full authorization of the emperor.”

For Russell, the images offer another important clue: “Whilst other coin-producing British Iron Age leaders portray obviously male warriors, Verica is depicted as a slender, feminine, bare-breasted figure riding on horseback.”

Verica’s identity also changes how Russell interprets the Roman account of the invasion. Historian Cassius Dio claimed that Claudius crossed the Channel because Verica persuaded him to do so. That story fits a broader pattern in Roman writing, which portrayed Claudius as weak-minded and ineffective, with women and freed slaves directing his decisions.

“The story of Claudius committing to something only because a woman told him to fits the trope of this emperor as being submissive and henpecked,” Russell said. “In effect, Dio was saying that the campaign was undertaken solely because of the whisperings of a barbarian femme fatale. Verica’s role was rather more central to the British expedition. Having her onboard ensured the project was a success as she provided tactical information and support on the ground.”

In this interpretation, Verica offered both a political justification for invasion and practical help in carrying it out. As Russell put it, “The invasion was Claudius’ great triumph, it being the only chance he had to prove he was a successful military leader. Verica provided the excuse for regime change, and the emperor seized it.”

Russell argues that Verica deserves recognition among Britain’s earliest influential female leaders. “We should take the archaeological evidence at face value,” he said, “and remember Verica as a female king and one of the earliest and most important of British female leaders. Had she not been deposed and fled to Claudius for military support, Rome may never have invaded Britain in the first place.”

The work follows earlier BU research into women’s place in Iron Age society. Published last year, that research involved Russell and university colleagues and found evidence of communities centered on women, where husbands moved to live with their wives’ communities.

The argument about Verica is presented in Caratacus: Great King of Britain, published by Bloomsbury in January (ISBN 9781350477902), and discussed in the latest edition of Current Archaeology.

#6396. Earth’s Ancient Oceans May Have Fooled Scientists About the Rise of Oxygen

Some of Earth’s best-known oxygen milestones may belong to the oceans, not the atmosphere, reshaping our understanding of the conditions that allowed complex life to evolve.

For billions of years, Earth had almost no oxygen in its atmosphere, making it a vastly different world from the one that supports complex life today. New research suggests oxygen accumulated in three major stages, with the deep ocean taking hundreds of millions of years to catch up.

Two geochemists at Chengdu University of Technology argue in The Innovation that scientists may have misjudged the timing of Earth’s oxygenation by using ancient ocean chemistry to estimate atmospheric conditions. Ocean chemistry is also influenced by nutrients, biological activity, circulation, and basin shape, making it an imperfect record of the air.

Instead, the researchers examined an oxygen isotope signature preserved in sedimentary sulfate. Reactions involving oxygen, ozone, and carbon dioxide produce a distinctive shortage of oxygen-17 in the atmosphere. This signature enters sulfate when sulfide minerals weather, providing a record of atmospheric oxygen.

The first major increase, the Great Oxidation Event, occurred between 2.4 billion and 2.1 billion years ago, raising oxygen from less than one-millionth of today’s level to between 0.1% and 10%.

The next increases occurred between 1.3 billion and 1.0 billion years ago and between 440 million and 410 million years ago, earlier than traditionally thought. The better-known Neoproterozoic and Paleozoic oxygenation events, dated to 800 million to 500 million and 420 million to 360 million years ago, may instead reflect ocean responses that lagged behind atmospheric changes by roughly 200 million and 30 million years.

Oxygen nevertheless remained scarce. Models based on the isotope evidence place mid-Proterozoic atmospheric oxygen at just 0.1% to 1% of modern levels. Charcoal, which requires roughly three-quarters of today’s oxygen concentration to form during burning, first appears around 420 million years ago.

Atmospheric and ocean oxygen generally increased together over billion-year timescales, although they could move in opposite directions over millions of years. When oxygen entered seawater containing accumulated organic carbon and sulfide, chemical reactions consumed the gas and could lower atmospheric levels. Some geological signals previously interpreted as oxygen increases may therefore indicate declines.

Oxygen also spread unevenly through the oceans. Photosynthetic microbes created localized oxygen-rich environments as early as 3 billion years ago, or earlier. These dominated during the Archean, before oxygen supplied from the atmosphere became increasingly important. The ocean interior did not become fully oxygenated until approximately 410 million years ago.

For life, the transition was gradual. An oxygen-free atmosphere severely limited organisms dependent on the gas, while fluctuating levels during the Proterozoic opened new habitats as animals evolved. After the third atmospheric increase, greater oxygen availability helped support larger bodies, active predation, and expansion into deeper waters.

The researchers caution that the isotope record has limited time resolution, oxygen concentrations after 1 billion years ago remain poorly constrained, and additional increases may have gone undetected. Their findings suggest that Earth’s transformation into an oxygen-rich world was shaped not only by rising atmospheric levels, but also by the long delay before oxygen reached the ocean depths.

Reference: “Stagewise oxygenation of the Earth’s atmosphere and oceans” by Haiyang Wang and Chao Li, 17 March 2026, The Innovation. DOI: 10.1016/j.xinn.2026.101353

Financial support was supported by the National Key Research and Development Program of China (grant no. 2022YFF0800100 to C.L.) and the National Natural Science Foundation of China (grant nos. 42425002 to C L. and 42572129 and 42103072 to H.W.).

#6395. Maple-Glazed Carrots

These maple-glazed carrots don’t hold back on the butter—or the brown sugar. Roasted with pure maple syrup and crushed red pepper flakes, they turn tender and glossy with a sweet-hot kick that complements everything from ham to lamb to green bean casserole.

The recipe began with Barbie—not the doll, but Andy Baraghani’s cousin’s former girlfriend. Her syrupy-sweet carrots became a fixture at family Christmas dinners. Some dishes are meant to last; some relationships aren’t.

For BA’s version, Andy traded the original’s hours-long cooking time for a hotter roast that gives the carrots browned edges and a buttery glaze. There’s no separate sauce to simmer: Everything goes straight onto a foil-lined (for easier cleanup) rimmed baking sheet, with regular tossing to coat the carrots in syrup as they cook. Finish with flaky salt for crunch and a welcome contrast to the sweetness.

No. This recipe calls for scrubbed, unpeeled carrots—give them a thorough cleaning and leave the skins on.

Keep the carrot pieces similar in thickness, halving or quartering larger ones lengthwise. Check the glaze each time you toss the carrots, especially once the edges begin browning: The sugars can darken quickly. Use tenderness and browned edges as your guide rather than waiting out the clock if the carrots are already done.

For a more savory version, try our Easy Roasted Carrots.

Place rack in middle of oven and preheat oven to 400°. Line a rimmed baking sheet with 3 sheets of foil (you’ll need it!). Cut 2 lb. medium carrots, tops trimmed to about ½", scrubbed, on a diagonal into 3" pieces (halved or quartered lengthwise if large).

Spread out carrots on foil. Evenly top with 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, ⅓ cup (packed; 70 g) light brown sugar, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, and ¾ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes. Season with kosher salt and toss to combine.

Roast carrots, tossing every 20 minutes, until tender and browned around the edges, 50–60 minutes. Watch closely as the carrots begin to brown; the glaze can darken quickly. Transfer to a platter and drizzle with any remaining syrup. Sprinkle with flaky sea salt (if using).

#6394. Arctic Bacteria May Be Using Sunlight and CO2 in a Way Scientists Never Expected

An Arctic bacterium’s genes hint at an unexpected way of using carbon dioxide, raising the possibility that similar survival strategies exist in oceans far beyond the polar regions.

In the Arctic Ocean, where nutrients and usable organic matter can be scarce, a tiny bacterium may have found a remarkable way to survive. Think of it as having a built-in solar charger and an unusual food supply. By capturing energy from sunlight and using a chemical called acetone, it may be able to turn carbon dioxide into some of the building blocks it needs to grow.

The bacterium, known as Porticoccus arcticus, lives in the frigid waters of the Beaufort Sea, north of the Yukon in the Arctic Ocean’s Canada Basin. At some locations, it accounted for up to 9 percent of detected bacteria, suggesting it is an important member of the region’s microbial community. In a study published in Nature Communications, researchers at Concordia University uncovered genetic evidence of an unusual metabolism that could help explain how these organisms survive in such a challenging environment.

One of the keys appears to be acetone, a chemical produced naturally by marine organisms, including microscopic algae, and through reactions between sunlight and dissolved organic matter. Scientists already knew that some marine bacteria could consume acetone, but P. arcticus appears to have a different way of putting it to use.

Its genes point to a process called acetone carboxylation, which combines acetone with carbon dioxide to produce compounds that can enter the cell’s central metabolic pathways. These chemical pathways allow cells to process carbon and make the materials they need to function and grow.

The researchers found the complete set of genes required for acetone carboxylation within the bacterium’s relatively small genome. They also identified multiple genes for proteorhodopsins, light-sensitive proteins that help cells capture energy from sunlight. Genes involved in both acetone processing and light capture were among the organism’s most active, suggesting that it may be able to use sunlight for energy while supplementing its carbon supply through acetone metabolism and carbon dioxide assimilation.

What makes this combination especially intriguing is that the researchers had not set out to look for bacteria with these abilities.

“The genomic composition of these organisms led us to reconstruct the different types of energy and carbon metabolisms that exist,” said David Walsh, a professor in Concordia’s Department of Biology and the study’s corresponding author. “That is how we found this very specific set of genes associated with the use of acetone, which was unexpected. We discovered that the organism’s genes were telling us about something we did not suspect was happening in an ecosystem. This was a surprise, as we were not actively looking for acetone-degrading bacteria that can use light.”

Walsh explained that the findings point to two distinct metabolic abilities, including a way of obtaining energy that researchers call photoheterotrophy.

“This study introduces two new discoveries,” he said. “The first is a group of organisms, P. arcticus, that has a unique metabolism that uses organic carbon while at the same time has the capacity to use light as an energy source. We call this process photoheterotrophy.

“The second discovery is the way the organism consumes acetone to also consume carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere. This acetone-mediated inorganic carbon assimilation combines what animals do — eating food, in this case, acetone — with what plants do: fixing CO2.”

The genetic evidence suggests that P. arcticus has developed a way to take advantage of several resources available near the ocean surface. However, the findings describe its potential metabolic capabilities rather than directly measuring how much carbon dioxide the bacteria take up.

Whether these abilities will help the bacterium cope with a warming Arctic Ocean remains uncertain. Walsh does not yet know how changing conditions will affect P. arcticus, although shifts in sea ice could alter the availability of sunlight and acetone, potentially changing where the organism can thrive.

The researchers also plan to investigate whether bacteria in other oceans and freshwater environments possess similar capabilities. Such investigations could help determine whether this unusual combination of sunlight capture and carbon assimilation is a specialized Arctic adaptation or a more widespread microbial survival strategy.

Reference: “Evidence of an acetone carboxylation pathway in photoheterotrophic bacteria from the Arctic Ocean” by Susan McLatchie, Sara Palestini, Asher Woodhead, Tony Gutierrez and David A. Walsh, 26 September 2026, Nature Communications. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78082-y

#6393. Behind the Scenes of the Inaugural Bon Appétit LIVE

This past weekend the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen in New York City opened its doors to the public for Bon Appétit Live, an immersive day of cooking demos and classes, talks with chefs and recipe experts, Test Kitchen tours, games, prizes, and plenty to eat and drink.

The day kicked off with a warm welcome from Bon Appétit’s editor-in-chief Jamila Robinson, who exclaimed that “the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen is the heart of our brand.” Robinson also shared that Bon Appétit just launched a new cooking app containing tens of thousands of recipes from the Test Kitchen archives.

Guests fueled up with an impressive array of curated breakfast treats alongside refreshing beverages from S.Pellegrino, before moving on to interactive experiences.

In the first class of the day, baking novices and aficionados alike joined senior Test Kitchen editor and BA Bake Club expert Jesse Szewczyk in the Test Kitchen for Pie Crust Fundamentals, presented by East Fork. The hands-on class featured guest Keia Mastrianni, brand storyteller and “unofficial pie lady” of East Fork. Mastrianni proclaimed her enthusiasm for pie making: “I love preaching the gospel of pie. My favorite thing is teaching people to make pie dough with their hands.” Szewczyk agreed, emphasizing the tactile nature of the process: “It’s a very physical thing to do…a recipe can be written, but teaching someone to make pie dough requires demonstration.” Participants were in luck as Szewczyk and Mastrianni demonstrated a buttery pie crust fortified with cream cheese, a recipe ideal for Thanksgiving developed by former senior Test Kitchen editor Shilpa Uskokovic. After Mastrianni shared crimping tips, participants made their own pie dough at stations throughout the kitchen, with Test Kitchen editors on hand to offer guidance. One participant, James, was particularly excited to be working with director of cooking Emma Laperruque. He enthused, “Before Emma’s and Chris [Morocco’s] recipes, I would burn water. [Bon Appétit] has made cooking really accessible, and I built a lot of confidence. I love the simplicity of Emma’s recipes…they are all so flavorful and so good.”

Each guest left ready for holiday baking season with new pie-making skills, and a ceramic pie dish from East Fork’s new bakeware collection, featuring clay and glaze made in-house with materials sourced in the Southeast. Before moving on to their next experience, Mastrianni encouraged everyone to keep honing their skills, emphasizing, “Practice makes pie. Progress, not perfection.”

Meanwhile, in the neighboring Demo Kitchen, a Pasta Boot Camp was underway with Bon Appétit senior cooking editor Kelsey Jane Youngman and chef Stefano Secchi. Secchi, chef and partner of New York City’s Rezdôra (recipient of one Michelin star) and Massara, honed his craft in Modena, Italy, under legendary chef Massimo Bottura.

After walking guests through the fundamentals of making and shaping fresh pasta by hand, Secchi demonstrated a filled ravioli dish aptly named Holiday in Parma. Made with 00 flour and egg dough, the ravioli was piped with a chestnut and Parmesan filling and served with a rich reduction of chicken broth, butter, and saba (a traditional Italian syrup made from slowly simmered grape must).

While guests savored their pasta in the Demo Kitchen, a lively panel discussion was underway on the 34th floor. Moderated by editor-in-chief Jamila Robinson, the Bringing Culture to Cooking panel featured chefs Fariyal Abdullahi (executive chef, Hav & Mar, NYC), Nicholas Bazik (chef and owner, Provenance, Philadelphia, a Bon Appétit Best New Restaurant of 2025), and Vijay Kumar (executive chef and partner, Semma, NYC, a Best New Restaurant of 2022). The conversation explored how culture, identity, and personal experience inform each chef’s cooking. The chefs shared some of their favorite home-cooking ingredients, such as Chef Bazik’s fermented lime juice, a versatile seasoning made by combining fresh lime juice with salt at a 2% ratio by weight. Chef Abdullahi championed berbere, the Ethiopian spice blend she likened to “Ethiopian salt” for its ubiquity in the country’s cooking. Abdullahi cautioned that store-bought blends are convenient but not necessarily of the highest-possible quality. “You should make it at home!” she encouraged.

Back in the Test Kitchen, Visit Maine hosted Lobster 101, a hands-on lobster class and oyster tasting with Bon Appétit’s manager of audience strategy Carly Westerfield and Krista Tripp, founder of Aphrodite Oysters in South Thomaston, Maine. Each participant received a whole, steamed Maine lobster and the ingredients and tools needed to transform it into a creamy, decadent lobster dip. Under Westerfield’s guidance, the class learned how to break down their lobsters, extract the meat, and assemble a dip made with cream cheese, mayonnaise, celery, chives, and lemon juice. The approachable demonstration demystified the process and showed guests how easily they could prepare a luxurious appetizer at home, just in time for the holidays.

Participants worked with hard-shell lobsters, but Tripp encouraged them to visit Maine and sample both hard-shell and soft-shell varieties. She explained that soft-shell lobsters, typically in season from July through August, have a sweeter, more tender meat. The two are actually the same animal at different stages of its molting cycle: a soft-shell lobster has recently shed its old shell, leaving a newer, more pliable one that is easier to crack. The class concluded with a tasting of Aphrodite Oysters, grown in the waters off South Thomaston, Maine. The medium-size oysters were briny and subtly sweet, reflecting the cold, brackish waters of the Lower Weskeag River where they were grown. A small squeeze of lemon was all that was needed to enhance their flavor as guests tilted their heads back, slurped, and allowed themselves to be transported to the rugged coast of Maine.

Meanwhile, in the Demo Kitchen, Bon Appétit director of culture Joseph Hernandez was joined by Matt Conroy, chef at Washington, DC’s Maison Bar à Vins, for a live cooking demonstration of one of Chef Conroy’s favorite dishes. Named one of Bon Appétit’s Best New Restaurants of 2026, the restaurant pairs French-inspired cooking with an eclectic wine list and seasonal cocktails. Chef Conroy prepared a new fall salad made of chicory, pear, and smoked blue cheese, finished with a Banyuls vinaigrette.

In the cafeteria, guests gathered for a live version of the Dear Bon Appétit advice column. Bon Appétit director of cooking Emma Laperruque presented questions about home cooking and holiday entertaining to chef Amanda Freitag. One attendee asked Freitag how to handle undercooked turkey legs and thighs each year. Freitag recommended removing the legs and cooking them separately, as in this BA recipe for Gravy-Braised Turkey from Jesse Szewczyk.

Next, food stylist Thu Buser showcased her exceptional culinary artistry by decorating an elaborate “snake cake” with vibrant green swirls and flowers. Then, a break for lunch with BA’s Best Mozzarella Sticks, a variety of salads and skewers, hot honey salmon, smoothies, and a cranberry maple mule.

While attendees grazed and mingled, Jamila Robinson joined legendary chef and restaurateur Marcus Samuelsson to discuss Back to Green: Rediscovering a World of Delicious, Healthy Eating, his new global plant-forward cookbook coauthored by Robinson. Samuelsson captured the atmosphere of the event, remarking, “What a party we are having here…the energy is amazing!”

The final demonstration of the day featured Cornmeal Shortcakes with Blueberry Compote presented by Visit Maine with Jesse Szewczyk and Ron Howard of Brodis Blueberries. Featuring a recipe from Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firsker, the shortcakes showcased farm-fresh wild blueberries grown on a ninth-generation family farm. As Szewczyk prepared the recipe, Howard discussed the importance of wild blueberries to Maine’s agricultural heritage. A native crop, they can be traced back to the end of the last Ice Age, predating lobster as a symbol of the state. “Everyone should think of wild blueberries as the ultimate Maine crop,” Howard explained. After tasting the shortcakes, attendees would be hard-pressed to disagree. Szewczyk noted that compared with conventional blueberries, the wild blueberries produced a more saturated color and tasted more distinctly of blueberry.

The day ended on a sweet note with pastry chef Eunji Lee, winner of North America’s Best Pastry Chef Award from The 50. Attendees had a chance to meet Lee and sample pastries from Lysée, her pastry boutique influenced by Korean and French culture and inspired by New York City.

Bon Appétit Live brought together chefs, culinary personalities, and food editors for a day of conversations, cooking, tasting, and learning. Attendees experienced the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen firsthand, learned directly from chefs and editors, and engaged with the people and products behind the food. As editor-in-chief Jamila Robinson said, “Food is always an invitation…we are so happy to give everyone access to the same experiences we have.”

Bon Appétit LIVE 2026 was sponsored by East Fork, Visit Maine, and S.Pellegrino® Sparkling Natural Mineral Water with thanks to All-Clad, As Ever, Bachan’s, Better Sour, Field Company, Floura, Gimme Seaweed, GOODLES, Graza, Hedley & Bennett, Kann Coffee, Material Kitchen, Misen, Owala®, Rip Van, SharkNinja, and Staub.

#6392. Not All Physical Activity Protects Your Brain, Scientists Warn

Across 30 countries, researchers found that exercising during free time was linked to lower dementia risk, while physically demanding work was linked to higher risk.

After spending an entire day on your feet, going for a walk or bike ride might seem unnecessary. Yet new research suggests that being physically active at work may not provide the same protection against dementia as exercising in your free time.

A major analysis involving more than 4.2 million people found that those who were most physically active during their leisure time had a 24% lower risk of dementia compared with those who were least active. In contrast, physical activity performed on the job was associated with a 20% higher risk.

The findings, published in The Lancet Public Health, raise an important question about the familiar advice to move more. If physical activity is good for the brain, why might its benefits depend on where and how it takes place?

Researchers at the University of Southern California (USC) examined this question by combining evidence from 74 cohort and case-control studies conducted across 30 countries. The participants ranged in age from 45 to 93 and were followed for a median of 10 years. During that time, researchers tracked diagnoses of dementia from all causes, including Alzheimer’s disease and vascular dementia.

The analysis was led by David Raichlen, a professor of biological sciences and anthropology at the USC Dornsife College of Letters, Arts and Sciences. It is the first systematic investigation of whether the “physical activity paradox,” previously documented in cardiovascular research, also applies to dementia. The paradox describes how physically demanding occupations may fail to provide the same health benefits as recreational exercise and may even be associated with greater disease risk.

“The findings challenge the long-held assumption that ‘every move counts’ for brain health,” said Natan Feter, the study’s first author, a postdoctoral fellow in Raichlen’s Evolutionary Biology of Physical Activity Lab at USC and a researcher in the Graduate Program of Epidemiology at Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul in Brazil.

One possible explanation lies in what happens around the physical activity itself. Walking, cycling, running, swimming, and playing sports during leisure time are generally activities people can choose and adjust to their comfort level. They may also provide opportunities to socialize, relax, and reduce stress.

A physically demanding job often presents very different circumstances. Workers may spend hours standing, repeatedly lifting heavy objects, or completing strenuous tasks with little opportunity for recovery. Unlike a recreational workout, these activities may occur alongside workplace hazards and pressures that extend well beyond the physical effort involved.

Manual occupations, for example, can expose workers to greater psychosocial stress, less control over their working conditions, and higher levels of air and noise pollution. These factors have independently been linked to dementia risk. Workers may also struggle to find time or energy for recreational exercise, particularly when access to safe places for physical activity is limited.

For these reasons, the researchers believe the higher dementia risk associated with occupational activity is unlikely to result from movement itself. Instead, the working conditions and broader social environments surrounding physically demanding jobs may help explain the difference.

The relationship also changed depending on how much activity people performed. Higher levels of leisure-time exercise were associated with progressively lower dementia risk, although the association eventually leveled off. Occupational activity followed the opposite pattern, with dementia risk increasing alongside greater activity before reaching a similar plateau.

Not every form of daily movement could be evaluated with the same confidence. Household physical activity appeared to be beneficial, although that finding came from just one study. Active commuting was associated with a modestly higher dementia risk, but only two studies examined this relationship. The researchers emphasized that more evidence is needed before firm conclusions can be drawn about either activity.

There are also important limits to what the larger analysis can establish.

Because the studies were observational, the findings cannot prove that physically demanding work causes dementia or that leisure-time exercise directly prevents it. Nearly all the studies relied on participants reporting their own physical activity, which can introduce errors in memory and reporting. Most of the evidence also came from high-income countries, despite expectations that low- and middle-income countries will experience the largest increases in dementia cases over the coming decades.

Even with these limitations, the contrasting associations remained after researchers accounted for factors including age, education, and chronic diseases. Multiple sensitivity analyses, which test whether findings hold under different analytical assumptions, produced consistent results. Feter said this consistency strengthens the case for taking the relationship seriously.

The importance of context may extend beyond physical activity. In a related study published in Alzheimer’s & Dementia the previous month, Raichlen, Feter, and their colleagues examined how different sedentary behaviors relate to brain structure.

They found that mentally engaging activities performed while sitting, such as working at a desk, were associated with greater volume in regions of the brain’s cortex compared with more passive activities, such as watching television. These regions included areas involved in executive function, which supports abilities such as planning and decision-making. Like the findings on physical activity, these associations do not establish cause and effect.

The researchers stress that their findings should not discourage people from working physically demanding jobs. Instead, they suggest that dementia prevention strategies need to account for the conditions under which people are active, including the opportunities they have to exercise for enjoyment outside work.

“In other words, when it comes to protecting the brain, the context of physical activity may matter just as much as movement itself,” Raichlen said. “Improving access to safe parks, walking trails and recreational facilities, ensuring people have adequate leisure time for exercise, and reducing harmful workplace exposures may ultimately prove as important as promoting physical activity itself.”

Reference: “Domain-specific physical activity levels and risk of dementia: a systematic review and meta-analysis” by Natan Feter, Paula Iso-Markku, Tiladia Markarian, Dylan M Luong, Jack Gunnink, Natália Schröder, Eduardo Lucia Caputo, Jayne Feter, Anamika Nanda, Sarah Hourihan, Gustavo S da Silva, Ashley Ventura, Daniela Benzano Bumaguin, Yann C Klimentidis, Gene E Alexander, Daniel Umpierre, Pedro C Hallal, Airton José Rombaldi and David A Raichlen, September 2026, The Lancet Public Health. DOI: 10.1016/S2468-2667(26)00142-8

#6391. Tears of the Lion: Catching the 2026 Leonid Meteors

Why you should watch for the November Leonid meteors this year.

Itâs always worth being vigilant when skywatching in mid- to late November. Every year, a few Leonid meteors punctuate the November morning sky around the 17th. These silent harbingers are only a hint at the showerâs true storm potential, which culminates once every three decades.

The Leonid meteor shower can put on a true spectacle, and while 2026 isnât expected to be a âstorm year,â we could be due for some enhanced activity in the late 2020s going into the early 2030s.

The source of the Leonid meteor shower is periodic comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle. On a 33 year orbit, comet 55P reaches perihelion 0.975 Astronomical Units (AU) from the Sun just inside Earthâs orbit once again on May 20, 2031.

Hubble captures Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle. Credit: NASA/HST/STScI

In 2026 the Moon phase is favorable at 41% illuminated, reaching 1st quarter phase a day after the showerâs peak night on November 16-17th. This means the Moon sets in the west, right as the radiant rises to the east.

The peak of the 2026 Leonids is set for November 17th at 3:00 Universal Time (UT), favoring Europe towards dawn, and North America just a few hours later. While 2026 is projected to be a 20 meteors per hour peak year, you just never know what a particular shower might have in store.

The Leonids are also real fast movers, approaching the Earth nearly head-on with a combined velocity of close to 70 kilometers per second. This is very near the theoretical maximum for inner solar system meteors. Most years only see a paltry 20 or so meteors per hour, though when the parent comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle is near perihelion, great storms are possible.

The Leonids hail from the backwards, question mark-shaped âSickle of Leoâ asterism. The radiant tracks from the +3rd magnitude star Epsilon Leonis past the bright double star Algieba in November. If you can trace a meteorâs flight back to this region, itâs a Leonid.

As an added treat in 2026, the planets Mars and Jupiter are very nearby, along with the bright star Regulus and the antihelion point towards which our planet is currently headed.

The rising Leonid radiant in 2026. Credit: Stellarium.

The Leonids top out with great outbursts every 33 years. A loose definition for a âmeteor stormâ is when the zenithal hourly rate (ZHR) tops out at about a 1,000 per hour, which is a fast-paced rate of one meteor every 3-4 seconds. Keep in mind, the ZHR is an extrapolated, ideal rate, assuming dark skies with the showerâs radiant directly overhead at the zenith. Most observers will always see less in reality, as fainter meteors slip by.

Records of the Leonids go all the way back to Arab annuals dating from 902 AD. 1833 saw an historic storm from the shower, as frightened residents along the U.S. Eastern Seaboard awoke to a sky awash in meteors. This single event was not only responsible in part for several religious movements of the day in the U.S., but also helped to push the modern scientific understanding of meteors from a purely atmospheric phenomenon to one originating from space.

A depiction of the Great Leonid Storm of 1833, depicted in 1889 by Adolf Vollmy. Credit: Public Domain.

The morning of November 17, 1966 saw a formidable performance from the shower, with observed rates over the southwestern U.S. topping out at an estimated 160,000 per hour (!)

I still remember catching the 1998 Leonids from the deserts of Kuwait, a year before the advertised outburst in 1999. The meteors lit up the desert floor just seconds apart towards sunrise with brilliant photo-flash flares. The spectacle continued right up until dawn. To date, it was still one of the best meteor showers Iâve ever witnessed.

Are we in for another great âmeteor stormâ in or around 2033? Well, we passed the mid-point in 2017. We did see a steady uptick in meteor activity through the late 1990s leading up to 1999. A caveat, however is in order with the approach of the Leonids in the early 2030s. Current models suggest we wonât see any great storms on the 2031 and 2064 passes of the comet, with 2099 being the next great âstorm yearâ. We may, however, still see respectable showers in excess of 100 per hour in the early 2030s laid down by older streams, topping the annual Perseid and Geminid meteors.

A Leonid double-shot. Credit: Eliot Herman

Observing a meteor shower is as simple as laying back and watching the sky, no special equipment needed. All you need is clear, dark skies and patience. Youâll see more in the early morning hours, as Earth hurdles headlong into the oncoming meteor stream. Imaging Leonids is a simple as setting up a tripod-mounted DSLR camera equipped with a wide-field lens to take long exposure shots of the sky, and seeing what turns up. An intervalometer hand control works great to automate this process.

An all-sky capture featuring a Leonid meteor. Credit: Eliot Herman.

Finally, be sure to count and record what you see, and send those observations to the International Meteor Organization.

Weâll see what the coming years has in store for the November Leonid meteors. One thing is for certain: youâll see zero meteors if you donât try. Time will tell if the coming years see the Leonids roar once again.

David Dickinson is a freelance science writer and long-time sky watcher. He has built telescopes and observatories, chased eclipses, and travels and observes with his wife, Myscha, on a mission to get âeyes on the skyâ worldwide. NASA's Swift Observatory went out in a blaze of glory this week, but it left behind millions of images of the universe that could fuel discoveries for decades.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Early Wednesday (Nov. 4), NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory fell out of space, burning up in the sky over Sumatra. It was a fitting, fiery end for a telescope that spent 22 years studying the most powerful explosions in the universe — and, even with Swift gone, its observations will continue to feed scientific curiosity for years to come.

Swift's most important contributions to astronomy are not exactly eye candy. Designed to swivel toward deep-space explosions at a moment's notice, Swift excelled at capturing bright, fleeting and faraway specks of light. The multiwavelength observatory was equipped with optical, ultraviolet (UV) and X-ray instruments, allowing it to catch cosmic bursts of energy across the electromagnetic spectrum, zeroing in on flares of light that other telescopes might miss.

One of its most significant detections was a gamma-ray burst — an incredibly bright blast, likely emitted by a giant star as it exploded in a supernova before collapsing into a black hole. Swift's famous image of GRB 221009A, or the BOAT ‪—‬ short for "brightest of all time" ‪—‬ looks like a speckled orange bull's-eye, caused by waves from the explosion rippling across space.

How the Swift Observatory saw the gamma-ray burst GRB 221009A, which may be the most energetic emission of this kind ever seen.

But Swift also took millions of observations of the nearby universe, including galaxies in our backyard. One of its most jaw-dropping images is this 24-hour exposure of the Andromeda galaxy (M31), located about 2.5 million light-years from Earth.

Andromeda is the closest major galaxy to ours, and it may be destined for a shared fate. Scientists suspect that Andromeda and the Milky Way are drawing closer together and might eventually collide. The merger would add Andromeda's roughly 1 trillion stars to our sky, though there probably wouldn't be any life left on Earth to appreciate it.

In Swift's view of our encroaching neighbor, captured with the observatory's ultraviolet instrument, tens of thousands of Andromeda's stars shine like sapphires set in a sparkling ring.

According to NASA, the observatory detected some 20,000 ultraviolet light sources in this image, captured over two months from May to July 2008. These sources include thousands of dense, hot star clusters scattered across Andromeda's 150,000-light-year-wide ring, as well as the distant galaxy M32 (seen as a bright orb of light to the bottom right of Andromeda's center).

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

In visible-light images of Andromeda taken with ground-based telescopes, the galaxy's bright center bleaches out many of the fiery young stars that emerge in Swift's view. While Swift likely won't be remembered best for shimmering starscapes like this one, it's a powerful reminder that looking at familiar structures in a new light can change everything.

#6389. Shape-Shifting Robotic "Slugs" Could One Day Crawl Across Alien Worlds

Robots have been a mainstay of our early space exploration efforts. But they normally have wheels. Or in some cases, rotors. While those solutions are great on flat ground, they struggle with jagged boulders or tight crevices. So engineers have been working on alternative robotic form factors, and a recent paper in Nature Machine Intelligence from researchers at Colorado State Universityâs Adaptive Robotics Lab, describes a unique morphology using a design principle typically seen in architecture rather than robotics - tensegrity.

Tensegrity was originally made popular by Buckminster Fuller in the mid-20th century. Itâs a blend of the words âtensionâ and âintegrityâ, and at its core it uses rigid rods that push outwards against elastic cables that pull inwards. So, instead of relying on heavy metal hinges, the rods âfloatâ on a web of tension.

This isnât the first time the idea has been brought to space exploration, though. NASA has been exploring its use cases for over a decade, perhaps most notably with the SUPERball - a spherical cage designed to withstand high-speed planetary landings without parachutes by absorbing the shocks of impact across its network of cables.

Fraser talks about some other robots that could end up exploring other worlds.

But this is one of the first times the idea has been applied to robotics. The CSU researchers have developed what they call the Tensegrity-based Continuum Robot (TeCoBot). Measuring in at around 587 mm (~2 ft) long and weighing around 600 grams, the cylindrical bot combined a squishy, flexible spine with adaptable dual mechanical claws, which provide the real interesting use cases of the technology.

TeCoBotâs body is made out of four stacked icosahedral tensegrity modules that create a continuous, flexible backbone. Each module is built around six lightweight rods suspended inside a 3D printed stretchy lattice. Three cables made up of 40-lb braided fishing wire run through the center of the robot, and by pulling on each of them with small motors attached to its base, the robot can bend in any direction - like an âelephantâs trunkâ as a press release puts it. It can also scrunch down to around half its original size if all three lines are pulled at the same time.

But whatâs most interesting about the technology is its modularity, which relies on the claws on either end. These claws are swappable, so if a robot needs to handle delicate cargo engineers can put a soft-padded claw on it. But, if needed, those soft pads can be swapped out for a heavier duty gripper claw that uses a worm gear to clamp and hold onto another gripper without draining any battery.

Fraser talks about the concept of "grey goo" - or self-replicating robots able to automate space exploration.

This unlocks all sorts of additional opportunities. As a stand-alone single robot, TeCoBot is already relatively capable - it can inch along like a caterpillar, roll sideways, and even climb vertically. It also exhibits what roboticists call âembodied intelligenceâ that means its body can naturally give way when bumped or when it runs into something without needing a whole control system to adjust to the changed environment.

But when they combine together, they unlock whole new operating modes. Using their claws to grab one another, three TeCoBots can self-configure into a wide variety of shapes. The paper discusses three robots wrapping themselves around a large pipe, and forming a H-shaped walker to crawl through tight spaces. But perhaps most interestingly for anyone who hates cleaning as much as this author, they are also capable of teaming up to clean off a table.

Those feats might not seem immediately applicable to space exploration, but the underlying modularity and adaptability would be extremely useful in the rough craters of the Moon or underground caverns on Mars. Weâve already reported on a snake robot designed to explore those exact locations, and this seems like a step up in functionality from that.

Video of the TeCoBot in action. Credit - Adaptive Robotics Lab YouTube Channel

That being said, it still has a long way to go before weâd see it on another heavenly body. Currently, engineers have to manually control the bots via a WiFi connection - which isnât exactly easy on deep space missions. But they do plan to make improvements on the design, upgrading the motors for faster movement and adding swarm intelligence to allow dozens of these modular robots to band together. If that development goes as planned, these elephant trunk styled robots might serve as some of our most intrepid deep space explorers.

#6388. FDA Approves Breakthrough Treatment That Helps Children With Type 1 Diabetes Keep Producing Insulin

For children with type 1 diabetes, managing blood sugar is a lifelong challenge, but a newly approved treatment offers hope of preserving their body’s ability to produce insulin.

For children newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes, insulin is essential for controlling blood sugar, but it cannot stop the immune system from destroying the cells that produce it. A newly approved treatment offers a way to slow that damage and preserve more of the body’s own insulin production. However, families have only a short window after diagnosis to consider the option.

In June 2026, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) expanded its approval of teplizumab to include children and adolescents ages 8 to 17 with newly diagnosed stage 3 type 1 diabetes. This is the stage when symptoms appear and insulin treatment becomes necessary. The expansion was granted through the FDA’s accelerated approval pathway, based on evidence that the drug helps preserve insulin production. Teplizumab was already approved for people ages 1 and older with stage 2 type 1 diabetes to delay progression to stage 3.

Type 1 diabetes develops when the immune system attacks beta cells in the pancreas, which produce insulin to help the body use energy from food and regulate blood sugar. Some of these cells usually remain when symptoms first appear. Teplizumab targets the immune cells responsible for the damage, potentially extending the “honeymoon” period when patients still produce some insulin themselves.

“Insulin is essential in stage 3 type 1 diabetes, but it doesn’t address the immune process that is destroying the cells that make insulin,” said Kimber Simmons, MD, MS, an associate professor of pediatrics at the University of Colorado Anschutz School of Medicine and a physician-scientist at the Barbara Davis Center for Diabetes. “Teplizumab gives us an opportunity to preserve some of the beta cells and insulin-producing capacity that a person still has. The goal is to intervene early enough to make a meaningful difference.”

Evidence supporting the expanded approval came from the PROTECT clinical trial, which involved 328 children and adolescents. After 78 weeks, participants who received teplizumab retained significantly more insulin-producing capacity than those given a placebo. Researchers measured this using C-peptide, a marker of how much insulin the body produces naturally.

Nearly 95% of children treated with teplizumab maintained a clinically meaningful level of their own insulin production, compared with about 79% of those receiving placebo. Separate studies involving people with type 1 diabetes have linked higher C-peptide levels with fewer episodes of severe low blood sugar, reduced insulin requirements, and a lower risk of certain complications, including diabetic eye disease.

The timing of treatment is particularly important. Teplizumab must be started within eight weeks of diagnosis, while participants in PROTECT began treatment within six weeks. Earlier research also suggested that starting treatment sooner may produce stronger responses.

Treatment involves two 12-day courses of daily intravenous infusions, typically six months apart. Potential side effects include rash, headache, nausea, and temporary reductions in lymphocytes, a type of white blood cell. More serious risks include cytokine release syndrome, an inflammatory reaction, infections, and viral reactivation. Experienced medical teams and careful monitoring are therefore necessary.

Teplizumab does not cure type 1 diabetes or eliminate the need for insulin. Instead, it introduces another way to manage the disease by addressing the underlying immune process.

To help clinicians and families navigate these decisions, Simmons led a national group of clinical trial investigators and pediatric diabetes specialists in developing practical guidance published in Diabetes Care. Supported by Breakthrough T1D, the guidance combines clinical trial evidence with experience in everyday patient care. It covers patient selection, potential benefits and risks, shared decision-making, safety monitoring, and treatment planning.

Simmons, who also practices at Children’s Hospital Colorado, co-authored the published results of both PROTECT and PETITE-T1D, a study examining teplizumab in children younger than 8 with stage 2 type 1 diabetes.

“Once a treatment is approved, the question becomes: How do we actually do this in the clinic?” said Simmons. “The way patients are treated in the real world doesn’t always line up perfectly with a clinical trial protocol. We wanted to give clinicians practical guidance so they can have informed conversations with families and make thoughtful, safe decisions.”

The guidance also addresses a longstanding challenge in medicine: translating research advances into routine care.

“Research shows that, on average, it takes 17 years for landmark medical breakthroughs to become widely adopted in routine clinical practice. Closing that gap is essential to getting the best science to people sooner,” said Breakthrough T1D Senior Vice President of Medical Affairs Anastasia Albanese-O’Neill, Ph.D., APRN, CDCES. “Breakthrough T1D is focused on efforts that will close this gap in a way that is safe and supports shared decision-making between clinicians and families. This new clinical guidance serves as an important tool that will help guide timely care for children with a new stage 3 type 1 diabetes diagnosis. We’re grateful to the leaders who provided their expertise and time to develop it.”

The authors emphasize that teplizumab should be incorporated into existing diabetes care rather than delivered through an entirely separate treatment system.

“We don’t want to create a separate pathway that fragments care,” said Simmons. “This is an opportunity to be thoughtful about how we use a new therapy while keeping the whole patient in view. Our specialty needs to stay focused on providing the best coordinated care we can.”

Reference: “Clinical Guidance for Disease-Modifying Immunotherapy in Children and Adolescents With New-Onset (Stage 3) Type 1 Diabetes” by Kimber M. Simmons, Adriana Weinberg, Emily Breidbart, Carla Demeterco-Berggren, Stephen Gitelman, Kevan C. Herold, Shideh Majidi, Daniel Moore, Amara Ogbonnaya-Whittlesey, Neha Patel, Jennifer L. Sherr, Emily K. Sims, Kupper Wintergerst and Michael J. Haller, 11 November 2026, Diabetes Care. DOI: 10.2337/dci26-0061
