In a key coastal area of Peru, violence was low despite the practice of human sacrifice.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Despite engaging in human sacrifice, the people who lived in the Lambayeque Valley of northern Peru had low levels of violence, a new study of their remains finds.

Human sacrifice occurred in the valley over the millennia. It's thought that at least some of these mass sacrifices were attempts to appease the gods in the wake of El Niño, a periodic weather phenomenon that can lead to intense rains and flooding in Peru and droughts in other parts of South and Central America.

"We have one example at the site of Sicán where around [A.D.] 1050/1100, around 200 individuals were killed and ritualistically buried during an intense El Niño event," study co-author Haagen Klaus, an anthropology professor at George Mason University in Virginia, told Live Science in an email.

Other human sacrifice findings include more than 200 children found near the modern-day town of Huanchaco who were sacrificed sometime between 600 and 800 years ago, possibly during an El Niño.

However, despite the occurrence of human sacrifice, levels of violence unrelated to sacrifice were actually quite low in the Lambayeque Valley. In the study, scientists analyzed the skeletal remains of 1,519 people from the Lambayeque Valley who lived between roughly 1500 B.C. and A.D. 1800, and whose remains were preserved enough to detect signs of violent trauma, including interpersonal violence.

A skull showing blunt force trauma that dates to the Chimu period, roughly 1375 to 1490.

Of these skeletons, "only 25 (1.6%) exhibited traumatic lesions consistent with interpersonal conflict, and 77 exhibited post-cranial traumatic lesions consistent with accidental trauma (5.1%)," Klaus and co-author Thomas Snyder, a bioarchaeologist at New York University, wrote in the paper, which was published Nov. 8 in the journal Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology.

The team didn't find any link between a person's sex and violence, they noted. The findings mean that despite the presence of human sacrifice, the amount of violence unrelated to sacrifice was low. This leaves a question: Why?

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

A healed fracture on the left leg of a person who lived sometime between 1000 to 650 B.C. The fracture may have been from an accident.

"Ritual violence may have alleviated non-ritual violence by creating spaces where social tensions could get worked out in a few different ways," Klaus said.

It's important to remember that other areas of Peru also practiced human sacrifice but didn't have the same low levels of interpersonal violence. Klaus noted that areas in the Peruvian highlands sometimes had higher rates of interpersonal violence. In their paper, Klaus and Snyder noted that societies that originated in the highlands, such as the Tiwanaku, Wari and Inca had to grapple with poorer soils and cold temperatures, and these challenges may have been a factor in increasing the levels of interpersonal violence.

The "evidence of sub-lethal and lethal violence forceful enough to break bone is significantly higher in some areas of Peru's highlands," Klaus said. He and Snyder noted in their paper that the inhabitants of the Lambayeque Valley may have had better access to marine and water resources, such as seafood and rivers that could be used for agricultural irrigation, than those who lived in highland areas. Access to these resources may have helped alleviate interpersonal violence in the valley by providing more food resources, they wrote.

Aside from practicing human sacrifice, people in the valley may have engaged in other practices that helped lower levels of interpersonal violence, researchers who were not involved in the new study told Live Science.

Environmental conditions may have helped reduce conflict or there could be "really unusual cultural practices in this region of avoiding or mediating conflict — both between and within groups," Elizabeth Arkush, an anthropology professor at the University of Pittsburgh, said in an email.

Constanza Ceruti, an anthropologist and explorer with the National Geographic Society, said in an email that she's glad that researchers are studying human sacrifices "after decades of being ignored as a taboo topic in academic discussion." She praised the study’s large sample size and noted that human sacrifice is a "phenomenon primarily associated [with] the manipulation and concentration of power by elites."

Jordi Rivera Prince, an anthropology professor at Tulane University, said that the findings dovetail with her excavations in the region, where she has "found little evidence of violent trauma during the Salinar (400-200 BCE), a period of great social change in the Andes."

Weston McCool, an archaeology professor at Cal Poly, said in an email that the newly published paper "is an interesting study that provides additional evidence for a sharp break in patterns of violence between the Andean coast and highlands." He noted that it "supports the hypothesis that coastal populations were buffered from terrestrial environmental downturns in ways that highland populations were not. The nature of that resilience, however, remains an important question for future research."

Snyder, T. J., & Klaus, H. D. (2026). Pax Lambayeque? Trauma, interpersonal violence, and environment over 3,000 years in the Lambayeque Valley Complex, Peru. Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology, 5, 1889466. https://doi.org/10.3389/fearc.2026.1889466

Owen Jarus is a regular contributor to Live Science who writes about archaeology and humans' past. He has also written for The Independent (UK), The Canadian Press (CP) and The Associated Press (AP), among others. Owen has a bachelor of arts degree from the University of Toronto and a journalism degree from Ryerson University.

#6365. Caramelized Cabbage Pasta

This pasta is the easiest way to cram an entire head of cabbage into one comforting dinner. The secret? Cooking it in butter over a long, relaxed period of time until it softens into a decadent, caramelized tangle. Paired with spaghetti, heavy cream, and some Dijon mustard and lemon zest to brighten everything up, this dish is a celebration of how versatile cabbage can be. Feel free to top your bowl with lots of fresh dill, or leave it unadorned with nothing more than an extra sprinkle of cheese.

Cook 12 oz. spaghetti in a large pot of boiling generously salted water, stirring occasionally, until very al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions. Drain, reserving 2 cups pasta cooking liquid. Set aside.

Melt 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pot over high heat. Add 1 large head of green cabbage (about 3 lb.), cored, thinly sliced, and 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and cook, stirring often, until cabbage is very tender and browned in spots, 18–25 minutes.

Add zest of 1 lemon, 2 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about 1 cup), 1½ cups heavy cream, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, and reserved pasta to cabbage and toss to coat. If sauce is too thick, add pasta cooking liquid a splash at a time, tossing constantly, until glossy. Taste pasta and season with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with finely chopped dill if desired.

#6364. Scientists Discover a Disturbing Link Between Cannabis Use and Earlier Psychosis

In studies where psychosis typically emerged at age 30 or later, cannabis users experienced it more than six years earlier, raising questions about cannabis use throughout adulthood.

Most discussions about cannabis and mental health focus on teenagers, but new research suggests the conversation should extend into adulthood. A large analysis found that among people who developed psychosis, cannabis users experienced their first episode an average of two and a half years earlier than non-users. The findings reveal a consistent association, although they do not prove that cannabis caused the difference.

Researchers at UNSW Sydney examined 149 studies involving more than 71,000 people, largely conducted in Europe, North America, and Australia since 2011. The analysis, published in Biological Psychiatry, focused mostly on people with schizophrenia.

Psychosis can involve hallucinations, delusions, disordered thinking, and changes in behavior. It is associated with schizophrenia and other mental illnesses and typically emerges in late adolescence or early adulthood. According to Psychosis Australia, up to 3% of adults experience a diagnosed disorder involving psychosis during their lifetime.

The researchers found that the age difference between cannabis users and non-users grew in studies where psychosis developed later in life. When the average age of onset was between 20 and 24, cannabis users experienced their first episode 1.6 years earlier. That difference increased to 4.43 years in studies with an average onset between ages 25 and 29, reaching 6.3 years when the average onset was 30 or older.

Chief investigator Matthew Large, a psychiatrist and Conjoint Professor at UNSW’s School of Clinical Medicine, said the findings suggest that the effects of cannabis use may accumulate over time.

“We’ve tended to focus on the dangers of using cannabis in adolescence, when the brain is still developing, but the risk doesn’t disappear once you’re in your 20s,” Prof. Large said. “What we’re seeing suggests a cumulative effect, where harm builds up over time, a bit like alcohol or nicotine.”

Interestingly, the researchers found no statistically significant difference in the age of psychosis onset between teenagers who used cannabis and those who did not. However, because psychosis rarely develops before the mid-teens, there is a limited window in which researchers could detect an earlier onset.

“There may be a biological floor, in that there is only so much earlier that onset can be shifted. In younger groups, strong development, genetic or other psychosis risk factors may dominate, making any cannabis-related age shift harder to detect,” Prof. Large said.

The analysis builds on previous research led by Large. A smaller 2011 meta-analysis found that psychosis began 2.7 years earlier among cannabis users, while a 2015 analysis found that psychosis typically developed 6.3 years after cannabis use began. Those earlier studies lacked sufficient data to compare different age groups.

Lead author Carly Stevens, from UNSW’s School of Biomedical Sciences, said the new age comparisons challenge the idea that delaying cannabis use until adulthood necessarily avoids its potential psychiatric risks.

“What we’ve found challenges the assumption that you’ll be fine if you wait to smoke weed until your mid-20s; that’s just not the case,” Ms Stevens said.

“There’s been so much emphasis on adolescents not smoking cannabis, which is important, but we need to broaden the warnings for everyone.”

An important limitation is that the research cannot establish whether cannabis directly causes psychosis or makes it develop earlier. Doing so would require experiments that deliberately expose people to potential harm, which Large said would be unethical. The findings also do not establish how likely an individual cannabis user is to develop psychosis.

“But the consistency of the evidence, particularly the strong effect in older adults who likely have been using cannabis for longer, does support the theory that cannabis plays a causal role in the timing of psychosis onset, and possibly the onset of some cases among people who would not have otherwise developed psychosis.”

For people who do develop psychosis, the timing of their first episode can affect important stages of life. Stevens noted that even a difference of a few years could interfere with opportunities that might otherwise shape someone’s future.

“People may miss out on study, job opportunities, travel and relationships in those years, and treatment can come with physical side effects that can make life harder as well,” she said.

Large believes reducing or stopping cannabis use could offer meaningful benefits if it helps delay psychosis, although the analysis did not directly test that possibility.

“It’s a major illness, which robs you of your shared reality with family, friends and all those around you,” he said. “If we can delay psychosis by even a few years, people will be more likely to reach crucial milestones in education and training, and develop strong support networks, which can protect against psychosocial decline.”

Delaying the onset of psychosis could also ease pressure on healthcare systems. According to Large, psychotic disorders account for up to 3% of health-related expenditure in developed nations.

The researchers believe their findings support clearer public health warnings about the potential psychiatric consequences of cannabis use, even while questions about causation remain unresolved.

“We can’t run direct experiments, so we have to go with the best evidence available,” Prof. Large said. “In my view, the threshold for health warnings about cannabis and psychosis has definitely been met.”

One concern is the expanding use of medical cannabis. Large said he has treated a growing number of people with psychosis who had been prescribed cannabis for conditions where evidence of benefit remains limited. He worries that its medical applications can lead people to underestimate potential risks.

“It’s got this therapeutic halo around it, which blinds people to the risk.”

The increasing popularity of cannabis edibles raises additional questions. Some products can contain higher concentrations of tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the main compound responsible for cannabis’s psychoactive effects.

Large also sees opportunities for harm reduction through cannabis legalization. Although legalization could increase access, government oversight could allow authorities to regulate THC potency, improve consumer education, and introduce requirements aimed at helping buyers understand potential health risks.

“You could tax it, regulate it, and require people to show they understand the risks before buying,” Prof. Large said.

For now, the researchers want to better understand the biological mechanisms that might connect prolonged cannabis exposure with the timing of psychosis. They are calling for more research involving older cannabis users, particularly as medical cannabis and high-potency products become more widely available.

Future studies will also need clearer, standardized measures of cannabis exposure to determine how different patterns and durations of use relate to psychosis onset.

Reference: “Cannabis Use and Age-Related Acceleration of Psychosis Onset: A Meta-Analysis” by Carly Stevens, Hannah Pincham and Matthew Large, 18 August 2026, Biological Psychiatry. DOI: 10.1016/j.biopsych.2026.06.025

#6363. The First Foreign Astronaut Will Visit China's Tiangong Space Station in Two Weeks

On November 25th, 2026, China's Shenzhou 24 mission will launch for the Tiangong space station atop a Long March 2F rocket. It will be the country's 18th crewed spaceflight and will see three taikonauts rendezvous with the Tianhe core module. Similar to previous Chinese crewed missions, the names of the crew are not expected to be announced until the day before the flight - except for one. On this particular flight, a Pakistani astronaut will accompany the pilot and commander, becoming the first foreigner to travel to Tiangong.

The China Manned Space Agency (CMSA) nominated Muhammad Zeeshan Ali and Khurram Daud from Pakistan's space agency, SUPARCO (The Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission). One of these astronauts will accompany the two Chinese taikonauts as a payload specialist, marking the first joint spaceflight involving Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of China's space program. After spending a week aboard the station, the Ali or Daud will return to Earth aboard the Shenzhou-23 spacecraft.

The process officially began in February 2025, when China and Pakistan signed an agreement in which Pakistani astronauts would be trained and selected to participate in missions to Tiangong. The two candidates were chosen after a rigorous selection process consisting of preliminary screenings, secondary evaluations, and final selection, which concluded in April 2026. Once Ali and Daud complete training in China, one will be selected for the mission while the other will serve as the backup astronaut.

This agreement represents an historic expansion of China's ambition in space and a major shift in the strategic partnership between the two nations. Previously, the two cooperated on the development of terrestrial infrastructure, and are now focused on collaborative deep-space exploration. For Pakistan, this represents an opportunity to send its first astronaut to space, edging out India by close to a year. Per India's Gaganyaan program, India's first crewed mission is expected to launch no sooner than Q2 2027.

For China, this is an important step toward the kind of international cooperation typical of NASA and the European Space Agency. It also aligns with their lunar ambitions, which will culminate in the creation of the International Lunar Research Station (ILRS). China's growth as a major space power continues and is now taking on partners!

#6362. The Best Holiday Cocktails, According to Eater Editors

Don’t let cocktails fall by the wayside in the flurry of holiday dinner prep — these drinks make the party

In the endless iterating that goes into devising a menu for a holiday dinner, there’s one finishing touch that really makes or breaks the vibe: the drinks. The wine and beer will, of course, flow — at these festive events, a bottle of Champagne or sparkling rose is likely to make an appearance — and it’s easy enough to throw together a gin and tonic or screwdriver. But nothing makes a holiday gathering feel chic, totally put together, gloriously intentional, like a batch cocktail, made-to-order martini, or gussied-up punch.

Now, we all have our preferences when it comes to strength, spirit, and format. The host’s bandwidth is also a consideration; do you want to make a lot of one thing, or tailor your options to your guests’ preferences? Those questions are for you to answer, but our staff is here to help by providing this rundown of six tried, vetted, and loved drinks to make at your own celebration.

Below, find Eater editor-approved recipes for cocktails that will add the most festive of feelings to every holiday gathering.

Stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

I host a holiday potluck with a core group of friends in December, and one of my favorite potential additions is whatever punch that drinks columnist M. Carrie Allan is cooking up over at the Washington Post. A favorite from 2022 was a meringue-topped citrus punch, featuring blood orange, Aperol, and a dramatic meringue topping. Said topping adds undeniable flair and drama to the presentation, but if you’re daunted by the idea, the punch itself is still a festive, not-too-sweet drink to serve, celebrating winter citrus. —Missy Frederick, editorial director, dining

Meaghan Dorman’s modern classic is a favorite year-round, but there’s something about the holidays that calls for Scotch. No shade to the nog freaks, but the subtly spiced sour is a pleasant counterpoint to the onslaught of holiday food and beverage maximalism. No need to break out the single malt either, your dusty bottle of Dewars or Monkey Shoulder will do just fine. —Allison Hamlin, director of network development

The French 75 — the effervescent classic cocktail made with gin, Champagne, and lemon — is already one of my easy-drinking favorites, and I like it even better in punch form, accented with an aesthetically pleasing ice block of cheery lemon slices. What makes it 77 instead of 75? The substitution of St-Germain (or any elderflower liqueur) for simple syrup, adding just a tiny touch of herbal complexity. It’s perfect for New Year’s Eve, but just as refreshing at Thanksgiving or any other holiday table where you want something light and zesty. —Hilary Pollack, deputy editor

As the de facto cook for Thanksgiving, I like to keep the drinks options simple so I can focus on food prep. This cocktail recipe requires only two ingredients, doesn’t require pre-batching, and is easy enough for people to pour on their own. I also like how it uses Basque cider, which is drier than the typical ciders, so it’s not too sweet while still tapping into that cozy fall feeling —Rayna Rossitto, editor, branded content

I grew up guzzling Broguiere’s eggnog, but I love the more tropical combination of rich, creamy coconut milk, rum, and cinnamon in coquito; the Puerto Rican holiday cocktail was first described to me as “eggnog, if it went on vacation,” and I haven’t looked back since. This version is by bartender Shannon Ponche, and gets extra dressed up in spice for the holidays with the addition of a homemade cinnamon simple syrup, a woody, nutty oloroso sherry, and a splash of spiced Braulio. —Francky Knapp, staff writer

There are two schools of thought on a post-dinner drink: You could go for a bracing digestif to “aid digestion,” or you could indulge in a liquid dessert that swaddles you in sugar, fat, and everything nice. I’m notoriously bad at decision making, so I tend to split the difference with an eggy flip tinged with something bitter. Together, a whole egg and syrup (in this case honey syrup) build a comforting base, while an entire 1.5 ounces of cocktail bitters (as opposed to the usual dash or two) ensure you don’t entirely fall asleep in your glass. Angostura is a great option, delivering some classic holiday spice, but any style of cocktail bitters would probably work, as would an amaro. Dry shaking (shaking the liquid ingredients without ice) is key to achieving a frothy texture, and don’t forget the half-ounce of whiskey, which punches up the rest of the flavors. —Nick Mancall-Bitel, editor

Several members of my husband’s family are Manhattan drinkers, so I expect that my decision to serve the Grandfather cocktail during Thanksgiving appetizers will be a hit. It’s a riff on the classic drink with a hint of fall, courtesy of the addition of Applejack, an apple brandy. It’s smooth and well-balanced. It’s also quite boozy, so I’ll probably look for a slightly lower-proof option to tide us over after that initial round. I’ve had success with a bourbon and ginger ale bar (with various sodas and mixers) in the past, as well as Smitten Kitchen’s fall sangria; maybe this year we’ll go with her (okay, still pretty boozy) apple cider Old Fashioneds. —Missy Frederick, cities director

#6361. Navigating Lunar Orbit Using Nothing But Shadows And A Power Meter

Humanity is quickly starting to saturate our ability to track all of the satellites we have in deep space. NASAâs Deep Space Network (DSN) has been the workhorse for tracking such things for decades, but is quickly being overwhelmed by the number of requests it receives. Which in turn makes it harder to track some of the missions that have been launched recently. A new paper, available in pre-print on arXiv, from Ian Down, James McElreath, and Manoranjan Majji, of Advanced Space, Space Exploration Engineering, and Texas A&M respectively, offer a no-cost solution to that tracking problem - use solar array data from a spacecraftâs eclipse to determine where it is.

Solar panel output is something every spacecraft already tracks, typically in the form of Maximum Power Point Tracking (MPPT), which is an algorithm designed to point a craftâs solar sails at the Sun to maximize the amount of incoming solar radiation it receives. But eclipses, where a spacecraft positions itself so that a body its orbiting is between it and the Sun, is also something every spacecraft experiences, at least for a little while.

Engineers usually spend a lot of time intentionally avoiding eclipses, because they can be really hard on the spacecraft itself. The solar arrays stop generating electricity, draining the battery, and everything on the craft gets much, much colder. However, the precise timing of how those blackouts travel across the solar panels of a spacecraft holds valuable information.

Fraser interviews astrodynamacist Dr. Aaron Rosengren, talking about the three-body problem of lunar orbits.

Astronomers know the exact positions of the Sun, Earth, and the Moon years in advance using advanced planetary maps. Given how much data weâve collected on those three bodies, we also know the precise shape and locations of the shadows those three bodies cast into space. Each shadow comes with two nested cones - the penumbra, where the Sun is partially blocked, and the umbra, where it is completely cut off.

When a spacecraft crosses into one of those cones, the amount of solar radiation hitting its solar panels drops precipitously, but its electronics continue to operate due to the on-board battery engineers placed there precisely to deal with these eclipses. By recording the precise timestamp where the voltage starts to drop, and when it starts to pick back up again after the spacecraft leaves the shadow, a navigation algorithm can determine its three dimensional location in space without needing any cameras, star trackers, or radio signals.

That sounds simple in theory, but in practice getting that precise measurement correct is difficult. The Moon has no atmosphere, so its shadow is very jagged and tracks the mountains and craters dotting its surface. Each of those features can change the eclipsesâ timing by a few seconds. Earth, on the other hand, is a whole other ball of wax - or ball of gas and rock as the case may be. Itâs squished slightly at the poles, and its atmosphere can blur the Sun, as well as enlarging its shadow, making it difficult to differentiate precisely what part of the planet the spacecraft is passing over at any given time.

Fraser talks about different techniques to find your way in the cosmos.

To solve this problem, the researchers turned to a dataset of over 22,000 historical observations of lunar craters being covered by Earthâs shadow, which was collected by astronomers between 1842 and 2011. Using this data, the algorithm was able to map certain parts of the Earthâs shadow to specific ground features, allowing a more granular idea of where the specific spacecraft is passing over during its eclipse.

To prove the system works, the researchers used another interesting data set - the actual flight telemetry from CAPSTONE, a CubeSat mission operated by Advanced Space, where Mr. Down, the lead author, works. CAPSTONE, which was intended to test the orbit for NASAâs now discontinued Lunar Gateway, recently completed its mission in July 2026. But on January 11th 2026, it traveled through the Moonâs shadow, with its solar panel voltage dropping from 23V to near zero, then picking back up to 31V when the panels hit sunlight again.

Using that data, the researchers timed the spacecraftâs entry and exit to the Moon shadow to within 15 seconds of the CAPSTONE's actual path. In addition to running the algorithm on real-life data, they also simulated a scenario where a spacecraft missed a check-in with ground stations and had its position uncertainty drift by several kilometers. Processing the eclipse data without any further information cut that uncertainty by more than 60 %

Perhaps the most important feature of this whole system is that it's essentially free. It doesnât require any additional hardware, or is âzero-Size Weight and Powerâ (zero-SWaP) in spacecraft jargon. To be clear, it doesnât entirely replace ground-based radio tracking. But it does provide a safety net. And as more and more spacecraft start venturing beyond low Earth orbit, and continue to overwhelm our active tracking systems, that zero-cost safety net could prove very valuable indeed.

I.M. Down, J. McElreath, & M. Majji - Eclipse Observables for Navigation in Cislunar Space

UT - A Small Satellite Could See a Perfect Solar Eclipse Every Month

UT - ESA's New Mission Can See a Solar Eclipse Every Day

UT - To Keep GPS Constellations From Drifting, Look To The Moon

#6360. A Five-Day Experiment Reveals a Surprising Secret of Deadly Brain Cancer

Researchers tracking glioblastoma cells in living mouse brain tissue discovered how quickly they can change their paths, revealing a hidden challenge in stopping this aggressive brain cancer.

Glioblastoma is one of the most aggressive forms of brain cancer, largely because its cells can spread deep into surrounding healthy tissue. Even after surgeons remove the main tumor, scattered cancer cells may remain in the brain and eventually contribute to the disease returning.

Understanding how these cells spread has been difficult because researchers have largely relied on images that capture only individual moments. Scientists at Uppsala University have now developed a method that lets them watch thousands of glioblastoma cells move through living brain tissue, revealing how they change their behavior over time. The findings, published in Nature Communications, could help researchers better understand why this cancer is so difficult to contain.

“Until now, we have mostly seen snapshots of how glioblastoma spreads. This method combines microscopy with artificial intelligence and allows us to watch the process unfold in living brain tissue. We could also compare tumors from different patients and investigate how they respond to treatment,” says Hitesh Mangukiya, researcher at the Department of Immunology, Genetics and Pathology at Uppsala University and one of the study’s lead authors.

The new method, called GlioTrace, combines automated microscopy with machine learning to follow individual cancer cells as they travel through brain tissue. To test it, the researchers collected glioblastoma cells from six patients and grew them as tumors in mouse brains. They then cut the brains into thin slices, kept the tissue alive in the laboratory, and photographed it at intervals of no more than two hours for up to five days.

A computer system identified and tracked individual tumor cells across the images, while statistical models helped researchers calculate when cells switched between different states. Unlike techniques that examine only small regions of the brain, GlioTrace can monitor cells across entire brain slices using standard microscopes.

The observations revealed that glioblastoma cells do not all spread in the same way. Some tumors showed a preference for traveling along blood vessels, while others spread more diffusely through the surrounding brain tissue. These differences were apparent between tumors derived from different patients.

Individual cells were also remarkably adaptable. A cancer cell moving along a blood vessel could later leave that route and travel independently through the tissue. Some cells changed their shape and movement patterns over just a few days, suggesting that their behavior is far less fixed than individual images might imply.

“What surprised us most was how flexible the tumor cells are. The same cell can change how it moves over just a few days. To develop treatments that stop tumor cells from spreading, we need to understand this ability to switch between different behaviors,” says Madeleine Skeppås, PhD student at Uppsala University and co-lead author of the study.

The team also used GlioTrace to examine how cancer treatments influence cell movement. Two drug substances reduced the movement and spread of tumor cells in the brain slices, although their effectiveness varied between patient-derived tumors. Even within the same research setting, cells with different movement patterns did not respond equally to the drugs.

Another experiment raised questions about what happens to invasive cells during treatment. In some tumor models, combining radiation with chemotherapy increased the proportion of cells with a particular shape. These cells were among the fastest moving and occupied a central position in the network of transitions between different cell states, indicating that they were closely connected to changes in cell behavior.

The findings suggest that certain highly invasive cells might persist during treatment. However, the researchers have not established whether these cells are more resistant to therapy or whether they contribute to tumor recurrence. Further studies will be needed to determine what this response means for treating glioblastoma.

“Using this method allows us to monitor, for the first time, how thousands of individual tumor cells move through living brain tissue and to see how they adapt their behavior in real time. It opens up new possibilities to understand and, in the long term, halt the invasion process,” says Sven Nelander, Professor of Integrative Cancer Research at Uppsala University.

An important part of GlioTrace is the computational analysis system developed by Skeppås together with colleagues at Chalmers University of Technology and the University of Gothenburg. The software processes microscopy images, recognizes the different shapes of cancer cells, and estimates how their characteristics change over time. It has also been made freely available, allowing other researchers to investigate how tumor cells interact with their surroundings and respond to potential treatments.

Although GlioTrace offers a more detailed view of cancer cell invasion, it remains a laboratory research method rather than a tool for making clinical decisions.

“We hope that the method will help us understand how tumor cells interact with their surroundings and identify treatments that can prevent cancer from spreading through the brain. However, for now, GlioTrace is a research method, and further studies are needed before it could be used to guide treatment decisions in patients,” says Hitesh Mangukiya.

Reference: “Reconstructing the single-cell spatiotemporal dynamics of glioblastoma invasion” by Hitesh Bhagavanbhai Mangukiya, Madeleine Skeppås, André Lasses Armatowski, Irem Uppman, Linnea Hallin, Filippa Kruse, Clara Nordquist, Soumi Kundu, Maria Berglund, Adam A. Malik, Cecilia Krona, Rebecka Jörnsten and Sven Nelander, 2 November 2026, Nature Communications. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78908-9

The research was supported by the Swedish Research Council, the Swedish Cancer Society, the Swedish Foundation for Strategic Research and the Knut and Alice Wallenberg Foundation.

A DNA analysis has confirmed that a Nazca infant who lived in southern Peru 1,600 years ago had a rare congenital condition called trisomy 13.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists in Peru have discovered the skeleton of an infant with a rare birth defect that left only one central eye socket in the child's skull. DNA analysis of the remains confirmed a chromosomal abnormality caused the deadly condition in the infant over 1,600 years ago, according to a new study.

"We cannot really say how long this individual survived," study co-author Lars Fehren-Schmitz, an anthropologist at the University of California, Santa Cruz, told Live Science in an email. But "the burial of this infant suggests that the Nasca treated this individual in death like most other infants."

The skeleton of this female infant was discovered alongside a second one inside a ceramic urn at the archaeological site of Jauranga in Peru's Palpa Valley, where numerous geoglyphs known as the Nazca Lines have been found. Archaeologists uncovered several dozen other burials dated to the Middle Nazca (also spelled Nasca) period (A.D. 325 to 440) at the site, but one of the co-buried infants had an extremely rare condition, researchers wrote in a study published Monday (Nov. 9) in the journal PNAS.

The infant had a very small skull and a single eye socket in the middle of her face, along with other developmental issues of the cranial bones. These traits match modern clinical descriptions of cyclopia, a lethal condition that occurs when the front part of a fetus's brain fails to divide into left and right hemispheres.

This condition can also cause alterations in the nasal structures, resulting in a missing nose or a tube-like nose above the single eye.

A medical illustration from 1891 of two infants with cyclopia.

"The cause of the malformation was present at fertilization, but manifestation occurs around the fourth to fifth week in utero [in the womb], when the frontal lobe of the brain has to divide," study first author Elsa Tomasto-Cagigao, an archaeologist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, told Live Science in an email.

Cyclopia is a rare condition, occurring in about 1 out of every 100,000 births. To learn more about the infant's short life, the researchers sequenced her genome. (DNA suggested the infant carried two X chromosomes, typical of a female.)

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The team detected an extra copy of chromosome 13, meaning the infant had a genetic condition called trisomy 13, or Patau syndrome. It's known to be a major chromosomal cause of cyclopia; that said, only a small percentage of trisomy 13 cases involve cyclopia.

While trisomy 13 is associated with advanced maternal age, it is not clear whether that was the case for this infant, Fehren-Schmitz said.

"This condition has been documented in historic and modern anatomical collections, but to my knowledge this is the first archaeological example of this developmental abnormality," Siân Halcrow, a bioarchaeologist at Durham University in the U.K. who was not involved in the study, told Live Science in an email.

The researchers' estimate of the infant's age at death suggests she may have survived for several weeks or months after birth, Halcrow pointed out. "This raises important questions about how infants with profound congenital differences were cared for and treated in past societies," she said.

The infant was buried in a ceramic urn, the researchers noted in the study, which was a common burial method in the Nazca period, along with a second female infant who had no skeletal abnormalities. "The baby with cyclopia was at the bottom of the jar, while the other baby was on top. Nevertheless, it appears that they were interred in a single event," Tomasto-Cagigao said. The genetic analysis showed that the two infants did not have the same mother.

A burial of two infants in one urn is unusual for this culture, the researchers said, but there is not enough archaeological evidence to conclude that the infant with cyclopia was given a different type of burial.

"The fact that the individual was buried with a 'healthy' individual in a regular cemetery, without any special grave goods, suggests that, to some extent, the individual was not treated differently in death, even though it had such a rare condition," Fehren-Schmitz said. "It was neither 'excluded' because of it nor treated in a 'special' way."

In ancient Andean societies, some people with disabilities took on special societal roles, such as ones associated with religious practices. "If that reflects Nasca society as a whole, we can't say based on one case," Fehren-Schmitz said, "but it does reflect the community this infant was part of, even if only briefly."

Tomasto-Cagigao, E., Reindel, M., Isla Cuadrado, J., Lund Valle, M., Kassadjikova, K., Harkins, K., Fehren-Schmitz, L. (2026). A Nasca-period perinatal burial reveals cyclopia associated with trisomy 13 in southern Peru. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. https://www.pnas.org/cgi/doi/10.1073/pnas.2625042123

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

#6358. This Rare Binary Star Emits Radio Pulses Every Few Minutes. Will It Eventually Explode?

Unusual electromagnetic signals permeate the cosmos, and they range from powerful and deadly gamma-rays down to generally harmless radio waves. The sources of many of these signals are well-understood, and in some cases, special spacecraft have been launched to monitor them. But some remain unexplained.

Radio waves are widespread throughout the cosmos because they come from objects with a wide variety of temperatures. Radio astronomy has been around for decades, so many of these are well-understood. But not all of them. Some of them have only been discovered more recently and are awaiting an explanation.

One of these phenomenon are called long-period radio transients (LPTs), and their periodic radio pulses range from a few minutes to several hours. That's important because it differentiates them from pulsars and their extremely short radio periods. Astronomers have only detected about 15 LPTs in total, and they've had difficulty explaining exactly what they are and how they generate their radio pulses.

There are different hypotheses invoked to explain them. They could be magnetars, which are neutron stars with extremely powerful magnetic fields that rotate very slowly. Or they could be something exotic and speculative, like strange dwarf pulsars.

But at least some of them have been confirmed to be White Dwarf-Main Sequence (WDMS) binaries, a binary star containing a white dwarf (WD) and another main sequence star. Astronomers have only been able to confirm the white dwarf's companion in a handful of cases, and in those, the companion is a red dwarf.

Now astronomers have identified for the first time a LPT that consists of a white dwarf with a Sun-like, G-type star as its companion. Their results are published in Nature Astronomy in a paper titled "A long-period transient with a Sun-like companion." The lead author is Dr. Sam McSweeney, who made this discovery while working as a researcher at the Curtin University node of ICRAR.

At the time of this research, there were only 12 detected LPTs, and the ones with identified components favoured WD and red dwarf pairs. "An optical follow-up confirmed that at least 4 (ouf of 12) long-period transients are binary systems comprising a white dwarf and an M dwarf," the authors write. But this newly-detected LPT, named GPM J071507â114153, bucks that trend. "It is a binary system comprising a low-mass white dwarf and a G-type star identified via optical spectroscopy."

âWe detected this system in a large survey using the MWA (Murchison Widefield Array) to scan the entire Milky Way visible from Australia. We then used the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa to determine its precise position,â said co-author Natasha Hurley-Walker, Associate Professor at the Curtin Institute of Radio Astronomy.

The MWA detected 214 separate pulses, and the MeerKAT pinpointed its location based on 33 detected pulses. 26 of MeerKAT's pulses were co-detected by the MWA.

The new LPT has a period of only 7.9âminutes, which is almost certainly from its rotation. The properties of its radio pulses, like its polarization, are modulated by a longer period of about 1.3âdays, which the researchers say is the binary system's orbital period.

Follow-up optical observations and spectrometry came from the Keck Telescopes. "The optical counterpart of J0715-1141 was observed with the low-resolution imaging spectrometer on the Keck 1 telescope on Mauna Kea, Hawaii," the authors write. Those observations were a pair of 1,200 second exposures. They let the researchers determine the nature of the WD's partner star.

This figure from the research shows the optical spectrum of the new LPT, J0715-1141, compared to model spectra from F-type, G-type, and K-type stars. The spectrum most closely matches that of a G-type, Sun-like star. "As a comparison, hotter F-type and cooler K-type stars show distinct spectral features not present in the data," the authors write. The three panels on the right highlight this in three different elements. Image Credit: McSweeney, S.J., Hurley-Walker, N., Bahramian, A. et al. A long-period transient with a Sun-like companion. Nat Astron (2026).

In this case, the WD's binary partner is a star like our Sun, which is far more massive and luminous than the M dwarfs (red dwarfs) found in other LPTs. So this rules out the idea that only WD-red dwarf pairs can generate LPTs.

Astronomers and astrophysicists want to know exactly how these radio pulses are generated. Can any of their observations help researchers determine the exact source of the radio pulses? Not exactly, but the clarity of the pulses helps narrow it down.

âThis is the first time the pulses are clear enough to see the white dwarf moving in its orbit around its companion, so we know that the pulsations are coming from a region close to the white dwarf, or possibly even from the white dwarf itself,â said lead author McSweeney.

"We conclude that in long-period transients powered by white dwarf binaries, the coherent radio pulsed emission crucially depends on its interaction with the companion star, which we show can be G-type stars in day-long orbits," the researchers write.

There's another suprise in these findings. The pulses from the WD let the researchers detect stellar flares from the Sun-like star as it passed in front of the WD.

âAs a bonus, we also saw the white dwarf moving behind a region with a strong magnetic field, most likely a âstellar prominenceâ, which is a large loop of plasma erupting from a starâs surface,â Hurley-Walker said. âItâs amazing that by using radio wavelengths we can detect the storms on a star over 5000 light-years away.â

This image shows a solar prominence from the Sun in 2010, with Earth shown for scale. The researchers were able to detect one of these coming from the main sequence star in the pair, as the white dwarf moved behind it. That's pretty impressive for a star that's 5,000 light years away. Image Credit: NASA/SDO

One questions astronomers ask is how these types of binaries form, and the researchers have a hypothesis for that. They say the system could've formed through binary evolution. "One possibility is that the present configuration of the system arises through post-common-envelope (CE) binary evolution," they write. The progenitor of the system most likely had an intermediate-mass primary with a lower-mass companion on a wider orbit. "As the primary evolved off the main sequence and expanded into a giant, unstable mass transfer initiated a CE phase, during which orbital energy and angular momentum were transferred to the envelope, leading to its ejection and substantial orbital shrinkage."

The primary star was left as an exposed stellar core, and evolved to become a WD, creating the situation the astronomers see today: a WD star with a G-type partner, that are still in a binary relationship, but detached from the common envelope they once shared.

As for the system's future, it could hold a cataclysmic explosion.

Binaries like this that have left their common envelopes, and that consist of a WD and a massive main-sequence star, are potential breeding grounds for eventual Type Ia supernovae. This can happen as their orbit decays and the WD accretes material from its companion. Once enough material builds up on the accreting WD, it explodes and destroys the WD. Or they could created a double degenerate WD-WD merger, if the main sequence companion collapses before the binary orbit decays.

Could the radio signals from LPTs be used to find the progenitors of these supernovae explosions?

"Radio detections of LPTs may offer a route to finding cooler WDs around hotter stars at greater distances than traditional ultraviolet and optical surveys," the authors write.

The upcoming Square Kilometre Array could be the key to this.

"In an era of larger and more sensitive radio surveys, such as those to be conducted by the Square Kilometre Array Observatory, this may form a new pathway for investigating the progenitors of type Ia supernovae," the authors write.

#6357. The Absolute Best Pie Recipes, According to Eater Staff

The dessert course is about to go off with a perfect pumpkin pie, chocolate peanut butter pie, a caramelized onion tart, and more

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

You don’t really need a holiday occasion to bake a pie, but it doesn’t hurt to let the spirit of the season introduce you to a few more festive recipes. Whether you’re a fan of savory dishes, prefer fruit pies, or love the wobble of a perfectly set custard pie, there is a pie for everyone — including Eater staffers.

We love a super-easy no-bake pie just as much as we love a more complex, picture-perfect creation. Here are some of our favorite pie recipes to make at home this holiday season and beyond.

Stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

Since I grew up in Los Angeles and had never heard of buttermilk pie, it may come as a surprise that it’s one of my go-to pies to make. I discovered it seven years ago on a Twitter thread about unique, regional pies and was fascinated enough by this classic Southern dessert to attempt it, trying the first recipe that came up on my Google search. This is that recipe, and it has been consistently easy and perfect since that very first pie I made. The filling is smooth and velvety with subtle notes of nutmeg and a kiss of lemon. It reminds me of dan tat, or Chinese egg tarts, but it’s way less fussy. Yes, you can make your own pie crust, but storebought works well here, too, because the real star is the wobbly buttermilk custard. — Kat Thompson, audience editor

When fall comes around, I turn to this tried and true caramelized onion and butternut squash tart from Food 52 over and over again. It’s a perfect savory option to bring to Friendsgiving, Thanksgiving, or any autumnal get together. What I love most about it is that it highlights flavors and ingredients of the season while standing out from the plentiful pumpkin and pecan pies that you’re sure to find at any gathering. To make it heartier, I sometimes add crumbled sausage to the mix. — Terri Ciccone, deputy director of audience development

The only thing my mom and I love more than re-invigorating this incredibly simple chess pie recipe is telling the (most likely made up) story behind the name. Trying on my grandmother’s Texas twang, we explain how a server at a diner was once asked the flavor of the custard pie that day. She said, “It’s just pie,” but with her Southern accent that was mistaken as “chess pie.” And so we got this simple custard pie, which is filled with evaporated milk and set perfectly with cornmeal. My mom started experimenting with adding edible lavender oil to the recipe, which has became my favorite way to bake it, but she’s also added a tablespoon or two of my dad’s “Mexican mocha” (spiced hot chocolate) mix to make an incredible chocolate custard pie with a kick. But even plain, this pie recipe is always a big hit. — Emily Venezky, social media manager

I have nothing but the utmost respect for people who lovingly make intricately crafted, high-maintenance pies with lattice crusts and the whole shebang, but my personal tried-and-true, always-go-back pie recipe is one I’ve frequently revisited since high school: no-bake chocolate peanut butter pie. I do not know the true origin of the semi-homemade, Sandra Lee-esque creation, but if you stumble upon some version of the five-ish-ingredient recipe that includes Cool Whip, like this one on the blog Crazy for Crust, that’s what I’m referring to. Rest assured that I generally have the taste and standards of a bougie person, but this extremely simple, absolutely-not-healthy recipe is just perfection. It’s sweet, salty, creamy, and simultaneously light, fluffy, rich, and decadent. Whenever I make it for a dinner party, holiday gathering, or potluck, it garners rave reviews (the word “orgasmic” has been used to describe it more than once). And as a child of the ‘90s, I love using an Oreo crust and Skippy peanut butter — forever crowd-pleasers. — Hilary Pollack, deputy editor

“We have Milk Bar at home, honey” is what comes to mind whenever I make this pie, which reminds me of the New York City bakery’s famous, albeit once salaciously named dessert (now called the Milk Bar Pie). This butterscotch pie from Smitten Kitchen packs the same gooey, buttery taste and a satisfyingly sticky consistency — I feel like it’s a pie for people who wish they could just eat caramelized graham cracker crusts and custards for dessert. — Francky Knapp, staff writer

This zingy citrus pie might evoke summertime, but that’s exactly why I make sure it’s on the table during the holidays. Somewhere between a lemon pie and an icebox pudding, Atlantic Beach Pie delivers the bracing acidity I crave after a marathon of rich food. It originated at a North Carolina seafood restaurant, acting as a clever loophole to the old wives’ tale that eating dessert after a seafood meal could be deadly. Believe the lore or not, this pie is bound to earn seconds, whether for its salty, buttery saltine crust, zippy custard filling, or cloud of velvety whipped cream. — Nat Belkov, deputy brand director

Claudia Fleming, adapted by Amanda Hesser for the New York Times

I am not a pie person, per se — I hate the pressure of making a flaky crust — but I don’t mind the less-stress approach of making a tart, which asks only that I press dough into a tart pan. This famous chocolate caramel tart, a version of which my mom made frequently when I was growing up, is a dish I would definitely have on my roster if Mythical Kitchen ever invited me onto Last Meals. With dark chocolate ganache, a caramel filling that’s made more complex by the addition of salt and creme fraiche, and a sprinkling of a little more flaky salt on top, it tastes like a slightly more sophisticated Twix Bar.

I once asked my mom to make it for an ex-boyfriend, with me talking it up to him as my favorite dessert ever, and when he told me it was “just okay” — and who says that, especially when presented with a free dessert that required the dessert-giver to make a caramel? — that was the final sign I needed that he was not the one for me. Lesson learned: My husband and I are very dessert-compatible. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter

#6356. A Common Gut Antibody May Be the Key to Preventing Colon Cancer Before It Starts

People who lack a common gut antibody face higher colorectal cancer risk, and experiments in mice are beginning to explain how that missing protection may matter.

Long before colon cancer develops, cells lining the intestine can begin dividing too quickly. Scientists at Rockefeller University have discovered that a common gut antibody helps keep this growth under control in mice, raising the possibility of preventing tumors before they form.

In a study published in Nature, mice lacking immunoglobulin A (IgA) developed more than twice as many colon tumors as mice with normal antibody levels. Giving the deficient mice IgA by mouth eliminated their increased cancer risk.

The findings may help explain why people with IgA deficiency, which affects about 1 in 500 Americans, face a higher risk of colorectal cancer.

“One intriguing aspect of this work is that it shows how a natural defense in the gut restrains the cell division that can lead to cancer,” says senior author Daniel Mucida, head of Rockefeller’s Laboratory of Mucosal Immunology. “Most cancer research focuses on trying to destroy a tumor that already exists, but what if we could intervene before tumors form?”

IgA is one of the immune system’s first lines of defense. Unlike antibodies that target specific pathogens, it can bind to many kinds of gut bacteria and even some healthy human cells. Scientists have long known that these antibodies are abundant in the digestive system, although their full purpose has remained unclear.

Gregory Donaldson, a former Rockefeller postdoctoral fellow who is now an assistant professor at UCLA, investigated whether IgA’s interactions with gut bacteria could explain its connection to cancer. He compared mice lacking IgA with normal mice raised alongside them, ensuring both groups encountered the same food and germs.

The increased cancer risk appeared across several different models of colon cancer. More importantly, the researchers found changes in genes controlling cell division before any tumors developed, suggesting that IgA influences cancer risk at an early stage.

The team traced this effect to DMBT1, a receptor on the surface of intestinal cells. Gabriella Lima dos Reis, a graduate student in Gabriel Victora’s laboratory, helped identify its role.

In the presence of gut bacteria, DMBT1 encourages intestinal cells to multiply. IgA acts like a brake by binding to the receptor and limiting that growth. Without IgA, the signal can become overactive, allowing cells to divide excessively and form tumors. The researchers found that removing gut bacteria or DMBT1 signaling also prevented this uncontrolled growth.

“If IgA is missing, epithelial cells that are performing their normal function—responding to bacteria by producing new cells—can keep dividing unchecked, leading to cancer,” Mucida says. “We think this homeostatic effect is IgA’s main function. This was a big surprise.”

The discovery could eventually lead to new ways of reducing colon cancer risk, particularly for people who have had polyps removed. Polyps increase the likelihood of developing colon cancer, and Mucida believes targeting this pathway could offer a way to lower that risk.

Donaldson also sees potential in beneficial gut bacteria. Although much research has focused on microbes that encourage tumor growth, some bacteria may help protect intestinal cells. One possibility is developing probiotics that stimulate protective IgA responses.

Both approaches remain speculative, and the findings have not established a cancer-prevention treatment for humans. However, the study suggests that understanding how gut bacteria, antibodies, and intestinal cells interact could reveal new opportunities to prevent cancer before it starts.

Reference: “Suppression of epithelial proliferation and tumorigenesis by IgA” by Gregory P. Donaldson, Gabriella Lima dos Reis, Marwa Saad, Christopher Wichmann, Izabela Mamede, Guo Chen, Caroline E. Harrer, Nicole L. DelGaudio, Dayu Zhang, Begüm Aydin, Tiago B. R. Castro, Sergei I. Grivennikov, Bernardo S. Reis, Elise G. Liu, Stephanie C. Eisenbarth, Kivanç Birsoy, Sohail F. Tavazoie, Beth M. Stadtmueller, Gabriel D. Victora and Daniel Mucida, 11 November 2026, Nature. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11264-2

#6355. This Supernova is 50 Million Light Years Away, But That's Close Enough For Astronomers

A new supernova has been spotted in NGC 1433, a spiral galaxy about 50 million light years away. That's pretty close for supernova observations, and it's an opportunity for detailed follow-up study. It's not a core-collapse supernova, where a massive star has burned through its fuel and collapses and explodes. It's a Type Ia supernova. That means it's happening in a binary star, where the exploding star is a white dwarf.

In type Ia supernova, a white dwarf, called the accretor star, draws material away from another star called the donor star. Material builds up on the surface of the white dwarf until it breaches the Chandrasekhar limit, about 1.44 solar masses. Then the white dwarf explodes and is obliterated. A type Ia supernova can also occur in a double white dwarf binary, where the two stars merge and explode.

This supernova is named SN 2026ahvu, where the suffix ahvu is a chronological identifier. It signifies that the supernova is the 41,855th transient discovered in 2026. But even though thousands of transients and supernovae have been found this year, this one is still particularly noteworthy for its relative proximity to Earth, and because it was detected early.

SN 2026ahvu was discovered on November 2nd by ATLAS, the Asteroid Terrestrial-impact Last Alert System. ATLAS is designed and optimized to detect incoming near-Earth Objects shortly before they reach Earth, but it can also detect other transients.

New transients are recorded on the Transient Name Server (TNS), a transient registry sanctioned by the International Astronomical Union (IAU). The TNS also hosts AstroNotes, where short notes are posted describing new transients when they're discovered.

The AstroNotes for SN 2026ahvu reads: "ATLAS operates with 4 x 0.5m telescopes in Hawaii (Haleakala and Mauna Loa), Chile (El Sauce) and South Africa (Sutherland), and a fifth unit in Tenerife, Canary Islands. We are robotically surveying the whole sky with a cadence of 1 day between -50 and +50 and 2 days in the polar regions, weather permitting. While carrying out the primary mission for Near-Earth Objects, we search for and publicly report stationary transients to the IAU Transient Name Server."

"We report a new transient source, most likely a supernova in the galaxy NGC 1433. We are submitting AstroNotes for transients that are either within 100 Mpc, or have some other interesting feature to bring to the community's attention, such as bright nuclear transients, slowly rising or rapidly fading objects."

In this case, the SN's brightness is rising, and that's important for observations. It gives astrophysicists an opportunity to observe the supernova from an earlier point in its evolution. When it was first discovered, its apparent magnitude was 17. A few days later, it was at 13.5. (Lower apparent magnitude means the object is brighter.)

The Dark Energy Camera on the VÃ­ctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope captured these images of NGC 1433 before and after SN 2026ahvu exploded. The before images are from the Dark Energy Survey, DECam's primary job. The after image was taken after ATLAS detected the supernova and alerted other astronomers. The orange star below and to the right is a foreground Milky Way star. Image Credit: Dark Energy Survey/DOE/FNAL/DECam/CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/. Acknowledgment: PIs: G. Narayan & T. Murphey (University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign) Image processing: M. Zamani & D. de Martin (NSF NOIRLab)

When supernovae are detected, astronomers are alerted and other telescopes watch closely. In this case, there are new images of SN 2026ahvu from the Dark Energy Camera (DECam) and the Gemini South telescope.

Type Ia supernovae are typically brightest for about 6 months, but their brightness inevitably drops over time. Their peak brightness lasts several days and is powered by the decay of an unstable nickel isotope, Nickel-56 (56Ni.) Then the decay of âµâ¶Co â âµâ¶Fe creates a weaker tail of light.

This simple schematic shows the typical light curve for a Type Ia supernova, relative to the Sun. The peak is primarily due to the decay of nickel-56 (56Ni), while the later stage is powered by 56-Cobalt to 56-Iron, which is stable. Image Credit: By Xenoforme~commonswiki (attribution as on the source page); SVG reconstruction: PJ Geest. - This file was derived from: SNIacurva.png, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/201323073

About 2 or 3 months after the initial explosion, the ejecta will have thinned out and expanded enough to form a nebula. At that point, when astronomers look at the spectra, they're seeing the composition of the entire exploded star, not just its core. It's a fairly well-understood progression, but there's always room for more observations and more refinement.

Type Ia supernovae are important because they serve as standard candles in the cosmic distance ladder. It's the system astronomers use to find distances to celestial objects that are way too distant for more direct measurements like parallax. So the more opportunities they have to study Type Ia supernovae, the more accurate the cosmic distance ladder is.

Beyond their scientific importance, supernova remnants are among the most visually stunning objects that exist.

This is the Crab Nebula, probably the most well-known supernova remnant. The Hubble captured this image of the nebula, showing it less than 1,000 years after its progenitor exploded. So it's possible that our descendants will see something similar when they observe SN 2026ahvu reads a millennium from now. Image Credit: By NASA, ESA, J. Hester and A. Loll (Arizona State University) - A Giant Hubble Mosaic of the Crab Nebula, Public Domain, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/516106

More images and observations, included detailed study of how the explosion's light changes over time, will follow. The supernova is also within reach of astrophotographers, so there could be some fantastic images arriving soon.

#6353. Ringing Black Holes Offer Precision Tests of Relativity

Black holes remain some of the most mysterious and awe-inspiring celestial objects ever studied. This primarily comes from the fact that they literally canât be observed unless they interact with something in its surrounding environment, most notably a star. Adding to their mystery, several types of black holes exist, including free-floating black holes that drift independently throughout space, stellar-mass and are produced from exploding stars, and supermassive black holes that exist at the center of galaxies like our own. But arguably one of the most mind-blowing mysteries about black holes is figuring out what happens when they collide, and even merge.

Now, a team of more than 70 researchers might be one step closer to solving this decades-long conundrum as they used a combination of computer models and a literature review to analyze how black holes behave when they collide, specifically focusing on a well-known âringingâ phenomenon that occurs when black holes collide and merge. In a recent study published in Classical and Quantum Gravity, the primary motivation behind the study was to advance black hole research by establishing a long-known method called black hole spectroscopy from a theoretical concept to a practical one. Black hole spectroscopy involves measuring the gravitational waves that are produced from two black holes colliding and merging, specifically focusing on the âringdownâ phase, or the waves produced from the newly merged black hole.

In the end, the researchers successfully found that hundreds of observed black hole mergersâ âringdownâ behavior match the longstanding Einstein's theory of General Relativity. While the researchers note current observational methods present limitations for providing more accurate measurements, they emphasize how next-generation ground-based gravitational wave detectors could have the necessary technology for more in-depth and accurate observations of gravitational waves.

âBy listening to the ringing of newly formed black holes, we are turning gravitational waves into a tool for exploring some of the deepest questions in physics, from the nature of gravity itself to the possibility of discovering entirely new forms of matter and energy,â said Dr. Gregorio Carullo, who is an assistant professor in the School of Physics and Astronomy at the University of Birmingham and a co-author on the study.

Introduced in mathematical equations and a longer paper in 1915 and 1916, respectively, Einsteinâs theory of General Relativity challenged the longstanding hypothesis that gravity acted as an invisible force. In contrast, Einstein proposed gravity behaved like a fabric in both space and time, woven together in a phenomenon called spacetime. As a result, massive celestial objects like stars and planets create curves and warps within this fabric, with the mathematical aspect of the theory also predicting the existence of black holes while also proposing the existence of gravitational waves. However, Einstein himself didnât believe they existed and took this belief to his death in 1955. The reason for his disbelief is because he was convinced that matter was not capable of collapsing inward on itself to create such a state where something like a black hole is produced.

It wasnât until 1964, nine years after Einstein passed away, that the first black hole was discovered, which astronomers designated as Cygnus X-1 and is locate about 7,200 light-years from Earth. And it wasnât for another 51 years that gravitational waves were first detected, 100 years after Einstein first proposed their existence in mathematical equations.

Going forward, the researchers of this latest study anticipate that next-generation observatories could unlock longstanding secrets abut black holes, including gaining insight into their formation and evolution, along with continuing to uphold or challenge theories from Einstein and other scientists.

What new insights into ringing black holes will researchers make in the coming years and decades? Only time will tell, and this is why we science!

#6352. Scientists Discover Alarming Signs of Extinction Risk Deep Beneath the Ocean

A changing ocean presents threats that population counts alone may not reveal, and genetic evidence from the Gulf suggests some deep-sea species are already vulnerable.

The deep ocean may no longer be the safe haven scientists once believed it was. Hundreds of meters beneath the Gulf’s surface, fish and shrimp are showing genetic warning signs linked to extinction risk, raising concerns that the global biodiversity crisis could threaten even some of the ocean’s most remote inhabitants.

A new study led by researchers at Florida International University (FIU) found evidence that five deep-sea species may be less resilient to environmental change than previously assumed. Led by FIU marine scientist Pedro A. Peres of the Bracken-Grissom Lab, the research examined three species of lanternfish and two species of deep-sea shrimp collected between 2011 and 2023.

The team analyzed genetic information from 486 specimens to investigate how these populations had changed and whether they could withstand future environmental pressures. According to Peres, the investigation is among only a handful of studies to track changes in the DNA of deep-sea animals over time.

All five species showed genetic warning signs associated with increased extinction risk. One lanternfish species, Diaphus dumerilii, had lost approximately 8% of its genetic diversity over just 12 years. That decline was comparable to, or greater than, losses recorded in some threatened and endangered animals over considerably longer periods.

The researchers also discovered that all five species had relatively small effective population sizes. This measure does not necessarily reflect how many animals are alive. Instead, it describes how many individuals effectively contribute their genes to future generations. A species can therefore have a large population while relying on a much smaller group to maintain its genetic diversity.

“This challenges the idea that deep-sea species are naturally more resilient because they occupy such vast environments,” Peres said. “It shows how much we can miss when we look only at population abundance without considering their genetic diversity and long-term viability.”

Genetic diversity helps explain why these findings matter. When individuals within a species carry different genetic traits, their population has more opportunities to adapt as conditions change. Losing that variation can make it harder to survive disease, environmental disturbances, and other threats.

Heather Bracken-Grissom, assistant director of the Institute of Environment’s Coastlines and Oceans Division, has spearheaded research into the genetic diversity and resilience of deep-sea species. As a co-author of the new study, she emphasized the consequences of losing that diversity.

“Genetic diversity provides the variation populations need to adapt to changing conditions, resist disease and recover from environmental disturbances,” she said. “When that diversity disappears, a species can also lose the ability to withstand future threats.”

The genetic findings are especially concerning when considered alongside predictions about the Gulf’s future. Using climate models, the researchers estimated how suitable deep-sea habitats could become for these species by 2050 and 2100. Their projections indicated that four of the five species could experience substantial reductions in suitable habitat, potentially losing as much as 70%.

Such losses could place additional pressure on populations already showing signs of limited genetic resilience. The possibility challenges a longstanding assumption that deep-sea animals are naturally protected by their extensive habitats and broad geographic distributions.

The findings also raise questions about the lasting consequences of the 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill. Earlier research documented substantial declines in deep-sea animal populations following the disaster, although the precise relationship between that event and the genetic patterns identified in the new study remains uncertain.

The researchers did not establish that the oil spill caused the genetic changes they observed. Their results instead suggest that some populations may have been vulnerable even before the disaster, potentially making environmental disturbances more consequential.

“Our results suggest some deep-sea populations may have already been genetically vulnerable before the Deepwater Horizon oil spill,” Peres said. “This has important implications for understanding the consequences of environmental disturbances. Events such as oil spills may affect populations that already have limited genetic resilience.”

The study, which also included FIU researcher Keith Sellers and Tracey T. Sutton of Nova Southeastern University, points to a gap in how scientists assess the health of marine ecosystems. Traditional surveys can reveal changes in population numbers, yet they may overlook genetic vulnerabilities that affect whether those populations can survive over the long term.

By examining DNA across multiple years, researchers can identify threats that might remain hidden in ordinary population counts. Peres believes this approach should become a greater priority as scientists work to understand the pressures facing deep-sea life.

“This study serves as a wake-up call for the scientific community,” Peres said, “highlighting the urgent need to integrate genetic monitoring into biodiversity assessments and emphasizing the importance of long-term monitoring to better understand and detect changes in marine populations over time.”

Reference: “Extinction risks in deep-sea populations revealed by genomic data and ecological niche modeling” by Pedro A. Peres, Keith Sellers, Tracey T. Sutton and Heather Bracken-Grissom, 12 November 2026, Nature Communications. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-79098-0
