#6309. Clouds block satellite cameras, so an AI learned how to redraw the ground beneath them

GeoCore-9B learned how to recreate the ground that is hidden beneath cloud cover in satellite photos.

A satellite picture of a flooded town is only worth something if the camera can see the town. On a cloudy day it can’t, and the picture shows cloud where the streets should be. A new AI model fills those streets back in.

It was built to know where on Earth it is looking and how much ground each pixel covers.

Jeonghyeok Do and Munchurl Kim of KAIST in South Korea built the model, called GeoCore-9B. Their paper is a preprint that has been accepted for presentation at NeurIPS 2026, an artificial intelligence conference. It has not yet been published in a journal.

The ground the model draws under a cloud is a reconstruction, not a photograph. Do and Kim make that point themselves, and they warn that realistic fake satellite imagery could be used to spread disinformation about disasters or geopolitical events.

Ordinary satellite pictures work like a camera. They record sunlight bouncing off the ground, so thick cloud or nighttime leaves them with nothing to record.

That matters most during floods and wildfires, when the weather is often bad and the ground is exactly what people need to see.

A radar satellite sends radio waves down and measures the echoes that come back. The method is called synthetic aperture radar, and it works at night and through cloud.

But its images don’t look like photographs, because brightness and texture in them mean different things. Do and Kim wanted one model for both problems.

Earlier attempts started with an AI built to generate ordinary photographs and then taught it about satellites. Do and Kim wrote that this builds in biases.

Ordinary photos are taken from eye level with a subject in the middle, while a satellite looks straight down at a scene with no center.

So they trained their AI model from scratch on satellite views alone, adjusting about 9 billion internal settings, known as parameters, as it learned.

The training set was 10 million satellite images, each paired with a sentence describing it. The note for a port mentioned ships and warehouses; the note for farmland mentioned a road between fields.

Each image also carried its latitude, longitude, and how much ground one pixel covers. A building looks very different when each pixel covers about 3 feet (1 meter) than when each covers about 105 feet (32 meters).

Without that number, a small building and a large industrial plant can have the same shape.

A model this large, trained from nothing, learns slowly and tends to produce scenes with no coherent layout. So Do and Kim brought in a second AI, already trained to recognize satellite imagery, as a teacher.

During training, the new model was scored on how well its internal picture of a scene agreed with the teacher’s picture of how roads connect and where field boundaries lie.

The teacher is switched off once training ends, so it adds no work when the model is in use. Without it, the team found, the model’s images had fragmented textures and distorted structures. With it, every score they tracked improved.

The team also tested what the model had absorbed about geography. Given only a latitude and longitude, with no text at all, it drew dense skyscrapers for the coordinates of New York City and ice fields for Antarctica. It drew sand dunes for the Sahara and forest for the Amazon.

The team checked 500 of these coordinate-only images generated by the model against all 10.5 million real world photos that were used as training images.

They found none that closely matched the real-world satellite images, suggesting that the AI was not simply copying existing photographs. However, they wrote that the test can’t rule out every form of memorization used by the AI model.

To put the model to work, Do and Kim froze it and trained a small set of extra settings for each task. This was far cheaper than retraining it.

On a public test set of cloudy and clear image pairs, GeoCore-9B outscored every program built specifically for cloud removal on two of three standard measures. Those were cover brightness and color accuracy, and how closely the structure matches the clear image.

On the third, how natural the image looks, it scored about the same as the best specialist. The roads and field boundaries in its reconstructions stayed where the clear images put them.

On a second public dataset, the model turned radar images into photo-like images. It scored best on the two measures of realism and fine detail, and it roughly matched the best specialist on structural similarity.

“By training the AI on where each satellite image was taken and the actual size of the terrain it shows, we made it possible to use a single model for multiple tasks such as cloud removal and image conversion,” said Kim, a professor in KAIST’s School of Electrical Engineering.

He added that he expects the work to make weather-limited satellite data more usable for assessing disasters and monitoring changes in forests and cities.

The model only produces ordinary color images. It can read a radar image but can’t generate one. In addition, it doesn’t handle the multispectral images, with light bands beyond visible color, that some Earth-observation satellites record.

One piece, the component that compresses each image before the model works on it, came from ordinary photography. On the cloud-removal images, it kept the main features but lost some faint local detail.

By their own account, the experiments can’t say how much of the gain came from the model’s size, its training data, or the teacher.

So far each task has been tested on a single public dataset. How the model performs on other satellites and regions is unknown, and that is the test Do and Kim plan next.

Do and Kim also want the model to predict changes on the ground: flooding, building damage, wildfire spread, and urban growth. The team plans to explore surveillance and reconnaissance as well.

The model’s code and weights are online, so other groups can run those tests.

The full study has been posted as a preprint on arXiv and accepted for presentation at NeurIPS 2026. It has not been published in a journal.

A man's appendix had to be removed, but not for dangerous inflammation, as you might expect.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The symptoms: The man went to the emergency room because he had a sharp pain in his lower-right abdomen.

What happened next: When doctors examined the man, the type of pain and the location of his discomfort suggested that he might have appendicitis, or inflammation of the appendix.

Appendicitis can be dangerous because it can cause the appendix to burst and release bacteria from the bowels into the abdominal cavity, thereby infecting the cavity's lining. This infection, called peritonitis, can spread to the bloodstream and cause the life-threatening condition sepsis, which kicks the immune system into overdrive.

Even though the patient had acute pain in his lower-right abdomen, he did not show signs of peritonitis, such as fever, nausea, symptoms of dehydration and an elevated heart rate, according to a report of his case. His doctors then performed abdominal ultrasound scans and found that the man's abdominal organs, including the appendix, appeared normal, with no signs of inflammation.

The report's authors did not include details about the man's treatment after this examination. But eight months later, he was still in pain and returned to the hospital for further evaluation, they noted.

The diagnosis: This time, when medical personnel questioned the man, he recalled that approximately 15 years earlier, he had accidentally swallowed a piece of a long bone containing edible marrow. The report does not mention if the man sought treatment immediately after swallowing this bone.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

At this second visit, doctors performed an abdominal X-ray and found a round object near the upper right of the man's pelvis. It measured about an inch (2.5 centimeters) long and a little over an inch (3 cm) wide.

According to a subsequent CT scan, the object contained bone tissue and was near the appendix. When the doctors looked inside the patient's abdomen with a laparoscope — a long, flexible tool with a camera at one end — they saw that the appendix was enlarged.

The treatment: Surgeons performed a laparoscopic appendectomy, which uses small incisions in the abdomen to insert instruments for removing the appendix. Inside the appendix was a hardened mass of fecal matter, called a fecaloma, which surrounded a long bone.

The organ's muscular walls had been stretched out by the mass, but there were no signs of inflammation. No complications developed after the surgery, and the patient was discharged two days later. The report does not describe any follow-up visits or treatments.

The appendix (orange) is a small, thin pouch of tissue attached to the colon.

What makes the case unique: It's relatively uncommon for people to accidentally swallow something indigestible and then require a medical visit for it. In the United States annually, about 120,000 people — roughly 90% of whom are children — are treated for ingesting foreign objects, and most of the objects are swallowed accidentally. Most commonly, the adults requiring treatment have ingested jewelry, while children are more likely to swallow coins, toys and batteries.

Typically, small, swallowed items pass harmlessly through the intestines within 48 hours; less than 1% require surgical intervention. Some objects, however, need immediate attention. For example, sharp items can tear the esophagus or puncture digestive organs. Batteries are hazardous if swallowed, as they contain corrosive acid that can leak into the gut. And small magnets are a big risk, especially if two or more are involved, since they may stick together through intestinal walls, which can tear holes in tissues or cause blockages and contortions in the intestines.

Swallowed foreign bodies rarely affect the appendix. Whether they enter the organ depends on the size of the opening into the appendix where it connects to the colon (which can vary between individuals), the dimensions of the ingested object, and the appendix's position in the body at the time. These objects cause approximately 0.005% cases of appendicitis, according to the man's case report. Such items recovered by surgeons through appendectomies include pieces of coal, nails, bits of enamel and glass, shells, dental crowns and bullets.

When a foreign body migrates to the appendix, it typically generates appendicitis within a few months, at most. However, this is not always the case. One report described a man who had eaten pigeons as a child and discovered more than 30 years later that he had 27 lead shot pellets in his appendix. Despite containing these pellets from the birds' flesh, his appendix was not inflamed.

"It is therefore possible, although rare, that a foreign body in the appendix even after many years (in our case, 15 years) does not lead to an authentic appendicitis either histologically or clinically," the authors of the marrowbone case report wrote.

They added that their patient was the first record in the scientific literature of a sizable bone lingering inside an appendix for more than a decade without causing significant inflammation. His pain was likely caused by physical shifting of the hard mass. His experience presented "a unique clinical picture," the doctors wrote.

"This case could offer a possible diagnostic and therapeutic option for appropriately treating patients with foreign bodies within the appendix," they said.

For more intriguing medical cases, check out our Diagnostic Dilemma archives.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Antonacci, N., Labombarda, M., Ricci, C., Buscemi, S., Casadei, R., & Minni, F. (2013). A bizarre foreign body in the appendix: A case report. World Journal of Gastrointestinal Surgery, 5(6), 195–198. https://doi.org/10.4240/wjgs.v5.i6.195

#6307. New hypothesis explains why the right side of the human brain controls the left side of the body

The brain's crossed wiring runs through every vertebrate group, and two neuroscientists trace it to the eyes of the first fishes.

A stroke on the right side of the brain weakens the left arm and leg. The brain is cross-wired that way, and for more than a century scientists have assumed there was an evolutionary reason for it.

Two neuroscientists have traced the crossing through every major group of living vertebrates. They now propose that evolution may never have selected it for the jobs it does.

On their reading, the crossed wiring may simply be inherited from the way the first fishes’ eyes were wired to their brains, some 500 million years ago.

Martin Wessendorf, an associate professor emeritus of neuroscience at the University of Minnesota, and Daniel Wang, a researcher in the University’s Department of Neuroscience, wrote the review.

It is a hypothesis built from more than a century of published anatomy rather than a new experiment. However, the authors wrote that it may be testable in fossils.

In an interview with Earth.com, Wang said the question reaches beyond his own field.

“This’ll be relevant to anyone who wants to know more about why brain injury on one side of the head often leads to loss of function on the opposite side of the body,” he said.

The crossing begins at the eye. The lens flips the image, so whatever sits to your right lands on the left side of each retina. The nerve fibers carrying the right half of the view then sort themselves at a junction behind the eyes and run to the left side of the brain.

One place that information goes is a structure in the midbrain called the optic tectum. It holds a map of the opposite half of visual space, and it fires fast turning and escape movements.

Every vertebrate examined appears to have one, lampreys and hagfish included, along with the crossing junction behind the eyes.

Living jawless fish carry both, so the authors conclude that the last common ancestor of all vertebrates probably did too. That puts the first crossed wiring in the Cambrian period, among jawless fishes that lived roughly 538 to 486 million years ago.

Anatomists call crossed wiring contralateral organization, and its age is what struck Wang.

“What surprised me the most was likely just how old the contralateral organization of the optic tectum is for vertebrates – spanning even to the Cambrian,” he told Earth.com.

Body senses crossed next. Two pathways carry touch, pain, temperature and body position from the spinal cord up to the brain, and both cross the midline in amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.

The one for light touch and body position is missing in fishes, so the authors trace it to the last common ancestor of the four-limbed animals.

Movement pathways cross too. One runs from the optic tectum down to the spinal cord and turns the body toward whatever just appeared at the edge of vision.

Lampreys and bony fish appear to have no such pathway. Sharks have one that mostly stays on its own side, and rays and lungfish have a crossed one.

Reptiles appear to have lost that pathway. A second crossed pathway, from a cluster of midbrain cells called the red nucleus, is thought to help control limbs.

True mammals appeared about 165 million years ago. By then, those crossed senses and movement pathways had already existed for almost 200 million years.

The pathway that lets you move one finger at a time is the special case. It runs from the cerebral cortex, the six-layered outer sheet found only in mammals, down to the spinal cord, and it crosses in the lower brainstem.

In most mammals, it ends where touch signals enter the cord and adjusts those signals. Few mammals besides primates, raccoons and kinkajous have a version that reaches the nerve cells that drive muscles.

So the circuit that gives humans fine control of their hands appears to be a sensory circuit put to a new use. Wang said that was the finding that surprised his co-author most.

“This demonstrates that circuitry that’s involved in one function can, with just a change or two, become a function that’s entirely different.”

The crossing isn’t universal in this pathway. In goats and elephants, it runs down both sides of the spinal cord, and in hedgehogs and moles it mostly stays on its own side. Even in humans, an estimated 10 to 25 percent of its fibers don’t cross.

Wang pointed to the goats and elephants, “so there’s a decent amount of diversity there,” he said. The authors read that variety as a sign that natural selection wasn’t strongly favoring the crossing in this pathway.

Isaac Newton proposed in 1704 that the junction behind the eyes sorts nerve fibers by visual field.

Ramón y Cajal, who later won a Nobel Prize for his work on the structure of the nervous system, went further in an 1898 paper. Once the visual map crossed, he proposed, it would pay for the maps of hearing, touch and movement to match it.

In computer models published in 2014, an animal controlled by the opposite side of its brain was likelier to survive a blow to one side of the head or body.

At least two other research groups have blamed a twist in the body plan, dating to the split between vertebrates and their invertebrate ancestors. That argument goes back to an 1822 dissection of a crayfish.

The authors see a problem with the twist. The visual system was probably crossed in the first vertebrates, but the pathways for touch, limb control and finger control didn’t exist yet.

So the authors doubt that a single ancient twist can explain them.

The authors’ own answer starts with the optic tectum. Its map of the opposite half of visual space sits on top. Beneath it, in register, sit maps of touch and hearing from the same half, and at the bottom sit the cells that fire movements.

Wessendorf and Wang propose that this stack biased the sensory and motor pathways that evolved later toward crossing.

When the cortex evolved, most of the pathways carrying signals into it were already crossed. A cortex wired to its own side would have needed extra crossings to collect vision, touch and hearing from the far side, or a rewiring of every older circuit.

The authors argue that either change would have carried a “wiring cost,” leaving mammals that were less energy-efficient, less intelligent, or both.

Not everything crosses. Smell and taste mostly stay on the same side, and the authors note that neither sense maps space the way vision, hearing and touch do.

The cerebellum, which coordinates movement, works the same side of the body it sits on.

“We propose that contralateral organization didn’t necessarily evolve as an adaptation, but because evolution is an engineer that builds with the foundation and materials it has at hand,” Wang and Wessendorf wrote.

The authors list what would test the idea. Their first prediction is that the last common ancestor of vertebrates had both the crossing junction and an optic tectum.

Cambrian fossils of jawless fish exist, and a fossilized brain cast from one could show whether both were there.

Wang said the finding that would complicate the idea is an early fossil vertebrate whose optic tectum handled vision on the same side rather than the opposite one.

The authors also predict that crossed pathways from the forebrain to the spinal cord will prove widespread in birds. Unfortunately, relatively few bird species have been examined.

Crocodilians appear not to have been checked, and the authors predict they have one too.

Hearing is the one sense the authors treat with caution. It appears to have evolved partly on its own in different lines.

What remains unknown is whether any Cambrian fish skull preserves enough of its brain to show the crossing.

Until one does, the idea rests on living anatomy. The next checks are in the fossil record, and in the birds and crocodilians whose spinal pathways have yet to be mapped.

The full study was published in the journal Frontiers in Neuroanatomy.

#6306. Billions of trees grow beyond forests – and counting them could change restoration plans

A satellite study counted 5.25 billion trees in Rwanda and Tanzania, finding more than half outside forests, from farmland to towns.

Count a country’s forests and you’ve counted its trees, or so the thinking goes. In Rwanda and Tanzania, most of the trees aren’t in the forests at all.

Researchers counted about 5.25 billion trees across the two countries from 2019 satellite images, and more than half stood on farms, in grassland and shrubland, and in towns.

Countries and organizations have pledged to plant more than a trillion trees worldwide since the Paris climate agreement of 2015.

A pledge needs a count of what is already there, and that count has mostly come from forest surveys that often exclude farmland.

Maurice Mugabowindekwe and Martin Brandt of the University of Copenhagen led the team, with colleagues at the Rwanda Space Agency, the University of Rwanda, and the Tanzania Forest Services Agency.

Their count covers only trees big enough to see from space. That means a crown of at least 32 square feet (3 square meters), or a height of at least 10 feet (3 meters).

The team sorted its count by the land cover map that the European Space Agency’s WorldCover project publishes.

Only 48.8% of the trees fell inside the class that map calls tree cover, which is roughly forest and woodland.

The other 51.2% were spread across everything else: shrubland held 22.1%, grassland 16.4%, and cropland 12%.

The rest, under 1%, stood in towns, wetlands, bare ground and mangroves. Counting only trees in the tree-cover category would leave out more than half the total.

Tanzania accounted for about 5.04 billion of the trees and Rwanda for about 213 million. The typical acre in Tanzania carried 17 trees (42 per hectare) and the typical acre in Rwanda 15 (37 per hectare).

A typical acre of forest carried about 25 (61 per hectare). Forest holds trees more thickly, but there is far more land outside it.

In 2015, a team writing in Nature estimated about 19.9 billion trees in Tanzania, nearly four times this count.

The estimates are not directly comparable: the earlier study included small trees beneath the canopy, while the new study also counted trees outside forests.

Older tree maps worked from pictures sharp enough to outline each crown, taken by drones, aircraft or satellites. Those images cost money, and clouds spoil many.

The Planet satellites the team used have a 10-foot (3-meter) pixel.

The freely available Sentinel-2 optical images and Sentinel-1 radar data have 33-foot (10-meter) pixels.

So the team stopped trying to outline crowns. They stacked 20 bands of data from the three satellite systems into one image and cut it into squares 315 feet (96 meters) on a side.

Then they trained a deep learning model to estimate how many trees each square held, from the patterns of color, texture and radar echo inside it.

The model learned from about 12 million tree crowns in 2,832 sample areas across nine African countries and India. People had marked those crowns by hand or pulled them from laser-scanner height maps.

The team also found that dropping the sharper Planet images and using only the two Sentinel satellites gave nearly the same accuracy.

Rwanda and Tanzania both run national forest inventories, in which crews measure the trees in fixed plots.

The team compared its predictions with 196 of those plots in Rwanda and 19,664 in Tanzania.

It counted only trees at least 8 inches (20 centimeters) thick at chest height, the size most likely to show from above.

The model undercounted in most landscapes. Its raw estimate was about 179 million trees for Rwanda and 3.79 billion for Tanzania.

Matching the field plots raised those figures by about a fifth and a third, respectively, to the 213 million and 5.04 billion reported.

The authors’ explanation is that overlapping crowns in dense forest blur into one signal at a 10-foot pixel.

Built-up areas and mangroves in Tanzania were overcounted instead, and the authors suspect buildings and wetland plants were being read as trees.

Even after correction, the Tanzania figure could be anywhere from 4.6 to 5.6 billion.

A survey of East African farms found an average of 79 trees per acre (195 per hectare).

At that density, the two countries’ 37.6 million acres (15.2 million hectares) of cropland could take about 2.3 billion more trees.

That would be nearly half as many again as the two countries hold now, and trees among crops can raise harvests as well, the authors added.

Tanzania’s own census counts far more cropland than the satellite map does, about 99 million acres (40 million hectares), half of it on smallholder farms.

On that figure, the authors wrote, smallholders alone could add around 3.4 billion trees “if they access adequate support and incentives.”

That is more trees than the count found in all of Tanzania’s forests.

The authors’ point is that a baseline like this one can guide where a government puts its restoration money, and where planting new trees would crowd out naturally open land.

Restoration programs across Africa, from national pledges to the Great Green Wall, have mostly had no such baseline, because operational tree-count systems remain largely unavailable, the authors wrote.

The satellites can’t see under a dense canopy, so the authors treat their own estimates for closed forest with caution.

The count also leaves out every tree too small to show at a 10-foot pixel, so it can’t yet tell whether newly planted seedlings survive.

The correction factors came from Rwandan and Tanzanian field plots, so they may not apply elsewhere.

To use this method elsewhere, researchers would need local field measurements to check and adjust the satellite estimates.

The data and code are publicly available. The team plans to incorporate field measurements into the model to better account for trees hidden beneath the canopy.

The researchers also hope to test the method in other regions and with data from other satellites.

The full study was published in the journal Journal of Remote Sensing.

NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope could capture images 30% sharper than — and remain operational for twice as long as — initially expected. Researchers say these "remarkable" developments could greatly enhance the volume and quality of the data they will analyze.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is nearing its final destination more than 1 million miles (1.6 million kilometers) from Earth, where it will soon scour the universe for a host of cosmological treasures, including an estimated 100,000 new alien worlds.

But even before its mission truly begins, recent developments suggest the state-of-the-art spacecraft could take better images than — and remain operational for more than twice as long as — initially expected, further delighting already-excited astronomers.

"It is fantastic to learn that Roman is not just reaching its design goals but exceeding them," Eamonn Kerins, an astronomer at the University of Manchester in the U.K. who will help lead one of Roman's major surveys, told Live Science.

Roman is NASA's latest flagship space telescope, following in the footsteps of iconic observatories like the Hubble Space Telescope and the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). The $4 billion machine ‪—‬ which is over 42 feet (12.7 meters) long and weighs around the same as a fully grown Tyrannosaurus rex ‪—‬ successfully launched into space on Aug. 30, more than a decade after scientists started building it.

The telescope is now en route to Lagrange point 2 (L2), a fixed point relative to our planet where Earth's gravity and the sun's gravity cancel each other out. There, Roman will join several other important spacecraft, including JWST and the European Space Agency's Euclid telescope.

Roman was launched into space on board one of SpaceX's Falcon heavy rockets. It lifted off Aug. 30 from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

During Roman's journey to L2, which is currently around 85% complete, mission scientists have remotely switched on the telescope's various instruments to test whether they function as expected. So far, this "commissioning process" has gone off without a hitch, and by the time Roman arrives in less than two weeks, it should be ready to snap its first in-depth images of the cosmos.

Researchers were already pumped to see what Roman will be able to do once it is in place and fully switched on. However, that excitement has further intensified in recent weeks, thanks to two postlaunch developments.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

First, a series of near-perfect rocket burns, executed during and shortly after launch, saved more than a decade's worth of fuel that can now be used to extend Roman's mission. Second, after remotely adjusting the telescope's mirror, researchers discovered it should be capable of snapping images with around 30% greater detail than engineers predicted.

The team that designed, launched and remotely commissioned the orbital observatory has "done an amazing job" and "their work has ensured that Roman is more than up to the task," Kerins said.

Shortly after Roman arrived in space on board a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket that lifted off from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida, mission scientists conducted two major burns, or engine firings, which gave the spacecraft enough momentum to escape Earth's orbit and make the journey to L2.

Roman is around the same size as a small truck and was packed into the nose cone of the Falcon Heavy rocket prior to launch.

Thanks to a combination of "exquisite planning by our orbital dynamics team" and "brilliant execution by the operations team," these burns were so precise that each one saved up to four years' worth of fuel, Jamie Dunn, director of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, said in a Sept. 14 statement.

On top of this, Roman ended up being much lighter than initially planned, which allowed engineers to pack another four years' worth of fuel into the spacecraft before launch. "Since Roman's [weight] was lower than we budgeted for, we were able to fill the propellant tanks to their capacity rather than only filling them as much as we needed," Alison Rao, the Roman propulsion lead at NASA Goddard, said in the statement.

In total, these savings could give Roman an additional 12 years of fuel, which could more than double the mission's planned 10-year lifespan. That means Roman could still be capturing images of the cosmos in 2048.

Given that Roman can collect data up to 1,000 times faster than Hubble, this extended lifespan will greatly enhance the amount of data the new space telescope will be able to capture. "With a 20-year Roman lifetime, we could, in theory, do over 20,000 years of Hubble survey work," Kerins said. "That's a lot of science!"

Roman is now on its way to L2, where the gravity of Earth and the sun cancel out, allowing it to remain in one place without expending much fuel.

This prolonged lifespan will let astronomers compare images of specific objects decades apart — such as expanding nebulas or colliding galaxies — allowing them to detect changes they otherwise might have missed.

It may also let them study objects or phenomena that we haven't even discovered yet, which is particularly exciting, Kerins noted. "The real show-stopper results will be new things we just aren't even thinking about right now," he said. "The possibilities are truly breathtaking."

There is also the chance that Roman's mission could be extended even further, because engineers often find clever ways of making active spacecraft last longer. For example, Hubble is more than two decades past its initial mission parameters, and the recently deceased Swift Observatory lasted 10 times longer than initially predicted before falling back to Earth last week.

Roman's secret weapon is arguably its Wide Field Instrument (WFI), made up of a 288-megapixel camera attached to a 7.9-foot (2.4 m) mirror, which will capture ultra-detailed images with a field of view roughly 100 times larger than Hubble's.

Roman's WFI consists of a 288-megapixel camera attached to a 7.9-foot (2.4 m) mirror. It will be capable of capturing images with a field of view 100 times greater than Hubble.

We have already seen the first WFI images — a series of blurry, green dots captured during a test of the instrument's 18 different light detectors ( see below). However, those photos were nothing like what WFI will capture in the future; those images will be so detailed that you would need dozens of high-definition TVs to properly display a single snap in full resolution, Kerins said.

After Roman completes the initial WFI commissioning phase, those images will be around 30% sharper than designers predicted. "All of the images from Roman's cosmic surveys will be even sharper than we expected," Alden Jurling, a senior optical engineer who works on Roman at NASA Goddard, said in an Oct. 14 statement. "It's a great outcome."

The improvements were first noticed after the WFI's car-sized mirror was realigned by just one-sixteenth the diameter of a human hair, demonstrating just how intricate the commissioning process has been. "Calibrating an instrument is like tuning a piano or guitar before a concert," Maxime Rizzo, a WFI systems engineer at NASA Goddard, said in the statement. "You adjust everything until it's just how you want it and then leave the settings alone so it performs consistently while you use it."

NASA released Roman's first photos on Sept. 15. Each small square represents one of the telescope's light detectors, and each blurry green spot is a distant star. (This is just a test image and does not represent how the telescope's proper photos will look.)

The improved image quality could really come to the fore during Roman's hunt for potentially habitable exoplanets, which is what Live Science's readers are most excited about for this mission.

Kerins, who is leading the Exoplanet Demographics Working Group for the Transits in the Roman Exoplanets Survey, is particularly excited about this development, but he said it does not necessarily guarantee that Roman will find more exoplanets than initially predicted.

The rest of Roman's commissioning phase is also proceeding as planned.

Roman's coronagraph instrument, which will block out the light from distant stars to allow WFI to spot alien worlds, has passed its main commissioning phase and is working as intended, according to a NASA blog post.

Roman has completed around 85% of its journey to L2 and should arrive at its final destination in the next few weeks. (The timeline in this image is a screenshot from Roman's commissioning process website, captured on Nov. 11.)

Meanwhile, a global network of ground stations, which will receive up to 1.4 terabytes of data from Roman every day, has established contact with the spacecraft and is receiving signals as expected, another blog post revealed.

All of these early wins raise hopes that Roman can have a long and successful career, and are a testament to the years of work that went into designing the spacecraft and planning the mission.

"What we're seeing now with the actual optical performance and estimated lifetime of Roman is just how good that design process has been," Kerins said. "It's a remarkable achievement. I can't wait to see what Roman is going to give us."

Harry is a U.K.-based senior staff writer at Live Science. He studied marine biology at the University of Exeter before training to become a journalist. He covers a wide range of topics including space exploration, planetary science, space weather, climate change, animal behavior and paleontology. His recent work on the solar maximum won "best space submission" at the 2024 Aerospace Media Awards and was shortlisted in the "top scoop" category at the NCTJ Awards for Excellence in 2023. He also writes Live Science's weekly Earth from space series.

#6303. At the Races: It's almost over

By Mary Ellen McIntire and Daniela Altimari

Voters are weighing in on whether to keep Republicans in control of Congress or give some power to Democrats amid mounting signs of dissatisfaction with President Donald Trump.

Democrats, who have expanded both the House and Senate battleground maps, are optimistic about their chances, while Republicans are hoping their base voters turn out — and help them defy the polls once again.

The expanded battleground map was evident in our final rankings of the most vulnerable senators, which included Sens. Roger Marshall of Kansas, Darline Graham of South Carolina and Cindy Hyde-Smith of Mississippi, three states that weren’t exactly expected to be part of the battleground at the beginning of the year.

Some of House Republicans’ best pickup opportunities come in districts that were redrawn in their favor, which is reflected in our final list of the most vulnerable House incumbents. Just two Democrats— Florida’s Darren Soto and Alabama’s Shomari Figures — rank among the 10 most endangered House members, while Republicans from the nation’s most competitive swing seats occupy most of the other spots.

Speaker Mike Johnson has spent the past several weeks crisscrossing the country hoping to save his narrow majority. He appeared Monday night with Rep. Jen Kiggans in the same Virginia district where Hakeem Jeffries, the top House Democrat, campaigned on Saturday. Earlier in the day, Johnson returned to Eastern North Carolina, home to a costly rematch between Democratic Rep. Don Davis and Republican Laurie Buckhout. Johnson also held a rally in a neighboring district that Trump would have carried by 14 points, a sign of GOP vulnerabilities even in conservative terrain. The speaker will begin Election Day in South Texas, where Republicans are hoping to flip two House seats while preserving another.

To mark Election Day, we’ve taken a look back over the past two years and identified 15 key moments that shaped the midterm campaign. We also have five questions we hope the election results will help us answer, including whether redistricting pays off for Republicans and how key constituencies that supported Trump and Republicans two years ago vote this time. And Roll Call photojournalists Bill Clark and Tom Williams shared the most memorable and striking images from their time on the trail this cycle.

Of course, it hasn’t been a quiet end to the campaign. Michigan Rep. Haley Stevens, who unsuccessfully sought the Democratic nomination for Senate this year, sent shockwaves across both parties Sunday when she appeared with and endorsed Republican Mike Rogers over primary rival Abdul El-Sayed.

That followed a major development in the Alaska Senate race, after The New York Times reported that aides to Democrat Mary Peltola helped recruit a candidate who shares a name with Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan. A federal judge on Sunday rejected a lawsuit from the Trump administration, which sought to delay certification of the Senate election if the incumbent Sullivan loses, as our colleague Michael Macagnone reported.

If your preferred way to watch results roll in is with a crowd, CQ Roll Call’s Nina Heller has a rundown of D.C. bars that will be airing election night results, many of which are offering deals on drinks and food.

Stay tuned to the Roll Call website for results and immediate takeaways. At the Races will be back in your inbox as usual on Thursday as we break the results down and look ahead to the next Congress.

#6302. A paleontologist hiking near Arches National Park may have found a new armored dinosaur

A new dinosaur bonebed discovered near Moab, Utah, may contain an unknown armored dinosaur species dating back 138 to 141 million years.

In mid-October 2026, the Utah Geological Survey (UGS) opened a new dinosaur excavation near Moab, in eastern Utah. The team calls the site the Ironstone Bonebed, and it lies north of Arches National Park.

The bonebed appears to contain the remains of a new species of armored dinosaur, the agency said. State Paleontologist Jim Kirkland is describing the animal and naming it in honor of Don DeBlieux, the Utah assistant state paleontologist.

The site is estimated at 138 million to 141 million years old. The UGS called it “currently tied as potentially the oldest Cretaceous dinosaur bonebed in North America.”

DeBlieux has said he spotted the first fossils while exploring the area on foot. They were a shoulder blade and an upper arm bone from an armored dinosaur.

He oversees the UGS field paleontology program and its fossil preparation lab. In 2002, he found a skull weathering out of sandstone near the middle of the Wahweap Formation, in southern Utah’s Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument.

That skull became the horned dinosaur Diabloceratops eatoni. DeBlieux spent more than 800 hours over two years removing the rock from around the bone.

Kirkland has said the crew has identified about four kinds of dinosaurs at the new site so far.

Kirkland, who has held his post since 1999, is known for naming numerous dinosaur species, most notably Utahraptor. After 25 years of working side by side with him, DeBlieux will retire at the end of 2026.

Geologically, the new locality is nearly equivalent to Doelling’s Bowl, a UGS site some six miles (10 kilometers) to the east.

DeBlieux also found Doelling’s Bowl, in 2005, when he came across the vertebrae and a hip bone of a dromaeosaurid, a raptor-like predator.

A 2012 study of Utah raptors named it Yurgovuchia doellingi and reported a bone bed covering tens of acres (at least several hectares).

Plant-eating iguanodonts, including one compared to Iguanacolossus, dominate it, with at least ten individuals. At least three polacanthine ankylosaurs, a group of armored dinosaurs, were also found there.

The bonebed lies in the lower Yellow Cat Member of the Cedar Mountain Formation, below a marker layer of calcrete. It yielded Mierasaurus bobyoungi, a long-necked sauropod descended from Jurassic turiasaurs of the Iberian Peninsula.

Kirkland and DeBlieux co-authored its 2017 description. By then, Doelling’s Bowl had also produced teeth from a large allosauroid predator and a new, still unnamed species of polacanthid ankylosaur.

“Ankylosaurs were so well protected that even their eyelids were armored,” Kirkland and Mark Loewen, then of the Utah Museum of Natural History, wrote in 2011.

At the time, the Cedar Mountain Formation had yielded more ankylosaur species than any other geologic formation in the world. Several more from it had been found but not yet described.

Gastonia burgei came from the basal Yellow Cat Member. It was closely related to Polacanthus foxi, from nearly age-equivalent rocks on England’s Isle of Wight.

Younger layers have produced other Cedar Mountain dinosaurs, including the ankylosaur Peloroplites cedrimontanus from the Ruby Ranch Member.

Utah’s first known nodosaurid, Animantarx ramaljonesi, was the first dinosaur discovered solely by technology. A radiological technician found it in 1994 by mapping low-level radiation across a quarry near the top of the formation.

Cedarpelta bilbyhallorum was then North America’s only known ankylosaurid from the Lower Cretaceous. Ankylosaurids are the branch of armored dinosaurs known for tail clubs and boxy skulls.

The UGS expects the new site to shed light on the transition from the Jurassic to the Cretaceous. A catastrophic event at the end of the Jurassic led to the near-complete extinction of Utah’s Morrison Formation dinosaurs, including Stegosaurus.

Across most of the western North American mountain belt, the gap between Jurassic and Cretaceous rocks spans 20 million to 25 million years.

In eastern Utah, microfossils, chemical signatures and uranium-lead dating of ancient soils cut it to five million to seven million years.

Kirkland, DeBlieux and two colleagues reported that revised dating in a 2025 conference abstract. In those rocks, an increase in larger coelurosaurs, a group of meat-eating dinosaurs, documents the extinction.

The ancient soils also point to a short wet interval after the drier Late Jurassic. Where Early Cretaceous wetlands formed in eastern Utah appears to have been controlled by movement of ancient salt deposits.

Kirkland has argued that the same salt tectonics explain why Utah’s oldest Cretaceous dinosaurs are restricted to northern Grand County.

As buried salt beds were squeezed into ridges, nearby ground subsided, and Lower Cretaceous sediments collected in the low areas.

Across much of the rest of North America, erosion was removing rock at the time. Salt movement peaked in the early Mesozoic, as reflected by the Salt Valley anticline at Arches National Park and the Moab fault.

The information was obtained from the Utah Geological Survey.

A new study supports a more nuanced approach to obesity diagnosis. Here's what to know.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Obesity is linked to a range of health problems ‪—‬ including heart disease, diabetes and early death ‪—‬ but it can be hard to know who is most at risk for these outcomes. Doctors and researchers often use body mass index (BMI) as a convenient tool to assess patients, but this metric does not account for individual differences in body composition, scientists have long argued.

"BMI misses a lot of information," Dr. Francesco Rubino, a professor of bariatric and metabolic surgery at King's College London, told Live Science.

Rubino recently chaired a team of 56 experts that was assembled to better define obesity and develop new diagnostic criteria for the condition. First proposed in January 2025, their new framework includes more body measurements beyond BMI and distinguishes between "preclinical" and "clinical" obesity.

Now, a new study published Wednesday (Nov. 11) in the journal Nature confirms that these new criteria could detect obesity with greater precision than BMI alone. In other words, with the new approach, more people would be accurately diagnosed with obesity and fewer people would be misdiagnosed than are with BMI alone.

Live Science spoke with Rubino and other experts to break down the new findings and learn what they mean for patients.

At the simplest level, obesity is excess body fat. There are special scans and exams that send weak electrical signals through the body to measure a person's body fat percentage directly, but criteria based on body measurements are more accessible across clinical settings.

BMI is the most common of these measurements, as it simply involves dividing a person's weight by their height squared. However, it does not account for individual differences in lean muscle mass or bone density.

BMI doesn't capture nuances and variation between patients, experts argue, and it limits what doctors can say about a given person's health risk.

Additionally, the different BMI categories — such as "overweight" and "obese" — don't carry the same risks for all patients. Certain racial and ethnic groups tend to experience health consequences, such as higher mortality rates, at different BMI levels than others do.

For a given patient being assessed for obesity, the proposed guidelines would suggest using at least one additional body measurement alongside BMI and having their doctor review their medical history for other signs of bodily or organ dysfunction.

The proposed body measurements are less influenced by a person's muscle mass or bone structure than BMI is. They include waist circumference, waist-to-hip ratio and waist-to-height ratio. Notably, because different ethnicities are associated with different fat distribution patterns in the body, the latest Nature study incorporated different waist circumference cutoffs based that varied by ethnicity.

In addition to these body measurements, the proposed criteria look at 18 conditions and signs of bodily or organ dysfunction that are related to obesity, such as cardiovascular diseases, joint pain and sleep apnea. (All 18 factors can be found detailed in this chart.)

Rubino and his colleagues — which together made up what's known as a Lancet Commission — defined "clinical obesity" as a disease state involving at least one of 18 forms of bodily dysfunction caused by excess fat tissue. Preclinical obesity, by contrast, is when a person is at risk of this disease state and may need interventions to avoid obesity-related dysfunction.

That means that two people with the same BMI, waist circumference and waist-to-height ratio may be classified differently, depending on whether they have other conditions. In the new study, between 77% and 91% of individuals with preclinical obesity did not progress to clinical obesity within 10 years, depending on the cohort analyzed.

This distinction can be complicated, though, as the diagnostic metrics for each form of dysfunction contain their own ambiguities.

"There needs to be more consensus on what's actually defining clinical obesity," said Dr. Aayush Visaria, an internal medicine instructor at Rutgers Robert Wood Johnson Medical School in New Jersey. Visaira was not involved in writing the new criteria but authored an analysis of the proposed measures.

The Lancet Commission argues that the categories of preclinical and clinical obesity could help doctors identify the people with the greatest need for treatment. The researchers tracked health outcomes using electronic health records from China, the United Kingdom, the United States and Spain, and they determined that their clinical obesity classification was better at flagging people's risk of death than BMI alone.

Changing the diagnostic criteria for obesity could, in turn, change who is recommended to receive weight-control medications.

They found no clear association between BMI and mortality risk, but clinical obesity was linked to a 69% greater risk of all-cause mortality, compared to no obesity.

The Lancet Commission's approach could drive a small net uptick in individuals diagnosed with obesity, according to the new study.

Under the current framework, "we are definitely missing some people who actually need obesity treatment but just did not meet the BMI criteria," said Dr. Jennifer Hwang, an instructor of medicine at the University of Chicago who has published her own analysis of the new criteria.

With the BMI-only approach, people with BMIs of 30 or higher are categorized as obese. With the new definition, some people with BMIs under 30 would be newly categorized as clinically obese, while a smaller group of people with high BMIs would suddenly not count as clinically obese, the Nature study predicted.

For instance, the former group might include people who have "overweight" BMIs but also have obesity-related dysfunction, while the latter group might include people with "obese" BMIs but without any dysfunction.

Overall, the new criteria would increase obesity prevalence by about 3.3% to 7.4%, the team predicted. The percentage varied depending on the group analyzed.

More research is needed to prove that the Lancet Commission's criteria would improve patient care and be practical to use in a clinical setting, Hwang said. She noted potential challenges in implementing both new aspects of the new framework. While the body measurements sound simple enough to use, clinicians would need training to perform them accurately.

Providers also may struggle with the new distinction between preclinical and clinical obesity. A 2025 analysis of the Lancet Commission framework noted that some patients who qualify for obesity medications under the Food and Drug Administration's guidelines may be recharacterized as having preclinical obesity and no longer receive a prescription.

Rubino and the rest of the Lancet Commission plan to continue validating their framework to see how it could best support personalized obesity treatment. For instance, they want to determine which forms of organ dysfunction are of greatest concern and develop a way of scoring each patient's level of risk.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

#6300. City crows let people get closer, but country crows can be bolder in their own way

City crows tolerate people better than rural crows, but unfamiliar objects near food can make them more cautious.

City crows let people get closer than rural crows do. But when researchers put a lamp base in a pile of peanuts, city crows were less likely than rural crows to take a peanut.

The study of American crows around Ithaca, New York, suggests that a crow’s fears are shaped by its past experience.

Two experiments were run by Dave Colucci and Anne Clark, biologists at Binghamton University. In the first experiment, objects were left next to food on crow territories.

In the second, Colucci walked toward crows and measured how close he got before they flew.

The evidence for greater wariness in city crows comes from a single object.

It also comes from only one of the three measures used by the team. In addition, the city sites were closer to suburbs than to a downtown.

In crows, Colucci said, fear of anything new exists side by side with a great deal of curiosity. The fear does not always prevail, he added, so a new opportunity is sometimes seized.

Ten crow families were chosen from parking lots, parks, and dead-end streets near Ithaca.

Another 10 families lived on farmland and natural areas in the nearby town of Dryden.

American crows live in family groups that share a territory.

On most days of the week, Colucci scattered two cups of unsalted peanuts in the shell on each territory.

The same spot was used each time. He continued until the family had fed there three times in a row.

A single object was then set in the middle of the peanuts on four separate mornings. The crows were filmed by a hidden camcorder. Colucci watched from at least 164 feet (50 meters) away.

The trials were run in July and August of 2019 and 2020. Four objects were used: a rock, an ear of corn in its husk, a takeout box, and a lamp base.

The box was paperboard, and the lamp base was made to look like wood.

Every crow was expected to find the lamp base new. Bright colors, shiny surfaces and sharp angles are typical of human-made things.

These features are probably better known to crows living in cities. None of them was present on the lamp base.

When only peanuts were offered, nearly every crow that came within about 10 feet (3 meters) took one.

The team estimated the probability of eating at 99% for such city crows and 97% for rural crows.

With the lamp base in place, the estimated probability dropped to 76% among rural crows and 53% among city crows.

Wariness of new things is called neophobia by biologists. By this measure, the city crows had more of it.

The other two measures concerned only the first crow of each family to arrive and to eat. Their timing was compared with that on days when no object was present.

With the lamp base in place, the first crow to arrive and the first to eat were about as quick in city families as in rural ones.

To Colucci and Clark, that result suggests both places have some bold crows.

Results from earlier experiments on city and country birds have not agreed with one another. Lower wariness in cities has been reported in some of them, higher wariness or no difference in others.

Colucci and Clark wrote that some of those experiments used human-made objects, which city animals may know better.

A second idea was tested with the corn and the takeout box. An ear of corn should be ordinary to a crow that lives beside farm fields.

That ear of corn should seem strange to a crow whose home is beside a parking lot. For a takeout box, the reverse should be true.

More rural crows were put off by the takeout box, and more city crows were put off by the corn.

The team could be confident of that pattern only in the share of crows that ate. In how quickly the first crow arrived or ate, the pattern was too weak to be sure of.

A one-mile (1.6 km) stretch of road was also walked in each setting once a week for three weeks. Every human-made object was recorded.

A total of 341 objects was counted, with 169 along the city road and 172 along the rural road. A typical object nevertheless remained in place for a shorter time along the city road.

Objects turned over faster along the city road, but city crows were still more reluctant to eat beside the lamp base.

City crows are thus exposed to a constant turnover of objects, yet their wariness of new things hasn’t been reduced.

The authors suggested that most litter may be treated by city crows as one category.

In the second experiment, crows were approached on foot by Colucci 145 times over three summers. These approaches took place across upstate New York and Quebec.

During some approaches his gaze was fixed directly on the crow. During others his whole face was tilted toward the ground. A camera on his chest streamed video to a phone in his hand so that his direction could be maintained.

The average crow took flight while he was still about 150 feet (45 meters) away. A distance of 33 feet (10 meters) or less was reached in only eight approaches.

Closer approaches were tolerated by city crows than by rural crows, as is usual for city animals. Rural crows fled from far away regardless of the direction of his gaze.

In the most built-up areas, crows let him get about 82 feet (25 meters) closer when his face was down. The authors wrote that the true effect of his gaze could be either small or large.

A similar but smaller effect was found in a 2013 study of crows in Seattle. To the authors’ knowledge, a difference between two populations in the use of human gaze had not been shown before.

Hunting is one possible explanation for the behavior of the rural crows.

Within city limits in New York, crows may not be hunted. Hunting them in rural areas is legal from September 1 to March 31.

The rural response was described by Clark, an associate professor emerita of biological sciences, as a blunt defense against predators. “Don’t take any chances, don’t stop to assess; let’s just be safe,” she said.

Clark added that such a habit would not work for city crows. People pass by too often in a city for a crow to take flight every time.

The peanut experiment also provided evidence of greater caution among rural crows. With no object present, the first city crow reached the peanuts at about four times the rural rate.

The number of people living within about half a mile (800 meters) gave the best prediction of a crow’s reaction. When smaller or larger circles were used, the predictions were poorer.

A circle of that size is larger than the territory held by a crow family.

It was suggested by the authors that crows average their experience of people over a wide area. They then adjust to the person approaching them.

Individual people who have threatened them are also remembered by crows.

The study leaves open whether city crows gain any advantage from being more cautious around an unfamiliar object. Two possible explanations have been put forward by the authors.

One is that cities contain dangers which cannot be predicted even by a crow that knows its neighborhood well.

The other concerns the crows that first settled in towns about 70 years ago. Those birds may have had little fear of new things, with caution proving useful only later.

It is also uncertain whether the lamp base was equally new to both groups. Its shape is perfectly symmetrical, and such symmetry is rare in natural objects.

City crows might therefore have found it more familiar than the team had intended.

Were that the case, the authors wrote, the difference between city and rural crows could be underestimated.

Future research could test whether wariness slows crows down when new problems have to be solved. It could also test whether cities hold more unfamiliar threats.

For comparisons of urban wildlife with rural animals, a first step was recommended by Colucci and Clark. They wrote that the objects present in each environment ought to be identified first.

The full study was published in the journal Behavioral Ecology.

#6298. Peregrine falcons are much smarter than we thought, using fake attacks to tire out their prey

A new study reveals that peregrine falcons deliberately use false attacks against their prey, making them much easier to catch later on.

When a peregrine falcon dives at a flock of birds and comes away with nothing, it looks like a failed hunt.

At one bay in British Columbia, some of those failed hunts may never have been meant to succeed. A study of peregrines and small shorebirds called Pacific dunlins suggests that early attacks send the flock into the air too soon.

A few hours later, the dunlins are often back on the ground, and that’s when the falcons make the most kills. If the researchers are right, the early attacks make the dunlins easier to catch later.

Ron Ydenberg and two colleagues at Simon Fraser University’s Centre for Wildlife Ecology published the analysis in October 2023. Their case rests on the timing of flights and kills at a single bay.

Predators are “imagined as clever in novels and movies, like the velociraptors in Jurassic Park,” Ydenberg said. But biologists who work from evidence, he added, tend to doubt such ideas.

Between 20,000 and 40,000 dunlins spend the winter at Boundary Bay, feeding on mudflats that the tide covers twice a day.

As the tide rises, the dunlins have to feed closer to the shoreline, where a falcon can ambush them from cover.

Like other shorebirds, dunlins used to rest on shore at high tide. During the 1990s, as more peregrines wintered at the bay, the dunlins largely stopped.

Now they often spend daytime high tides circling in a loose flock high over the bay. Almost every dunlin the falcons were seen to kill was outside that flock.

But circling takes energy. On days when the dunlins made these flights, they averaged 3.1 hours in the air.

By the team’s estimate, the three most dangerous hours for a dunlin on the ground run from one hour before high tide to two hours after.

On those days, the dunlins spent 89% of the hour before high tide in the air and 95% of the hour after.

But in the second hour after high tide, the dunlins were in the air only 44% of the time. The falcons did best in that hour, making 43 of the 139 kills recorded in 905 hours of watching.

The dunlins had done a lot of their flying earlier, more than an hour before high tide, when the danger was low. Compared with the safest schedule, their flights started early and ended early.

To explain the early flights, the researchers used a 2007 model inspired by killer whales hunting sea lions.

In that model, a predator can gain by making attacks that have little chance of success. The prey still has to flee, then make up the lost feeding time by taking more risks later.

At Boundary Bay, that would mean falcons attacking before high tide to send the dunlins up early.

The team couldn’t test the idea, because even experienced observers can’t easily tell a serious attack from a half-hearted one.

In data the team hasn’t published, peregrine hunts at the bay peak two to four hours before high tide, hours before the kills do.

The records come from Dick Dekker’s winter visits to Boundary Bay between 1994 and 2012.

Falcon attacks were recorded on 151 days. The dunlin flocks were timed from dawn to dusk on 34 days, and they made their high-tide flights on 23 of them.

The authors wrote that Dekker became “the world’s foremost watcher of wild falcons.”

The authors offered two other explanations.

Less skilled falcons might be the ones attacking early, while skilled falcons hunt just after high tide. Or the dunlins might land early because feeding is especially good on a falling tide.

To test those explanations, researchers would have to track individual falcons closely, Ydenberg said. That doesn’t look practical at Boundary Bay, where the falcons weren’t marked.

He added that the idea could be tested in other predators and their prey, where the same logic should apply.

The full study was published in the journal Frontiers in Ethology.

#6296. New species of flying frog discovered in a mountain pond called Coca-Cola Lake

Scientists identified a new flying frog species in Indonesia's mountains. DNA, body features, and calls helped confirm the discovery.

A seasonal pond sits high in the mountains of Sulawesi in Indonesia. Climbers know it as Coca-Cola Lake.

A new species of flying frog has been collected there and it has been named Rhacophorus kurniatiae.

Body measurements barely separate this frog from its closest relative. The difference shows up when the animals breed. The relative builds a nest of foam.

The new species leaves its eggs in a loose mass of jelly instead.

No other flying frog on Sulawesi has been documented laying its eggs in a loose, irregular mass of jelly.

The frogs were collected on November 18, 2011, by Wahyu Trilaksono. Trilaksono is a herpetologist with Indonesia’s National Research and Innovation Agency.

Four colleagues from Indonesia and the United States joined Trilaksono in describing the new species.

Thirty-one adults were collected in total. Every one of them came from that single pond.

Males measure 1.7 to 1.8 inches (43 to 47 millimeters) from snout to rump. Females are larger at 1.9 to 2.2 inches (49 to 57 millimeters). That is roughly the length of an AA battery.

The pond is found 6,155 feet (1,876 meters) up in the Mekongga Mountains. This range lies on the southeastern arm of Sulawesi.

The pond is not natural. It was created by a logging company as a place to store logs.

Rain and seepage fill the pond for part of the year. No stream runs into it or out of it. During the dry season, it shrinks to a few pools and exposed moss.

Loggers worked these mountains before they became a protected forest in 1994.

The 2011 trip belonged to a series of expeditions run for the ICBG Indonesia Project.

The project was a biological inventory of the mountains. Its Indonesian and American partners included the Museum of Wildlife and Fish Biology at the University of California, Davis.

The field team was led by Alan Hitch, who is a research affiliate at that museum. Hitch recalled reaching the pond on the way up the mountain. Green frogs were all over it.

“You don’t really see frogs in big congregations like that,” Hitch said.

Biologists describe an event like this as explosive breeding. Adults gather suddenly along the edge of the water for a brief burst of mating. Heavy rain appears to trigger it at Coca-Cola Lake.

Asian flying frogs are tree frogs. Their name comes from gliding, which is done on large webbed feet. A foam nest is where the typical flying frog lays its eggs.

Rhacophorus boeadii is the closest relative of the new frog, and it breeds that way. Scientists named it last year from mountains in central Sulawesi.

Coca-Cola Lake is shared with a third flying frog. Its eggs are packed into compact balls of gel.

R. kurniatiae does neither of these things. Its eggs are laid straight into an irregular mass of jelly that contains no foam. The mass hangs above the water or is loosely attached to whatever is nearby.

The frogs showed no preference for any plant species or leaf shape. The embryos stay inside the jelly until they become tadpoles.

The authors wrote that the habit may reflect an adaptation to water that comes and goes.

The team needed to check whether the pond frogs were a species of their own. Twenty-eight body measurements were taken on preserved specimens for that purpose.

The 81 specimens came from six flying frog species found on Sulawesi and nearby islands.

Eighteen of them were the new frog. Its females were compared with R. boeadii females. None of the 28 measurements differed reliably between them.

Three measurements did differ among males. These were eye width, the length of the first toe and the width of the pad on the fourth toe.

The DNA was close as well. One stretch of mitochondrial DNA differed by 2.19% to 2.43% between the two species. The gap between the new frog and the other four species was about 4% to 5.7%.

Andrew Engilis Jr. is the curator of the UC Davis museum and a co-author of the study.

Species can sometimes “look the same, but their behavior is different and their genetics are different,” Engilis said.

Animals like these are known to biologists as cryptic species.

A few features do set the new frog apart on close inspection. A small flap of skin is present on each heel. A fold of skin runs along its limbs and its third finger carries more webbing.

The call of one male was recorded on a digital camera at 6:40 p.m. It lasted about 1.4 seconds.

Four notes made up the call. A single short pulse opened it. Three notes of three to five pulses each came next. The call of R. boeadii is a single note.

The team also wanted to compare the call with that of the third flying frog at the lake.

Call measurements published in 2015 by Hellen Kurniati were used for this. She was a long-serving herpetologist at Indonesia’s Museum Zoologicum Bogoriense.

The new species has been named in honor of Kurniati. She died before it was described.

Only one recording from one male was good enough to be analyzed. The authors wrote that the opening note may be that male’s own variation. It may not be a trait of the whole species.

R. boeadii is known from two mountain regions in central Sulawesi. R. kurniatiae has been found only on the southeastern arm.

Two major faults run close to the line between those ranges. Faults are long breaks in Earth’s crust where blocks of land slide past each other.

The authors suggested that the faults may have acted as barriers, splitting an ancestral frog population in two.

A similar pattern is seen in the flying lizards and macaques of Sulawesi.

Closely related species live on different arms of the island. The idea has not been tested for the frogs. More genetic analysis will be needed for that, the authors wrote.

So far, researchers have found the frog only at Coca-Cola Lake.

This raises potential conservation concerns, the authors wrote. They pointed to pressure from farming, deforestation and climate variability across Sulawesi.

The amphibians of Sulawesi have been studied less than those of Java, Sumatra and Borneo.

Thirty-three amphibian species are known from the region and six of them are flying frogs. The researchers expect the true number to be higher.

Several species have been added by recent fieldwork. One of them is a fanged frog that nests on land.

Engilis said the region is a candidate for national park status. Continued species discovery could help speed that process, Engilis added.

The authors called for targeted surveys of the island’s mountain habitats.

Other high ponds in the Mekongga Mountains could be surveyed in the future. Such work could show whether Coca-Cola Lake is the frog’s only home.

The full study was published in the journal Zootaxa.
