#6295. Your favorite foods may soon contain less sodium

Most of the sodium Americans eat comes from packaged and prepared foods. A new FDA rule could help cut sodium at the source.

Starting in December, a new FDA rule will let food makers replace some or all of the added salt in products such as bread, cheese, and canned vegetables.

That could make a difference because Americans get more than 70% of their sodium from packaged and prepared foods.

One option is a salt blend that replaces some sodium chloride with potassium chloride. Few Americans use salt substitutes at home.

Daniel W. Jones, a professor emeritus at the University of Mississippi School of Medicine, chaired the committee that wrote the 2025 U.S. blood pressure guideline, which recommends potassium-enriched salt substitutes.

In the journal JAMA, Jones said the FDA rule could help reduce sodium intake.

Table salt is sodium chloride. In a potassium-enriched salt substitute, some of that sodium chloride is replaced with potassium chloride.

Potassium chloride is a salt made with potassium in place of sodium.

According to Jones, a blend of 25% to 30% potassium chloride is recommended. A higher proportion is not accepted by American tastes, which is part of the reason.

Stores sell a wider range, from blends of equal parts to pure potassium chloride. The equal-part products are usually labeled “light” salt.

Wanpen Vongpatanasin of UT Southwestern Medical Center directs the center’s section on hypertension.

Vongpatanasin noted that blood vessels are affected by sodium and potassium in opposite ways. Sodium makes arteries stiffer, while potassium generally relaxes the blood vessels.

“You get a twofer with a potassium-enriched salt substitute,” Jones said.

A person who switches consumes less sodium and more potassium, he added. Both changes are considered healthy.

Blood pressure is measured in millimeters of mercury, the units used in a reading such as 120 over 80. Jones noted that a blend with 25% potassium chloride lowers blood pressure by 5 to 7 points on average.

The top number is lowered by 8 to 10 points with most blood pressure drugs, he added.

Jones also explained the significance of such a drop for people with high blood pressure. Their risk of heart attack, heart failure, stroke, and kidney disease is reduced with every 10 points lost.

The reduction was estimated by Jones at about 15% to 20%.

The substitute was tested in a trial that was published in 2021 and conducted in 600 villages in rural China. The 20,995 participants had either survived a stroke or were at least 60 years old with high blood pressure.

The villages that received the potassium blend were selected at random and the remaining villages continued to use regular salt. One quarter of the blend consisted of potassium chloride.

The participants were followed for almost five years. About 29 strokes a year were recorded among every 1,000 people who cooked with the blend.

Roughly 34 strokes a year were recorded among every 1,000 people who used regular salt.

Deaths from any cause were also less frequent in the villages that used the blend. Blood pressure differed less than Jones’s average. The top number was about 3 points lower in villages using the blend.

Vongpatanasin and her colleagues examined how many people use these products. A national health survey of about 37,000 U.S. adults was analyzed for that purpose.

In the survey years 2013 and 2014, 5.4% of adults said they used a salt substitute. No other survey round recorded a higher share. By 2017 to 2020, that figure was 2.5%.

Use was low throughout and later fell by more than half. A substitute was rarely used by patients being treated for high blood pressure, either. Fewer than 1 in 10 of them reported it.

Taste is one reason. Vongpatanasin noted that potassium chloride can taste bitter or briny. The effect is stronger in larger amounts and for people who prefer heavily salted food.

She advised cooking with the substitute, along with other seasonings, instead of sprinkling it on cooked food. People become accustomed to the taste in about two weeks, Jones said.

Cost was also identified as a barrier in the 2025 guideline in which the World Health Organization suggested the switch. The guideline noted that the blends can cost more than regular salt and that public awareness is low.

A small consulting arrangement with the drugmaker AstraZeneca has been disclosed by Vongpatanasin.

She is also named as a co-inventor on a University of Texas patent for potassium magnesium citrate. No revenue has been generated by that patent to date.

Only a small part of dietary sodium is changed when a household switches completely to a substitute.

Roughly 11% of the sodium eaten by Americans is added during cooking or at the table. That estimate was reported by the FDA.

Average intake in the United States has been put at about 3,400 milligrams a day by the same agency. About 2,300 milligrams of sodium are contained in one teaspoon of table salt.

Federal dietary advice sets that amount as the daily limit, and the 2025 heart guideline aims for less than 1,500.

The recommendation of the WHO applies only to salt that people add themselves.

This limit was explained by Rain Yamamoto, a scientist in the nutrition and food safety department of the agency.

The advice is most relevant in countries where most salt is consumed through home cooking, Yamamoto said. The United States does not belong to that group of countries.

“Standards of identity” are maintained by the FDA for foods such as bread, sour cream, and mayonnaise.

The ingredients that a product needs before it can carry such a name are listed in each standard. Salt was allowed or required under 139 of those standards while a substitute was not permitted.

In October, the agency issued a final rule that lifted the restriction on substitutes in all 139 standards. Some or all of the salt in those foods may be replaced when the rule takes effect in December.

The affected foods include mayonnaise, salad dressing, many cheeses, canned vegetables, canned fish, bread, and pasta.

Potassium-enriched salt is not suitable for every patient. People with chronic kidney disease, especially end-stage disease, should not use potassium-based substitutes.

Other types of substitute such as herb blends can still be used by those patients.

Blood potassium can also be raised by several kinds of medicine. Some diuretics are included in that group and are commonly known as water pills.

Two common families of blood pressure drugs are included as well. These are the ACE inhibitors such as enalapril and the angiotensin receptor blockers such as losartan.

A doctor should be consulted first by patients on those drugs so that blood potassium can be monitored.

The WHO’s recommendation excludes pregnant women and children because evidence in these groups is limited.

Serious events linked to high blood potassium occurred at similar rates in both groups.

However, the trial had excluded people with serious kidney disease and people who were taking potassium supplements. Blood potassium was also not tested routinely during the trial.

No new labeling requirements were added by the FDA rule, which makes those exclusions relevant to packaged food.

A required warning about high potassium on those foods was declined by the agency. Potassium chloride will still be listed by name among the ingredients.

Use of a substitute is allowed by the FDA rule but no manufacturer is obliged to change a recipe.

No minimum level of replacement was set and no penalties were listed for companies that keep regular salt.

The rule leaves the choice of substitute to manufacturers.

Potassium chloride is mentioned in the rule as one example beside yeast extracts, MSG, and amino acids. Sodium in bread or cheese could therefore be lowered by a manufacturer with no potassium added.

A related question was left open by the 2021 trial in China. The blend was used for home cooking in that trial and people who ate most meals elsewhere had been excluded.

Packaged food that already contains the blend was not examined in that trial.

Concern about the rest of the diet was expressed by Sotiria Everett, who is a dietitian at Stony Brook University. Little effect is expected from cooking with a substitute if deli meats, cheese, and bacon are still eaten, she said.

A fruit or vegetable at every meal was recommended by Everett because potassium intake is then increased naturally.

The rule was published on October 13 and takes effect 60 days later in December. A report on progress toward the voluntary sodium targets of the FDA is also expected later in 2026.

The decision to use potassium salt in pursuit of those targets will be made by each manufacturer.

The full report was published in the journal JAMA.

Scientists have discovered that a known mushroom, Galerina indica, contains both psychedelic chemicals and deadly toxins.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A tiny brown mushroom found in Florida's swamps is the first known fungus to contain both psilocybin, the chemical compound in psychedelic mushrooms; and amatoxin, the poisonous substance in the world's deadliest mushrooms.

The species, Galerina indica, has been nicknamed the "dark magic mushroom" and was characterized in a study published Wednesday (Nov. 11) in the journal Current Biology.

"There is no species of mushroom anywhere, in any group, that has been known to produce both at the same time," study first author Andrew Kunik, a fungal biology researcher at the University of Florida, told Live Science. "So it's quite remarkable."

Exactly why the dark magic mushroom has evolved to contain these two compounds is unclear, but the authors told Live Science that they may give the fungus a powerful defense against being eaten.

The ability to produce either psychedelic or toxic chemicals has evolved multiple times across fungal lineages. A process called horizontal gene transfer, which is widespread among fungi, has played a part in that process.

In horizontal gene transfer an organism passes new genetic material to another, as opposed to vertical gene transfer, in which a parent passes genetic material to offspring. It can lead to unexpected genetic combinations and, in bacteria, plays a key role in the development of antibiotic resistance.

The tiny mushrooms seem to have acquired both psychedelic and toxic compounds via horizontal gene transfer.

Some of the world's deadliest mushrooms, from the Amanita genus, stop cells from producing proteins and can cause death through liver failure. Past work has shown these mushrooms shared the ability to produce their poisonous amatoxins via horizontal gene transfer with mushrooms from the unrelated genera Galerina and Lepiota. Some mushrooms have acquired the ability to produce psilocybin via horizontal gene transfer as well.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

But Kunik and colleagues weren't looking for specific chemicals when they began hunting for Galerina mushrooms in the swamps of Florida; they just wanted to learn more about the mushrooms' chemical makeup, as not all Florida Galerina mushrooms had been characterized before.

To find them both together in one mushroom, I never expected to find that.

They collected five specimens from Galerina, a genus that contains over 300 species worldwide, many of which are poisonous. Among the samples they collected were small G. indica specimens that grew on moss-covered palm trunks. The largest mushrooms were only about 0.2 inches (0.5 centimeters) tall, with caps up to about 0.1 inches (0.25 cm) wide.

Chemical analyses revealed that the dark magic mushroom contained both psilocybin and amatoxins, including one amatoxin that had never been documented in mushrooms. The new amatoxin wasn't wholly unexpected, given that other species of Galerina produce closely related amatoxins, Kunik said.

The production of psilocybin alongside the amatoxins was more of a surprise for the research team.

"To find them both together in one mushroom, I never expected to find that," study co-author Matthew E. Smith, a plant pathologist at the University of Florida, told Live Science. "We were shocked."

To understand how the tiny, deadly mushroom acquired its mind-altering, liver-poisoning abilities, the team compared the genes of G. indica with those of other psilocybin-producing mushrooms, finding the genes shared a common evolutionary origin — even though the mushrooms themselves are distantly related.

Scanning electron microscopy image of the spores from the “dark magic mushroom”.

The researchers also found G. indica’s psilocybin-producing genes are arranged in a different order than in other psilocybin-producing fungi, which suggests the gene cluster was rearranged during its evolutionary history, a clue that horizontal gene transfer happened.

G. indica seems to have acquired the ability to produce psilocybin via horizontal gene transfer from unrelated fungi about 15.5 million years ago, based on reconstructions of Galerina’s evolutionary history from DNA analysis, Smith said. However, it’s possible that psilocybin-producing genes entered the lineage through two separate horizontal gene transfer events, possibly as recently as 6 million years ago, Kunik noted. Collecting and sequencing more Galerina specimens could help untangle their evolutionary history.

The findings are surprising, said Hannah Reynolds, a fungal ecologist at Western Connecticut State University who was not involved with the new research. "What was exciting about this paper was seeing both of these [compounds] present, seeing that this gene cluster jumped in, got rearranged, maybe came in twice — it's very cool," Reynolds told Live Science.

The ability to produce two types of incapacitating chemicals could form a powerful defense against being eaten, because organisms that would normally eat them would have difficulty evolving defenses against both, Kunik speculated.

But the idea that this duo of compounds prevents the mushroom from being eaten is just a hypothesis. To buttress that idea, further research might tweak the genes of the dark magic mushroom to observe how removing one compound affects the species' role in the food web, Kunik suggested.

Tropical and subtropical mushrooms are historically understudied, so there is likely much more incredible fungal diversity right under our feet, Smith said.

Kunik et al. (2026). "The 'dark magic mushroom' co-produces amatoxins and psilocybin." Current Biology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2026.10.041

Olivia Ferrari is a New York City-based freelance journalist with a background in research and science communication. Olivia has lived and worked in the U.K., Costa Rica, Panama and Colombia. Her writing focuses on wildlife, environmental justice, climate change, and social science.

#6291. America’s biggest data centers use nearly as much electricity as an entire state

A study estimates that 403 major U.S. data centers used 82 terawatt-hours of electricity in a year, with natural gas and coal supplying more than half.

Every backed-up photo, every chatbot answer and every streamed show lives somewhere called the cloud, which sounds like nowhere at all. It is a set of windowless warehouses.

At the high end of the estimate, 403 of the largest U.S. data centers together used nearly as much electricity in a year as Indiana uses statewide.

More than half of that electricity came from burning gas and coal.

A team led by the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and the Harvard Data Science Initiative mapped 403 of these buildings, known as hyperscale data centers.

The researchers then estimated what each one drew from the grid between May 2024 and April 2025.

The totals are estimates built from each building’s electrical capacity, not meter readings.

“Data centers are growing incredibly fast, driven largely by AI, and decisions about where to build them and how to power them are being made right now,” said lead author Gianluca Guidi, a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics.

“But there’s very little facility-level information about their environmental footprint.”

“Our study helps fill that gap,” Guidi added.

Hyperscale data centers are the largest class of data center, the kind that runs cloud services and trains big AI models. The buildings in the sample had an average electrical capacity of about 40 megawatts.

The team started with 675 candidate sites from a commercial database and kept the 403 it could confirm. Each address was matched to a rooftop and its footprint checked against OpenStreetMap.

Then the researchers looked at satellite and aerial images for the signs of a data center: big uniform roofs, cooling equipment and a substation next door.

Virginia had 142 of the 403, more than any other state. Oregon had 56 and Ohio 38.

No data center runs at its full rated capacity every hour, and the companies don’t publish their real loads. So the team multiplied each facility’s capacity by the hours in a year and by a load factor.

The researchers ran four versions of that factor, from a light load to one meant to bracket heavy AI training.

Across the four versions, the 403 facilities used an estimated 68 to 99 terawatt-hours of electricity over the year. The central estimate is about 82 terawatt-hours, or roughly 1.8% of all the electricity the country used.

Indiana, Michigan and Tennessee each use about 100 terawatt-hours a year. So at the high end these warehouses matched a whole state, and even the central estimate covers most of one state’s use.

The central figure is about 3.6 times a 2021 estimate of what hyperscale centers used in 2018. Projections of AI’s appetite for electricity look ahead; this study counts the buildings that exist now.

To work out where the electricity came from, and the power emissions behind it, the team assigned each data center to its regional grid operator.

The team then allocated the data centers’ electricity demand across power plants in each region based on how much electricity each plant generated.

The plant-by-plant generation and emissions figures came from the Environmental Protection Agency.

On that basis, 53.9% of the electricity came from fossil fuels: 38.2% from natural gas and 15.2% from coal.

Nuclear plants supplied 20.9%, and hydro, wind, solar, biomass and geothermal together supplied 25.3%. Nuclear and renewables together fell short of half.

The result was about 25.7 million metric tons (28.3 million U.S. tons) of carbon dioxide under the central version, and 21 to 31 million metric tons across all four.

A 2021 study estimated that U.S. hyperscale data centers were responsible for greenhouse gas emissions equivalent to about 10.5 million metric tons of carbon dioxide in 2018.

Virginia alone accounted for about 21 terawatt-hours, roughly a quarter of the total. Oregon followed with about 11, Ohio with about 9 and Iowa with about 7.

Virginia, Oregon, Ohio and Iowa together made up more than half of the electricity use, so the industry is heavily concentrated.

Oregon’s data centers drew more electricity than Ohio’s. Yet Oregon’s were tied to about 1.3 million metric tons of carbon dioxide and Ohio’s to 2.9 million, because Oregon’s grid runs far cleaner.

The fuel mix behind each state’s grid decides the carbon.

Virginia’s data centers were tied to about 7 million metric tons, the most of any state.

PJM, the grid operator serving Virginia, oversaw the region with the highest data center electricity demand. Its territory spans parts of 13 states and the District of Columbia.

There, about 60% of the attributed electricity came from fossil fuels and 33% from nuclear plants.

The method gives each data center the average fuel mix of its regional power grid. It doesn’t trace which plant physically fed which building.

It also doesn’t count the renewable power contracts some operators sign, unless that power shows up in the regional mix. The authors wrote that the numbers describe the grid, not any company’s performance.

Measured that way, the data centers’ electricity was slightly cleaner than the national average: about 314 grams of carbon dioxide per kilowatt-hour against 348 for the country.

About 23% of the demand, though, sat in regions dirtier than that average.

The data also can’t separate AI work from ordinary cloud computing inside a building. And the 272 candidate sites the team couldn’t verify were left out, so the totals likely run low for the industry as a whole.

Guidi said the picture has already moved on.

“The data center boom hasn’t slowed down since our study period ended in April 2025. New facilities have been built, existing campuses have expanded, and demand for AI computing continues to grow,” he said.

The researchers estimated electricity use and carbon dioxide emissions.

The team plans to examine the health effects next, according to study co-author Francesca Dominici, director of the Harvard Data Science Initiative.

“The fossil fuel power plants in the regional electricity systems associated with this demand also release other pollutants, such as fine particulate matter, nitrogen oxides, and sulfur dioxide, that are directly linked to heart and lung disease and premature death,” Dominici said.

The people who breathe those pollutants live near the power plants, which may be far from any data center.

Earth.com has covered the industry’s other local footprints, from heat zones around server farms to the one in four data centers in water-stressed regions.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Sustainability.

#6290. In California’s Central Valley, Democrats hope to harvest fruits of Proposition 50

By Sean Campbell, Nicholas Corral, Jules Cox, Aden Max Juarez, Caitlin Roehmholdt, Jose Trejo and Maybeline Tucker

BAKERSFIELD, Calif. — In a final get-out-the-vote push Monday, California’s two U.S. senators joined Randy Villegas at a labor union headquarters in the Central Valley district that could be critical to Democrats’ attempts to win back control of the House.

The 22nd District, spanning farmland from north of Fresno to south of Bakersfield, was redrawn via Proposition 50 to weaken six-term Republican Rep. David Valadao’s chance of reelection.

Valadao, who lost his seat once in 2018 during a Democratic takeover in President Donald Trump’s first term, is facing an even tougher environment now thanks to redistricting, high prices and the war in Iran. Inside Elections lists the race as a Toss-up.

“This is still very much a battleground district for California and for the country,” Democratic Sen. Alex Padilla told reporters after the rally Monday morning. “That's why you see the level of commitment from so many volunteers knocking on doors, making the phone calls, getting out the vote.”

Valadao has defied the odds before. He won the seat back in 2020 after losing by less than 1,000 votes in 2018 and has held it since. He is the only congressional Republican who voted to impeach Trump in 2021 who is still serving in the House. Trump won the counties in the 22nd District in 2024, but under the new lines, the district would only have gone for Trump by 1.5 percentage points, one reason why party and labor leaders made the trip Monday in a final push.

Villegas, a mechanic and progressive college professor, wore Converse and cheered as speaker after speaker proclaimed he would be the winner once votes are counted in California.

Introducing himself as the Robin to Padilla’s Batman, Democratic Sen. Adam B. Schiff said Californians “need a champion like Randy in Congress.” He egged on the crowd: “Are you so over David Valadao?”

Padilla, center, and Schiff, right, campaigned for Villegas on Monday. (USC Annenberg Media)

The senators are not the only big names to stump in the district. In September and October, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., as well as House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., appeared in the Central Valley. When asked, Villegas pushed back against the notion that his race was only competitive because of the favorably redrawn district.

“This is a district that we would’ve been competitive in regardless,” Villegas told reporters after the morning canvass kickoff. “Our message is one that has resonated across the political spectrum.”

Addressing the crowd in both English and Spanish, Villegas dropped a few curse words to punctuate his get-out-the-vote messaging. He told the labor activists gathered in the standing-room-only rally that when their sunscreen and sweat dripped in their eyes while canvassing later, they should remember, “That is the pain David Valadao and Republicans are going to be feeling.”

Cathy Abernathy, a Republican consultant and prominent GOP activist in Bakersfield, said Villegas is “too far” left for the Central Valley, but she stopped short of saying she was confident Valadao could win. She also criticized Prop 50 and the way Democrats redrew the lines to break up cities and counties and said she would support national reform of the redistricting process.

“David Valadao, he's resilient. He's a fighter. He has constantly gone against the odds,” said Matthew Martin, chair of the Kern County Young Republicans, taking a moment to chat with reporters after sending get-out-the-vote text messages in the Republican Party headquarters in Bakersfield. If it wasn’t for Prop 50 shifting the makeup of the district so dramatically, “I think this would be more of a slam dunk for David Valadao,” he said.

Martin predicted that Latinos age 45 and under would be the deciding factor in the election. The district is 74 percent Latino, according to 2020 Census data.

Prop 50, pushed by Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom and approved by voters last year, 64 percent to 36 percent, redrew the 22nd to make it easier for a Democrat to win. Valadao's own home base of Hanford, where his family owns a dairy farm, was carved out of his district.

Valadao posted a photo of himself on Facebook dropping his ballot in a drop box in Hanford. His campaign did not respond to multiple requests from reporters seeking to cover activity on the ground.

Instead, Valadao joined California Republican gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton at a rally last Thursday. He also posted on his Facebook page about celebrating the birthday of the founder of the Sikh religion, Guru Nanak. At the event with Johnson last month, the congressman said, “We’ve got a lot on the line. We’ve got to keep fighting all the way towards the end.”

The district is at the epicenter of multiple nationwide fights: It saw early immigration enforcement raids during Trump’s second term, and changes to Medicaid through the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” are expected to have a major impact. Roughly six in 10 residents in the district are enrolled in the state’s Medicaid program, known in California as Medi-Cal.

For Republican voter Kevin Caid, Trump was top of mind as he dropped off his ballot at California State University, Bakersfield. He lives in the neighboring district represented by Republican Rep. Vince Fong. Caid voted Republican down the ballot, saying his top issues were taxes and keeping a nuclear weapon out of Iranian hands.

“If gas is high, you know, that’s the price it takes,” Caid said.

Linda Fiddler, a canvasser for the Villegas campaign, is a long-time campaign volunteer in the district, having worked on Democratic campaigns since 2010. She described Villegas as a “game changer” compared to previous Democratic candidates.

“They never distinguished themselves from the Republican,” Fiddler said. She attributes Valadao’s previous success to voters lacking a strong reason to vote against him. She hopes Villegas’ messaging of “you deserve more” is that reason.

Jacob Brunell, 28, the field director for the Westside Democratic Headquarters, said he’s canvassed multiple times in Bakersfield, but this time he felt the excitement and noticed Republican voters crossing party lines.

“This is an area that has been consistently, throughout time, screwed over by land developers, by energy owners,” Brunell said. “I think [voters] are happy to see a Bernie Sanders-backed progressive taking on this fight and hopefully winning the election.”

Bakersfield Vice Mayor Manpreet Kaur said that in this land of farm workers, she has seen young people turning out to vote at the same level as voters aged 60 to 65, and said she believes it is to protect their immigrant families.

“Children of immigrants are becoming that protective barrier between Trump's illegal operations being carried out and harming our families and our communities,” Kaur said. “The immigrant struggle is everyone's struggle, whether they admit it or not.”

Jon Rodriguez, 26, a Latino voter from Bakersfield, said immigration was the biggest issue driving his vote after Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity increased in East Bakersfield. While he lives in the bordering 20th District, represented by Fong and packed with more Republicans by Prop 50, Rodriguez said he would have voted for Villegas if he could have.

“Whether they're citizens or noncitizens, whether they have a visa here or they have full-time citizenship, they're still scared because they know by the color of their skin they're going to be targeted,” Rodriguez said after dropping off his ballot at a voting station at California State University, Bakersfield.

Andres Ramirez, 21, of Bakersfield, said he voted for Villegas. Because his parents are in the process of applying for U.S. citizenship, he said he hopes having Democrats in office will protect them from being deported.

“With Trump, he's wanting to deport us,” Ramirez said. “But I'm legal here, so I make sure that he doesn't want to, like, attack us.”

Democrats have focused their attack ads on Valadao’s vote for Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill Act,” which imposed a work requirement for Medicaid eligibility. Cecilia Torres, 30, cited that vote as she cast her ballot at CSU Bakersfield.

“I do kind of fear for my health care, and will it be affordable? Will I have it, even?” Torres said. “I really hope to see him removed from office and never again see him on the ballot.”

Dolores Huerta, a liberal labor icon who endorsed Villegas in the primary, died in Bakersfield last week at age 96. Chants of “Sí se puede,” a phrase coined by Huerta meaning, “Yes, we can,” broke out during Villegas’ Monday morning rally.

“It is everything,” Villegas said when asked what Huerta’s legacy meant to him. “One thing that I'll always take to heart is her own words: that every moment is a potential organizing opportunity, every person is a potential activist, and every minute is a chance to change the world.”

This story was reported from California by students from the University of Southern California Annenberg School for Communication and Journalism. Direct questions to christina.bellantoni@usc.edu

#6289. Unusual warmth has reached the seafloor off Canada’s Pacific coast – and scientists may know why

A seafloor sensor off Vancouver Island logged its highest temperature since monitoring began in 2009, and researchers say El Niño may be behind the spike.

El Niño is usually described as a warming of the surface waters in the tropical Pacific.

This fall, sensors off Canada’s west coast recorded unusually warm water hundreds of feet below the surface.

One seafloor sensor logged its highest temperature since monitoring began there in 2009. The scientists who operate the sensor said the warm pulse is consistent with a strong El Niño.

The sensors are operated by Ocean Networks Canada, an ocean-monitoring initiative of the University of Victoria.

The readings were announced by the organization itself this week. They have not yet been published as a study.

The record was set at a site called Barkley Canyon Upper Slope, off Vancouver Island. A sensor rests on the seafloor there, about 1,300 feet (400 meters) down. That depth is roughly a quarter of a mile.

On November 8, the water at this site reached 46.8°F (8.21°C).

Jay Cullen is the interim president and chief executive of Ocean Networks Canada.

“We’re seeing significant warming not just at the surface, but hundreds of meters below it,” Cullen said.

The November 8 reading was 4.5°F (2.49°C) above the long-term average for the site. It was also 1.6°F (0.89°C) warmer than the previous record, which was set in 2019.

The water has cooled since then, but normal temperatures have not returned. In mid-November, it was still about 2.9°F (1.6°C) warmer than average.

Warm water has been found at other sites too. The Barkley Canyon sensor is one part of a much larger network. Roughly 530 miles (850 kilometers) of seafloor cable connect its five main research sites.

One of those sites is Clayoquot Slope, which lies more than 3,900 feet (1,200 meters) down. Temperatures well above average are being recorded there as well.

Since late summer, sites between 1,300 and 4,100 feet (400 and 1,250 meters) deep have logged record seasonal temperatures.

The deepest site is the exception. At Cascadia Basin, about 8,700 feet (2,650 meters) down, temperatures remain within their usual range.

El Niño was declared by the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration in June.

On November 12, the agency’s Climate Prediction Center said El Niño was still strengthening.

A strong or very strong event was judged likely to continue into early 2027. The chance of that was put at more than 79%.

How can El Niño affect waters off Canada’s Pacific coast?

Steve Mihaly is a senior scientist at Ocean Networks Canada. According to Mihaly, the energy of a strong El Niño travels north from the equatorial Pacific.

It moves as waves that follow the coastline, and oceanographers call them coastal trapped waves.

Sea level has also been above normal since the warm water arrived. The rise was recorded by tide gauges at Bamfield and Tofino, two communities on Vancouver Island.

Pressure recorders on the seafloor picked it up as well. By mid-November, sea level was about 10 inches (25 centimeters) above normal. Local wind and atmospheric effects were accounted for first.

The scientists then attributed about 6 inches (15 centimeters) of the rise to the waves.

At Barkley Canyon Upper Slope, the water temperature began climbing sharply in late October and reached a record on November 8.

Mihaly said northwest winds persisted into the fall, pushing warmer surface water offshore and drawing colder water upward.

This process, known as upwelling, helped mask the warming at depth.

A second network, called VENUS, is run by Ocean Networks Canada in the Salish Sea.

These sheltered waters are shared by British Columbia and Washington State. The VENUS sensors reach depths of about 980 feet (300 meters).

Temperatures in the Strait of Georgia, which is part of that sea, have been above average throughout 2026.

Jordan Watson is the science director of Ocean Networks Canada.

“Since the start of 2026, the VENUS observatory has shown temperatures consistently higher than we’ve previously observed,” Watson said. “And this was before any El Niño effects started to appear.”

Watson described the area as known for migrating salmon, spawning herring, and marine mammals.

Warming from El Niño could add to the already high temperatures there. That would put more stress on marine ecosystems, the organization said.

So far, only temperatures and sea levels have been reported by the scientists. No effects on marine life have been reported yet.

The record is also a short one. Monitoring at Barkley Canyon began in 2009, so it covers less than two decades.

The scientists were not certain about the cause either. They said the warming likely marks the arrival of El Niño’s effects on Canada’s Pacific coast.

Cullen noted that conditions will be monitored closely over the coming months.

A new tool is also being planned by Ocean Networks Canada and CIOOS Pacific, a regional ocean-data group. It will track ocean conditions across the region.

The seafloor data will be combined with measurements from other groups around the Salish Sea.

Fisheries and Oceans Canada and the University of Washington are among them. More details will be shared later this year, the partners said.

Live and long-term readings can be viewed on Ocean Networks Canada’s data dashboard.

A proposed tabletop quantum sensor could match the precision of the best satellite measurements of frame dragging, a subtle effect predicted by Einstein's general relativity.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists have proposed a new tabletop device to detect the subtle way Earth's daily spin on its axis twists the space-time around it ‪—‬ an effect predicted by Einstein's general relativity.

If built, the sensor could measure the quantum effect known as frame dragging with the same precision as the best satellite experiments, but in minutes instead of years, the researchers proposed in a new study.

The research, published Sept. 17 in the journal Physical Review Letters, aimed to address a classic mismatch in physics. Picture a ring of clocks bolted to a spinning merry-go-round. You synchronize each clock with its neighbor around the ring. Then, you compare the last clock with the first. They don't match.

"It is impossible to synchronize that collection of clocks when you're in a rotating frame," Kai-Isaak Ellers, a physics graduate student at the University of California, Berkeley (UC Berkeley) and first author of the study, told Live Science.

A photo of scientists working on NASA's Gravity Probe B in 2003. This device measured Earth's frame-dragging from space, confirming Einstein's predictions with an 18% margin of error.

Einstein's theory of general relativity predicts that a massive, spinning object drags the fabric of space-time along with it, just like a spoon twirling in honey. The effect is clearly visible around supermassive objects, like the Milky Way's central black hole. But around Earth, the effect is very faint.

So far, scientists have measured Earth's frame dragging only from orbit. They tracked how the twisting of space-time slowly shifts spinning gyroscopes or the paths of satellites. In 2011, NASA's Gravity Probe B satellite, which carried four gyroscopes, confirmed Einstein's prediction with a margin of error of about 18%. Satellites tracked with lasers have since done even better. In July, researchers reported in the journal Nature that the LARES-2 satellite had shrunk that margin of error to just 0.2%.

However, that took about three years of laser tracking. Researchers also had to account for the fact that Earth bulges at the equator and its mass is spread unevenly, which gives the planet’s gravity small irregularities that tug on satellites far more strongly than frame dragging does. To subtract those tugs, the team relied on detailed maps of Earth's gravity made by other satellites.

Measuring frame dragging more precisely is a way to stress-test general relativity. Several alternative theories of gravity predict a slightly different amount of twisting, and a lab-based measurement would also be free of the modeling assumptions that satellite experiments depend on, Ellers said.

The new device is a loop of superfluid helium-4 — helium chilled until it flows without friction and behaves like a single, giant quantum object. The loop is interrupted by a thin barrier riddled with tiny holes, called a Josephson junction. Superfluid helium can slip through the holes, but ordinary liquid helium cannot.

"That's where the quantum behavior comes from," said K. Birgitta Whaley, a quantum physicist at UC Berkeley and a co-author of the study.

As Earth spins and drags space-time, it nudges the quantum state of the helium flowing through the junction. That nudge shifts the frequency at which the helium sloshes back and forth in the loop, which the researchers could detect.

A visualization of Earth's uneven gravity field taken by NASA's Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment in 2009. The lumpiness of our planet's gravitational field makes it harder to precisely measure relativistic effects.

Superfluid devices, many of them built at UC Berkeley, have detected Earth's rotation since the late 1990s. But the helium-4 versions built around a Josephson junction, like the new design, have worked within about a hundredth of a degree of 2.17 K (minus 455.76 Fahrenheit, or minus 270.98 Celsius), the temperature at which helium-4 becomes a superfluid. At that temperature, a lingering fraction of "normal" helium mixed in with the superfluid adds noise.

Instead, the team calculated how the device would behave at a few thousandths of a degree above absolute zero. Below 0.7 K, the noise changed character, and the team found it drops sharply as the helium gets colder. One key finding in the new paper is the result of the team's thermal noise analysis, which showed how sensitive these devices could be at millikelvin temperatures, Elles said.

The catch is the barrier. Earlier helium-4 devices used holes about 90 nanometers wide. Working at these frigid temperatures demands much smaller holes, about 1 nanometer across ‪—‬ roughly the size of a helium atom. Keith Schwab, a physicist at Caltech and co-author of the study, and his collaborators are developing such materials, but they haven't been built into a working sensor yet.

If they can be, the researchers calculate that the device could measure frame dragging to 0.2% precision in about 35 minutes. If its vibrating membrane were made from the lowest-loss crystals, such as quartz or sapphire, that could drop to about one second, they said.

"This seems to be a very serendipitous discovery that at millikelvin, we can get this high sensitivity," Whaley told Live Science.

The signal corresponds to a time difference of about 10-35 seconds between helium flowing one way around the loop and the other — the same mismatch as the clocks on the metaphorical merry-go-round.

"The interesting thing about it is just how small it is," Whaley said. "It's not so far off from the Planck time," about 10-44 seconds, the shortest slice of time before the known laws of physics are expected to break down. This experiment is still a billion times too large to reach that limit, Whaley said. But future helium experiments could help explore whether time flows smoothly, like a ramp, or ticks forward in tiny, indivisible jumps, like the frames of a movie.

Ellers, K.-I., Christodoulou, M., Schwab, K. C., & Whaley, K. B. (2026). Quantum sensing of gravitational frame dragging with a superfluid ⁴He gyrometer. Physical Review Letters, 137(12), 121404. https://doi.org/10.1103/q3v9-rjm9

Larissa G. Capella is a science writer based in Washington state. #6286. Howler monkey droppings hold clues about the fragmented forests they live in

In southern Mexico, the mix of gut bacteria in howler monkeys varied with forest patch size, the trees growing there, and how well the patches were connected.

Howler monkeys can survive in small patches of forest.

A study in southern Mexico found that the mix of bacteria in their guts varied with the size of those patches, the trees growing there, and how well the patches were connected.

Researchers found these patterns in droppings from adult male mantled howler monkeys.

Repeating that sampling could help conservationists track changes over time without capturing the animals.

The study was led by Tabor Whitney while she was a doctoral student at Northwestern University. She worked with primate researchers at Universidad Veracruzana in Mexico.

The work was carried out in the Los Tuxtlas Biosphere Reserve in the state of Veracruz. About 60% of the original forest cover in the reserve has been lost. The remaining forest is broken into patches among pastures, farm fields, and towns.

The 10 study patches ranged from about 5 acres to nearly 500 acres (2 to 199 hectares). Farmland or pasture bordered every one of them.

Whitney and field assistants followed adult male howlers in October and November, during the 2022 rainy season. When a male defecated, the fresh droppings were collected from the ground with sterile sticks.

The team tested the droppings for three things. The first was the bacteria in them. The second was the fatty acids that those bacteria produce. The third was the breakdown products of stress hormones.

The trees in every patch were also measured. Across patches, average trunk width ranged from about 10 to 16 inches (25 to 42 centimeters).

Biologists call the community of microbes in an animal’s gut its microbiome.

“An awesome takeaway of the study is the knowledge the gut microbiome is the most sensitive to ecological change,” Whitney said.

Gut bacteria were analyzed in 41 samples from 32 males. Monkeys from different patches carried different mixes of bacteria.

These differences were linked to all four measures of a patch’s size and layout. Its area and its distance from other forest were among those measures. All seven measures of the trees growing in the patch were linked to the differences too.

Plant fiber is digested by some of the bacteria involved. One such group is Prevotella, and monkeys in larger patches carried more of it.

A different group of bacteria was most common where trees were small. The same was true where few rows of trees linked a patch to other forest.

Only one forest measure predicted the diversity of bacteria carried by a monkey. That measure was trunk thickness. Less variety was found in monkeys from patches with thicker-trunked trees.

The authors suggested that monkeys in mature forest may eat a narrower diet. Fewer kinds of microbes may be taken in as a result.

The team also tested distances to the nearest houses and roads. Neither distance predicted any of the three health measures in the main analysis.

Stress hormone levels were measured in 36 males. They didn’t differ clearly from patch to patch. One pattern, however, was the reverse of what the team had predicted.

Males in larger patches tended to have higher hormone levels, not lower ones.

Higher levels were also found in patches with more fig trees. Figs are a central part of the howler diet.

The authors explained the result in social terms. Several howler groups are supported by larger patches. More than one group may be attracted to the same place by fig trees.

Hormone levels could be raised by competition during encounters with rival groups, not by food shortage. Ordinary demands such as reproduction and fighting infection are also known to raise these hormones.

A monkey with a high level is therefore not necessarily in trouble.

Plant fiber is fermented by gut bacteria, and small fatty acids are released in the process.

Those acids are used by the animal for energy. These acids also help maintain the gut lining and the immune system.

No difference between patches was found in the amounts of these acids. Instead, the team’s attention was drawn to the balance between propionate and butyrate, two of the acids.

A surplus of propionate over butyrate has been proposed as a sign of an unbalanced gut. That pattern has been documented both in people and in wild primates that are short of food.

More propionate than butyrate was present in the droppings from all 10 patches.

In four of the 10 forest patches, the ratio of propionate to butyrate was about 2.6 or higher.

Human studies have linked that threshold to gut disorders. Whether it signals a health problem in howler monkeys remains unknown.

The authors wrote that a reduction in butyrate-producing bacteria may be indicated by the pattern. The reduction may extend across the whole landscape.

The researchers also raised the possibility of long-term effects on the monkeys’ gut lining and immune function.

Howlers in southern Mexico suffered a mass die-off in 2024. Up to 31% of some local populations died from the combined effects of extreme heat, drought, and habitat degradation.

Baseline health records are needed if early warning signs of decline are to be detected, the authors wrote.

Two conservation priorities were recommended by the authors. Patches of mature, varied forest should be protected and enlarged. Rows of trees and wooded strips along rivers should keep those patches connected.

The researchers also suggested that a wider variety of trees be planted, including fruiting species. Howlers would then be able to move through the canopy in search of food and mates.

Permission from local landowners was needed before the team could reach the monkeys.

“Landowners we’ve spoken with are really open to these conversations,” Whitney said.

“They’ve said they love seeing the monkeys, and if they can help them travel on the trees, they’re very interested in it.”

She said the same sampling could be repeated every five or 10 years. Changes could then be compared over time, and the effect of conservation work could be checked.

Every sample came from an adult male. All of the samples were collected in a single rainy season.

Female and young howlers have different energy and hormone demands. The results therefore can’t be assumed to apply to them.

The gut bacteria samples were also limited and unevenly distributed across patches. Some patches supplied one sample, while others supplied as many as 12.

The team identified which bacteria were present. What those bacteria were doing inside the monkeys was not measured.

The study found links between forest features and gut bacteria.

Further research could test whether changes to the forest lead to changes in the monkeys’ gut bacteria.

The authors also noted that forests across Los Tuxtlas may be too uniformly degraded.

That could explain why the fatty acids varied so little. Comparisons with other landscapes are needed, they wrote.

Future research could pair repeated sampling with long-term records of the monkeys’ behavior. Such work could test whether these signals change as the forest does.

The team is now preparing a study comparing the gut bacteria of male and female howlers.

The full study was published in the journal Animal Conservation.

#6285. GLP-1s Extend Life Span, New Research Suggests. Could They Be Key to Human Longevity?

This may mean the drug also has benefits outside of diabetes management.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

Roughly 11 percent of American adults are on a GLP-1 for weight loss, according to a 2026 Gallup survey; so chances are, you likely know someone who is using one for diabetes management, obesity treatment, or heart health—but the benefits might not stop there. Now, semaglutide, the popular GLP-1 medication found in Ozempic and Wegovy, is drawing serious attention from longevity experts.

A recent study published in Nature found that semaglutide administered to female mice late in life significantly extended their life span. The results pose a legitimate question: Could GLP-1 drugs lengthen human lives as well?

To understand whether GLP-1s have anti-aging benefits, researchers put mice that were 20 months old—or roughly 60 human years—on a semaglutide regimen for the rest of their lives. There was also a control group of female mice the same age that received saline injections instead of the semaglutide. The team targeted older, non-obese, non-diabetic female mice to minimize the effects of male aggression and injury, consistent with previous long-term aging research, according to study author Danica Chen, PhD, professor of metabolic biology and nutrition at the University of California, Berkeley.The results? The median life span of the mice that received the GLP-1 drug increased from 742 days to 834 days, roughly a 12 percent extension. The researchers also saw reduced inflammation and preserved cognitive and muscle function in the GLP-1 group.

But there’s a rub here: This study was done in mice, which are a far cry from human adults, meaning we don’t yet know the effects of GLP-1s on people—at least not yet. However, there has been research that suggests lower-calorie diets lead to longer life spans in humans. “The general cause of aging is accumulation of cellular damage,” Chen says. She explains that calorie restriction can reduce cell damage and improve the function of tissues (a group of similar cells working together to perform a specific task), both of which contribute to a longer life span.

Michael Corley, PhD, associate professor of medicine at the University of California San Diego, thinks the Nature study is “important and exciting” because it looks beyond the established metabolic benefits of GLP-1 drugs and tests whether they can influence the biological aging process. (Biological age denotes how well the body is functioning on cellular and molecular levels, while chronological age refers to the number of years a person has been alive.)

“The finding that semaglutide extended life span by approximately 12 percent in older female mice, while improving several measures of physical and cognitive function, adds important evidence to the emerging field of GLP-1 therapies as potential gerotherapeutics,” or treatments that target the root of aging, Corley says. In fact, Corley was involved in a separate study, published earlier this year in Nature Communications, that found that 32 weeks of semaglutide treatment improved multiple epigenetic aging clocks, including measures of biological age and the pace of aging.

Findings presented at the 2026 Aging Research and Drug Discovery Meeting have also strengthened this emerging picture, Corley explains. Novo Nordisk, a Danish pharmaceutical company with locations around the world, reported that semaglutide improved measures of biological aging across multiple organ systems, including the heart and kidneys.

Likewise, Eli Lilly, an American pharmaceutical company headquartered in Indiana, presented findings that tirzepatide—another GLP-1 medication, which is found in prescriptions like Mounjaro and Zepbound—positively influenced several epigenetic aging clocks, including organ-specific markers that measure the biological age of the heart, kidney, liver, and immune system.

“Together, these independent observations suggest that GLP-1-based therapies may affect biological aging through multiple molecular pathways,” Corley says. “The new mouse study is particularly interesting because it extends these molecular observations to actual life span, while also demonstrating improvements in several hallmarks of aging.”

So, could GLP-1 drugs actually extend the life span of humans? Corley thinks the more compelling opportunity isn’t necessarily extending life span, but extending health span—or the number of years people live in good health, free from chronic disease and disability.

“Human life span has biological constraints, and it is unlikely that GLP-1 drugs alone will dramatically extend the maximum limits of human longevity,” he says. “However, by reducing the burden of cardiovascular disease, metabolic dysfunction, and other age-related conditions, these medications could help more people remain healthy and independent for longer, potentially increasing average life span without fundamentally changing the upper limits of human longevity.”

However, improvements in biological aging don’t necessarily translate into longer lives, Corley cautions.

“The critical next step is determining whether these molecular changes predict meaningful improvements in physical function, cognition, and resilience,” Corley says. “I think the greatest potential of GLP-1 therapies is not to push humans beyond the limits of longevity, but to help more people reach older ages while maintaining their health, function, and independence.”

To find out whether or not GLP-1 drugs can eventually be used as a legitimate longevity tactic in humans, Chen says clinical trials in humans are an important next step. For now, GLP-1s remain a titan of diabetes and weight management—but their role in human longevity remains to be seen.

#6284. Man charged in spree of powder-filled letters that rattled Congress

Federal officials unsealed charges Tuesday against an Oklahoma man accused of mailing hundreds of letters containing suspicious substances to members of Congress and other officials last month and ahead of the 2024 election.

The court records, unsealed in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Oklahoma, show officials filed a complaint against Robin Martin with two charges: conveying false or misleading information and hoaxes and mailing threatening communications. Martin is set to make his first court appearance Tuesday; information for an attorney was not immediately available.

The complaint alleges Martin sent more than 700 letters to election officials across the country as well as letters to members of Congress of both parties containing suspicious substances. The substances have so far tested as nontoxic and are believed to be yeast or flour, the complaint says.

The complaint alleges that Martin started sending letters with suspicious substances ahead of the 2024 election, addressing them to election officials in all 50 states. Some of those letters had messages written on them that could only be shown by exposure to ultraviolet light, the complaint says.

The mailings contained letters that claimed President Donald Trump won the 2020 election and raised concerns about issues with the 2024 count. Tests of the suspicious white substances included with the letters revealed they were nontoxic, the complaint says.

The 2024 letters had a return address of a business office in Maryland, while the 2026 letters had a return address previously tied to a Democratic Socialists of America office. Neither of those addresses were connected to the sender, the complaint says.

The complaint says that DSA provided officials with documents showing that someone identifying themselves as “George Livingston” contacted DSA officials in October and said they would be arrested for “TREASON AGAINST THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA.” Those messages contained some similarities to the 2024 letters, according to the complaint.

Investigators later tracked down Martin’s phone to places where the letters were sent from and also tracked his car on surveillance footage. The complaint also says investigators tracked purchases he made, including turmeric and vinegar, that could have been used to create an ink that would be visible under UV light.

The case is separate from one announced last week against an Illinois man accused of sending threatening messages to members of Congress.

The missing 1.2 billion years of geological history at the Grand Canyon finally has an explanation.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

More than a billion years of geological history is missing from the walls of the Grand Canyon, and now, scientists may know why.

In the canyon's sides, ancient metamorphic and igneous rocks that formed 1.7 billion years ago sit directly under younger sedimentary rocks laid down 500 million years ago. The 1.2 billion-year chunk of history in between wasn't preserved — leaving a geological gap known as the Great Unconformity.

This missing period was a very important time in Earth's history, because it was just before and during the Cambrian explosion, which saw a huge diversification of life on Earth. The Great Unconformity is not only at the Grand Canyon; there are big gaps in the rock layers of that time across North America, the Baltic region of Europe and in northern China. Researchers have long debated why this unconformity exists.

The unconformity is sharply evident in the transition between Cambrian Tapeats Sandstone and Proterozoic Brahma Schist in the Grand Canyon.

Now, a new model of the movement of Earth's middle layer, the mantle, has revealed an explanation: The slow, heat-driven circulation of the mantle pushed these three regions upward during the time when the Great Unconformity was formed, according to new research published Nov. 4 in the journal Nature.

This uplift would have helped facilitate erosion, meaning sediments formed at that time sloughed off the continents and landed in the ocean. Importantly, the model also shows that in the past 540 million years, these same areas started sinking instead of rising, creating areas for sediments to get caught and then keep piling up in neat layers on the continents — marking the point where the Great Unconformity ends. This matches what geologists can see in North America, the Baltics and northern China.

"We looked at, where are the best places that the mantle would help create a Great Unconformity?" study co-author Nicolas Flament, a geoscientist at the University of Wollongong in Australia, told Live Science. "And these three places turned out to be three places where it's known to be quite extensive."

Erosion during Neoproterozoic times, followed by sedimentation during early Phanerozoic times, formed the Great Unconformity. Bottom: Dynamic uplift was followed by subsidence for Laurentia ('LAU'), Baltica ('BAL') and North China ('NCH').

The cause of the Great Unconformity is hotly debated, with some arguing that a global deep freeze known as Snowball Earth could have shoveled sediment off the continents in this period. Glaciation probably played a major role in erosion, Flament said, but the new study suggests that the key driver was deep within the planet. Without the mantle pushing the continents upward, glaciers and other erosive forces would have had no slope to push sediments down, he said.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Earth is in a constant state of recycling crust through plate tectonics, said Shanan Peters, a geologist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who was not involved in the study. Oceanic crust sinks back into the mantle through the process of subduction ‪—‬ when one tectonic plate dives beneath another. The chemicals it carries down with it get released back into the atmosphere via volcanic eruptions, linking the mantle with the atmosphere.

And tectonics aren't steady. As continents break up and join back together over eons, different materials get pushed into the crust. For example, the ancient Paleo-Tethys ocean, which lapped off the shores of the supercontinent Pangaea until it closed about 200 million years ago, was rich in carbon-bearing sediments that eroded from the continents, Peters said. When the ocean floor was subducted back into the mantle, this carbon was pushed into the depths of the planet.

It contributes to the environment in which complex life evolved.

Today, in contrast, most of Earth's subduction is around the Pacific Rim, and much of the Pacific seafloor is remote from continents, so the seafloor is relatively starved of carbon. What's getting pushed into the mantle now is therefore a different chemical composition than what existed 200 million years ago.

In that sense, referring to the Great Unconformity as "missing information" isn't accurate, Peters told Live Science. Instead, the absence of a rock record in those places at that time reveals something about the processes going on back then — and hints at how geology might have been affecting the atmosphere, and thus life's evolution.

The geological processes occurring during the time of the Great Unconformity may have set the stage for the Cambrian explosion, Peters said. For example, the crystalline rocks exposed on the surface at that time may have released elements like potassium, iron, manganese and carbon into the seas at an increased rate, prompting marine life to invent biomineralization — shells — in response and possibly shifting the composition of Earth's atmosphere to be more oxygen-rich, Peters said.

Flament agreed that the geological changes had significant knock-on effects for life. "It contributes to the environment in which complex life evolved," Flament said.

What's particularly interesting about the Great Unconformity is how it reveals not just a period of erosion but also a switch back to the deposition of sediments. The new paper provides an explanation for both, Peters said, and changes in the mantle are just the planetary-scale process to explain this big-picture phenomenon.

"This seems to me to be the only reasonable way to go back and forth between this state over time," he said.

There are still questions about what else the continents were doing in this time period. Peters leads an effort called Macrostrat that is pulling together observations of rock layers around the world, and Flament said he hopes that database will help ground-truth the new models' findings.

"So far in Africa and Russia, we don’t have as comprehensive a database," he said. "Once that is done, we can go and check whether the idea works."

Editor's Note: This story was updated at 10:30 p.m. E.D.T. to note that James Price, not Tia Ghose, edited this story.

Archaeologists have found a 2,200-year-old golden bear in an Iron Age burial in Kazakhstan that may have held seven people.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The gold bear would have been worn on a headdress.

Archaeologists in Kazakhstan have discovered a unique gold bear figurine in a 2,200-year-old burial mound that looters had hit but failed to empty completely.

The sculpted bear stands on its hind limbs and holds a pot-like container between its front paws. The artifact would have been worn as part of a headdress, and holes at its base indicate that it could have been sewn onto the garment, according to a translated statement from the Kazakhstan government.

The 2,200-year-old gold bear is a unique find in Kazakhstan.

The gold bear was unearthed at an Early Iron Age burial mound at the Karagaily burial ground in the southern city of Almaty, along with a surprisingly high number of human bones for a single burial mound.

Although other gold-crafted animals have been found in the region, the newly unearthed bear is the first of its kind.

"The sculpted bear figurine is unique to Kazakhstan. No similar finds have been discovered previously," Lyazzat Sagyndykova, director of the Almaty Museums Association, which conducted the excavation, said in the statement. "This discovery allows us to trace cultural parallels across the whole of Eurasia, from the Black Sea region to Altai."

Archaeologists in Kazakhstan excavated a 2,200-year-old burial mound.

The figurine dates to the Saka period, named for a nomadic horseback-riding people from Iran who lived on the Eurasian Steppe and Tarim Basin of what is now western China. Archaeologists have found comparable gold objects at other excavations in Kazakhstan, according to the statement. For example, a headdress element shaped like a small leopard previously came to light at the Almaty Kok-Kainar burial ground, which dates to the fourth century B.C. Also, the headdress of Kazakhstan's famous "Golden Man," a young Iron Age warrior buried in an extraordinarily lavish grave, also has a gold, sheep-shaped decorative element.

It's unclear which bear species the figurine depicts, but today Kazakhstan is home to two subspecies of brown bear: the Tien Shan or Himalayan brown bear (Ursus arctos isabellinus), which lives in the Tien Shan Mountains in the southeast, and the East Siberian brown bear (Ursus arctos collaris) in the Altai Mountains in the east, according to a study published earlier this year.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Preliminary analyses date the recently excavated site to the fourth to third centuries B.C., according to the statement. Based on the number of bones they excavated, experts suspect that the mound, which is around 8 feet (2.4 meters) tall and roughly 85 feet (26 m) wide, may have been the final resting place for four adults and three children.

Archaeologists found a surprising number of human bones in the burial mound.

"Of particular interest is the unusually large number of human remains in a single burial mound, as such burials are atypical for Kazakhstan," Marat Mugalovich Nurpeisov, a senior research fellow at the Almaty Museums Association, said in the statement. "As a rule, burial mounds of a comparable size were intended for the burial of one or two people."

Archaeologists also found pieces of Saka pottery, most of which had been strewn about after the burial had been looted in ancient times, according to the statement. The thieves left behind a 10-foot (3 m) looting pit.

"Research into the Karagaily burial ground is ongoing," Nurpeisov said in the statement. "To clarify the circumstances of the burial and determine the exact number of individuals interred, further analyses are planned, including the involvement of anthropologists."

After all of the investigations are finished, some of the artifacts will be put on display at the Almaty Museum, according to the statement.

#6279. This may be the best evidence yet that dinosaur blood can fossilize

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Minerals may have preserved remnants of ancient blood in a dinosaur bone, but some are skeptical

Using a technique called scanning electron microscopy to peer inside an 115 million-year-old dinosaur limb bone, researchers captured images of tiny ellipsoid structures, about 20 micrometers in diameter, that may be fossilized red blood cells. Molecular analyses found preserved heme — the oxygen-carrying component of hemoglobin — in the bone.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The life and times of a dinosaur may be written in its blood — if blood can be preserved in bone.

Tiny microstructures found in the limb bones of a fossilized 115-million-year-old specimen are the remnants of red blood cells, researchers report November 2 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The team says these are both the oldest red blood cell structures yet identified and the first to be chemically proven. But not everyone is as sanguine about that conclusion.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The ability to identify such structures could offer a powerful molecular window into the physiology of long-extinct animals, including their metabolism and even activity levels, says paleontologist Kliti Grice of Curtin University in Bentley, Australia.

The bone, from a fossil-rich site in northeastern Brazil called Mina Pedra Branca, belonged to the dinosaur Aratasaurus museunacionali. Grice and her colleagues used a variety of chemical and imaging analyses to study the Cretaceous Period specimen.

Maurilio Oliveira/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0)

The team prepared thin cross-sectional slices of bone and imaged details of the limb bone’s internal structure with focused electron beams. That revealed ellipse-shaped microstructures within the limb’s fossilized network of blood vessels.

A map of the ellipsoids’ chemical element composition revealed that they were full of iron, carbon and nitrogen, all components of a biomolecule called heme. Heme is an iron-bearing, ring-shaped molecule found in hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen throughout the body.

Then, the researchers used a technique that identifies molecules by how they scatter laser light. Those analyses suggested the presence of porphyrins, ringlike organic compounds found in blood — and the precursors of heme. Finally, they ruled out contamination from other porphyrins, such as the pigment chlorophyll, by separating and identifying the molecular contents of a bone extract. That experiment also suggested heme.

Taken together, these findings point unequivocally to the preservation of molecular traces of ancient blood, the team says. They also offer a clue to a novel pathway that might preserve those traces for so many millions of years.

Blood cells decompose within days of the death of an organism. Only unusual and fast-acting environmental and biochemical conditions could have stopped decay and held those tissues in place as the organism fossilizes.

In this fossil, the secret ingredient was a manganese oxide mineral called hausmannite, the researchers say. The team’s analyses had found the mineral within the ellipsoid structures. That mineral, they propose, may have acted as a time capsule, preserving the cellular structures and protecting the molecules within, including collagen amino acids.

Distinguishing fossilized blood cells from nonorganic minerals that formed within a fossil after the organism’s death is a tricky task. During fossilization, mineral-rich fluids seep in and around the bones, and the minerals that form within the fossil can bear a strong resemblance to bodily structures.

In a 1997 study, two paleontologists analyzed tiny spheres found inside the limb of a fossil, possibly a pterosaur. The spheres were once thought to be the fossilized remnants of ancient blood cells, but the duo determined that the spheres were instead pyrite, an iron mineral that had been deposited in the bones after death.

Those paleontologists suggested that, going forward, several criteria should be met before proposing a blood cell origin for fossilized structures, including comparing the shape of the structures with that of living related organisms and identifying certain biomarkers in the structures. One of those biomarkers is heme compounds.

Grice and her colleagues say that their study meets these criteria. Unlike the pyrite, hausmannite was crucial to preservation, “rather than simply a mineral that replaced biological material after it had disappeared,” she says. The close spatial relationship between the hausmannite, the blood cell-like structures and the chemical signatures of heme “raises the possibility that mineralization helped stabilize, entomb and protect components of the original biological material during fossilization.”

But Mary Schweitzer, a paleontologist at North Carolina State University in Raleigh who was not involved in the new study, says she doesn’t think these findings do fully meet those criteria.

The heme biomarkers, for example, don’t appear to be localized to the round structures alone, as would be expected in fossilized blood cells, but come from analysis of the entire bone. The proposed red blood cells also differ in size and shape compared with red blood cells from living birds and reptiles, she says.

Schweitzer is no stranger to skepticism over the discovery of ephemeral tissues in fossils. In 2005, she and her colleagues reported the first recovery of flexible, soft-tissue blood vessels from the 68-million-year-old fossilized leg bone of a Tyrannosaurus rex. It was a landmark study that sparked debate, including over how it would even be possible to preserve such tissues through deep time, as well as the most surefire way to detect them in the present.

“I am not convinced” that the research team has definitively identified heme compounds, Schweitzer says. “I do applaud them for bringing a plethora of methods to the study. Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, and that does require state-of-the-art technology.”

No one really knows what a dinosaur’s red blood cell shape would be, let alone how the process of fossilization might distort the original shape of the structures, or allow heme-related molecules to escape their cellular confines over time, Grice says.

And, she says, her team’s interpretation of the evidence doesn’t just rely on the observations of those structures. “[It] rests on the convergence of anatomy, morphology, mineralogy, elemental analysis and molecular chemistry,” she says. “That combination is critical.”

As for whether other fossils might have molecular traces that have been preserved by hausmannite, “we simply don’t know yet,” Grice says. “But this type of preservation may not be quite as rare as we currently think.”

K. Grice et al. Heme signatures in mineralized red blood cells within vascular canals of a 115-million-year-old dinosaur bone. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. 2026. doi: 10.1073/pnas.2614248123

D.M. Martill and D.M. Unwin. Small spheres in fossil bones: Blood corpuscles or diagenetic products? Palaeontology. 1997.
