Willsey: The principle is to try and get these things as small as possible to disrupt the least amount of tissue as possible, and then to get them really, really close to the individual cells, the neurons themselves that have the information we’re trying to record.

Sanders: The goal here is to restore a person’s ability to talk.

Willsey: So in the ideal situation, the electrodes would sit, you know, right next to those neurons. This type of technology that’s very intuitive, that can record activity from the brain in kind of a high-throughput way, can put the words up at a good speed and a good accuracy, allows them to kind of regain the ability to communicate with others close to how they maybe were before they had the illness. So that truly is very powerful.

Sanders: You might remember that Casey’s implant, called the BrainGate 2 system, requires ports on his head that are connected to external wires.

Casey: What is annoying about this device is really easy to answer. It is not portable, and it is not implanted only inside my head.

Sanders: Unlike Casey’s implant, the Paradromics device is fully implantable. That means it’s wireless. This summer, Willsey implanted Paradromic’s device in a volunteer’s brain. The brain belonged to a 68-year-old woman who lives in Michigan. She has primary lateral sclerosis, a disease that has taken away most of her ability to talk. So far, the Paradromics system is up and running, and the volunteer is testing her abilities out.

Here she is talking with Willsey and other researchers in a video provided by Paradromics. You’ll hear her natural voice, which is hard to understand, and then a digital voice speaking the words her brain implant decoded.

[Audio] I love the change of seasons in Michigan. And my favorite one is the fall. I love the change of seasons in Michigan. And my favorite one is the fall. Yeah, it’s good.

Sanders: This volunteer has used the device to talk to her grandkids on the phone. But this is just the very beginning for this research project. There’s so much more to test.Casey is still working on his system, too — particularly, streamlining the process. When Casey uses his brain-computer interface, it decodes speech signals from his brain, then puts words on a screen. Casey then selects a button, using his eye movements or his brain-computer interface, to say these words out loud with a digital voice. Here’s Casey.

Casey: It is not fast enough to provide enough instant conversation with other people that need to slow down to talk to me.

Sanders: But scientists want to skip this middle part — the words written on a screen. They want instead to go straight to speech, and perhaps make conversations faster. Casey says this goal to go directly from brain signals to a speaking digital voice would be his top priority.

Casey: That one is the holy grail of what this will become in terms of speech. It will allow you to have a seamless conversation. I am talking about, yes, I will intend to talk, and then it will just translate that automatically into speech, like we do, and you are doing right now.

Sanders: In an earlier episode, we talked about attempts to do just this with Casey’s system, to push it to do what they call brain-to-voice. Early attempts were hard to decipher. But it has already improved, by a lot. In the latest tests, this brain-to-voice process produces words that are understandable – reaching about 95 percent accuracy for listeners. Here’s Casey speaking test sentences. It comes from a preprint manuscript posted on the website bioRxiv.

[Audio] The day is not over yet. Please come in with me.

Sanders: Scientists have another thing on their to-do list. And this one goes beyond the words themselves. Here’s Gilja, from Paradromics.

Gilja: Let’s say I identify whether a sentence is a statement or a question. Well, now you can pass that information on to speech synthesis, so that you get these two different versions.

Sanders: The same words could be a statement or a question. You see what he means. You see what he means? And that information can be pulled out from a person’s brain activity.

Gilja: If I’m decoding prosodic information, if I’m decoding speed, when a word is meant to appear, that can also be passed on to modern speech synthesis systems, so that you’re more accurately capturing the prosody that somebody intends. Same thing with loudness, right? So you can see how as that information becomes available from the neural channels, it can be provided to the AI speech synthesis to get closer to the intended voice in the moment that the individual wants to generate.

Sanders: All of these signals can be collected and used to build a more accurate voice — one that says things exactly how a person intends to say them, like a Minnesotan’s ooftah or a slow southern hey y’all. Now, today’s voice clones can add these emotional layers onto words already. Here’s what Jules told me when I asked him about whether his voice clone can do it.

Jules: Oh, there are plenty of things it does that are all the above. But one thing in particular is how it inserts tone and inflections on words. Sometimes my wife will get mad because my response can come off with some sass.

Sanders: So there’s loudness, emphasis, pitch — all of these things contribute to what words means. But imagine if a brain implant can pick up these cues directly — no typing required. Here’s Hochberg.

Hochberg: There’s a lot that can be conveyed through the emphasis, through the tone, through even the humor that can sometimes be conveyed by the way that somebody who’s able-bodied may speak a particular sentence. All of those, I think, really can be captured by these implantable brain-computer interfaces by harnessing the rich neural activity that’s available from the brain. We should be able to restore a lot of that.

Sanders: Sergey Stavisky is one of the UC Davis researchers working with Casey and Hochberg. He and his colleagues are working on some of these ideas.

Stavisky: And even now we’re continuing to improve that and actually adding additional layers. So we have one forward-looking project where we can maybe decode the kind of emotional valence of how he’s trying to say it. Is he trying to say something in an angry way or in a surprised way or in a happy-sounding way, to kind of further make it more expressive.

Sanders: They’re even trying  to decode singing. Well, OK, it’s really more of a hum at this point, he says. But those sorts of tone shifts could, in theory, be deciphered.

Stavisky: We definitely have our work cut out for us on the singing and melody side of things.

Sanders: All sorts of voice signals could be pulled from brain activity.

Stavisky: Ultimately, we want people to be in full control of what they’re communicating. This should come from their intent. So, yeah, we are trying to decode all of the aspects of his voice, whether it’s the pitch, the timbre, the loudness, the intonation, which word he’s stressing. All of that, ideally, we would decode from brain activity, including kind of all of that emotional nuance.

Sanders: Voice clones can speak with various emotions. You heard my voice clone do just that in earlier episodes. But the difference here is that a person wouldn’t have to type in the instructions. They would come straight from their brain, seamlessly. Other nonverbal signals can be pulled from the brain, too.

Samantha Brosler: In the past five years or so, there have been a lot of advancements in the field of BCIs for restoring individual functions to people with paralysis.

Sanders: That’s Samantha Brosler, a bioengineer at the University of California, San Francisco. Some brain-computer interfaces can pick up movements. We haven’t talked much about them, but these implants have their own very successful research history. They’ve allowed people to control a robotic arm, for instance.

Brosler: Most of these devices so far have been designed to restore one function at a time, whereas in reality, frequently people who are paralyzed are missing both the ability to speak and perform body movements. And so in this study, we asked whether a single brain implant could be used to decode both speech and movement at the same time.

Sanders: It turns out, it could. She and her colleagues were able to decode gestures for communication — things like thumbs up, or a head nodding yes — and words. This combo approach is a more natural way of getting a point across.

Brosler: We naturally use gestures alongside our speech. So for example, some gestures can substitute for speech entirely, like nodding yes, shaking your head no, waving, shrugging, giving a thumbs up. But they can also add or change the meaning of what we’re saying. So for example, if you say maybe combined with nod head yes, that has a very different, you know, meaning than if you say maybe and shrug or shake your head no.

Sanders: My kids know that a slow maybe with a skeptical eyebrow raise is much closer to a no than my fast upbeat maybe with a little head nod. There is so much subtext in our body language.

Brosler: So I think of, you know, gestures and body movements as an additional communication channel that can work together with speech to add expressivity to what we’re trying to say.

Sanders: In the study, the output was a digital avatar who looked like the person. Success looked like the avatar moving and getting the word right.

Brosler: And the idea is that we enable the participants to use speech and gestures alone or together. So in theory, someone could say hello while waving.

Sanders: The researchers started simple, with just a few phrases — hello, bye, good idea, how’s it going, let’s go — and just a few gestures, like a shrug or a point, a fist pump, thumbs up.

Brosler: Of course, ultimately, we’re hoping to expand this to even larger vocabulary and more range of body movements across the whole body to help allow people more expression in their communication.

Sanders: The sheer number of different approaches to restoring communication is a sign that this neurotechnology is coming fast. Here’s Willsey.

Willsey: I think it’s good. There’s a lot of players that are entering into the field that have a variety of different ideas where they can run the clinical trials and see how these different devices stack up.

Sanders: There are lots of reasons to be optimistic about the future here, and it’s a future that isn’t even that far off. Here’s David Brandman, one of the researchers at UC Davis who works with Casey. He’s also the neurosurgeon who implanted Casey’s device.

Brandman: I think I’m about five years away from being able to meet a patient with ALS and having the following conversation, and saying, you know, Ms. Smith, I’m sorry you’ve been diagnosed with ALS. I don’t have a cure for you, but I do have a device that I can implant that can help you communicate despite facing a future of paralysis. It’s a device that would be implanted. It’s fully wirelessly. It’s cosmetically invisible, and you’d be able to use it to communicate your needs and have a meaningful conversation with friends and family. So I think that kind of conversation is about five to 10 years away.

Sanders: It’s a beautiful vision. When you’ve been a reporter as long as I have, you’re skeptical when scientists say something big is just five to 10 years away. But in this case, I see it.

It’s easy to get drawn into the technical details here. Different types of implants, the decoding processes, AI-powered voice clones and what they can do and can’t do — what they should do and shouldn’t do. But if you step back and really look, you’ll see that this research is all propelled by a very simple and powerful fact: The human voice is too important to lose.

Casey: What does my voice mean to me? It means so much. I think it is the most important thing that I have lost in this whole disease.

Sanders: So now we are here, in this moment, as Jules would say, right here, right now. And right now, the human voice is shifting and changing, expanding in ways that were completely unthinkable even just a few years ago. The future of the human voice and its many replicas is anybody’s guess.

Sanders: In one of Jules’ comedy sets, the one he did in November of 2024, he wheels out onto the stage as the song “Walking on Sunshine” plays.

As the crowd settles and finishes their clapping and woo-ing, Jules pauses. You can’t see this, but he wiggles his eyebrows — a lot. The crowd goes crazy every time. He hasn’t said a single word yet. After another pause, he deadpans with his voice clone: “That is all the time I have. My Make-A-Wish covered only a few minutes. Goodnight, everybody.”

And with that, Jules takes control and he’s off on a tear, ripping through stories of a weatherman who seems too happy about standing out in hurricanes, the exquisite guilt trips lovingly crafted by his Cuban parents, and the indignities of having body parts shaved with his sister right there in the room. Jules has the audience laughing so hard. It’s magnificent.

MA: And being backstage and then seeing him come out, like roll out in his wheelchair and everybody go nuts because they’re like, what is going on here? Like, this doesn’t make sense. And every time I was like, this is like life. This is love. This is passion. This is like, what else is there? Like, I don’t know that there’s anything else more powerful than what this guy is doing here and what I can help him do.

Sanders: I get what MA meant when she said that comedy is something that heals. When his set actually does come to a close, he tells the audience. [Audio] Now you have to watch me slowly get off this stage. Goodnight, everybody.

Sanders: It’s hilarious. It’s happy. It’s sad. It’s perfect.

This is The Deep End, Talk to Me. I’m Laura Sanders. If you like this podcast, tell your friends and leave us a review. It helps the show a lot. Send us your questions and your comments at podcasts@sciencenews.org.

#6247. 2026 Full Moon calendar: When to see the Full Moon and phases

The phenomenon of a Full Moon arises when our planet, Earth, is precisely sandwiched between the Sun and the Moon. This alignment ensures the entire side of the Moon that faces us gleams under sunlight. Thanks to the Moon’s orbit around Earth, the angle of sunlight hitting the lunar surface and being reflected back to our planet changes. That creates different lunar phases.

The next Full Moon will be the November Beaver Moon, which occurs at 9:54 a.m. EST on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026. It will also be a Super Moon.

We’ll update this article multiple times each week with the latest moonrise, moonset, Full Moon schedule, and some of what you can see in the sky each week.

Here’s the complete list of Full Moons this year and their traditional names.

(All times Eastern; * denotes a Super Moon.)

The images below show the day-by-day phases of the Moon in November. The Full Moon this month will be on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026.

The times below for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location. All other times are Eastern unless otherwise specified. For more details on upcoming sky events, check out our full Sky This Week column

Sunrise: 6:49 A.M.Sunset: 4:41 P.M.Moonrise: 1:19 P.M.Moonset: 12:03 A.M.Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (67%)

Thursday, November 19Sunrise: 6:50 A.M.Sunset: 4:40 P.M.Moonrise: 1:41 P.M.Moonset: 1:07 A.M.Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (76%)

Friday, November 20The Moon passes 5° north of Neptune at 8 A.M. EST; 12 hours later, our satellite passes 7° north of Saturn at 8 P.M. EST. The trio is visible in the southeastern sky two hours after sunset, forming a triangle with the Moon to the upper left of Saturn, and Neptune to Saturn’s right. Only the Moon and Saturn are visible to the naked eye, while Neptune will require optical aid.

Sunrise: 6:51 A.M.Sunset: 4:40 P.M.Moonrise: 2:04 P.M.Moonset: 2:12 A.M.Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (84%)

The phases of the Moon are: New Moon, waxing crescent, First Quarter, waxing gibbous, Full Moon, waning gibbous, Last Quarter, and waning crescent. A cycle starting from one Full Moon to its next counterpart, termed the synodic month or lunar month, lasts about 29.5 days.

Though a Full Moon only occurs during the exact moment when Earth, Moon, and Sun form a perfect alignment, to our eyes, the Moon seems Full for around three days.

There are a wide variety of specialized names used to identify distinct types or timings of Full Moons. These names primarily trace back to a blend of cultural, agricultural, and natural observations about the Moon, aimed at allowing humans to not only predict seasonal changes, but also track the passage of time.

For instance, almost every month’s Full Moon boasts a name sourced from Native American, Colonial American, or other North American traditions, with their titles mirroring seasonal shifts and nature’s events.

Wolf Moon (January): Inspired by the cries of hungry wolves.

Snow Moon (February): A nod to the month’s often heavy snowfall.

Worm Moon (March): Named after the earthworms that signal thawing grounds.

Pink Moon (April): In honor of the blossoming pink wildflowers.

Flower Moon (May): Celebrating the bloom of flowers.

Strawberry Moon (June): Marks the prime strawberry harvest season.

Buck Moon (July): Recognizing the new antlers on bucks.

Sturgeon Moon (August): Named after the abundant sturgeon fish.

Corn Moon (September): Signifying the corn harvesting period.

Hunter’s Moon (October): Commemorating the hunting season preceding winter.

Beaver Moon (November): Reflects the time when beavers are busy building their winter dams.

Cold Moon (December): Evocative of winter’s chill.

In addition, there are a few additional names for Full Moons that commonly make their way into public conversations and news.

Super Moon: This term is reserved for a Full Moon that aligns with the lunar perigee, which is the Moon’s nearest point to Earth in its orbit. This proximity renders the Full Moon unusually large and luminous. For a Full Moon to earn the Super Moon tag, it should be within approximately 90 percent of its closest distance to Earth.

Blue Moon: A Blue Moon is the second Full Moon in a month that experiences two Full Moons. This phenomenon graces our skies roughly every 2.7 years. Though the term suggests a color, Blue Moons aren’t truly blue. Very occasionally, atmospheric conditions such as recent volcanic eruptions might lend the Moon a slightly blueish tint, but this hue isn’t tied to the term.

Black Moon: A Black Moon is a recent, unofficial term that can describe one of two situations. Either the third of four New Moons in a single astronomical season or the second of two New Moons in a month is a Black Moon. As its name suggests, the Black Moon is completely dark, as it is a New Moon that occurs when the Moon is between the Sun and Earth. The New Moon cannot be observed except during a total solar eclipse.

Harvest Moon: Occurring closest to the autumnal equinox, typically in September, the Harvest Moon is often renowned for a distinct orange tint it might display. This Full Moon rises close to sunset and sets near sunrise, providing extended hours of bright moonlight. Historically, this was invaluable to farmers gathering their produce.

What is the difference between a Full Moon and a New Moon? A Full Moon is witnessed when Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, making the entire Moon’s face visible. Conversely, during a New Moon, the Moon lies between Earth and the Sun, shrouding its Earth-facing side in darkness.

How does the Full Moon influence tides? The Moon’s gravitational tug causes Earth’s waters to bulge, birthing tides. During both Full and New Moons, the Sun, Earth, and Moon are in alignment, generating “spring tides.” These tides can swing exceptionally high or low due to the combined gravitational influences of the Sun and Moon.

A common antibiotic may be linked to a higher risk of miscarriage and stillbirth when used early in pregnancy, a new study suggests.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Taking doxycycline, a commonly prescribed antibiotic, during the first trimester of pregnancy may increase the risk of pregnancy loss, a new study suggests.

The antibiotic is broad-spectrum, meaning it targets a wide range of bacteria. It's often used to treat acne, respiratory infections and sexually transmitted infections, such as chlamydia and syphilis. Doctors generally avoid prescribing the drug during the second and third trimesters because it belongs to a class of antibiotics that can bind to calcium in developing bones. Animal studies suggest that this may disrupt fetal bone development.

However, evidence on doxycycline's safety during early pregnancy has been mixed and limited. The new study, published Tuesday (Nov. 10) in the journal Annals of Internal Medicine, provides clearer evidence of a link between doxycycline use in the first trimester and pregnancy loss.

"I would advise physicians to carefully consider the benefit-risk balance when prescribing doxycycline to women who are pregnant or planning a pregnancy," study first author Almut Winterstein, a pharmacist and drug-safety researcher at the University of Florida, told Live Science in an email.

Using information from two U.S. insurance databases, the researchers analyzed 224,870 pregnancies in people ages 12 to 55. More than 218,230 of these patients were treated for respiratory tract infections, and over 6,630 were treated for acne, between conception and the end of the first trimester. About 4,385 of the women filled a prescription for doxycycline during that time frame, while the others received an alternative antibiotic.

Among women with respiratory infections, those prescribed doxycycline had a 40% to 54% higher risk of pregnancy loss, compared with those prescribed amoxicillin, another broad-spectrum antibiotic in a different class. The exact level of risk varied between the two databases.

The researchers also compared the doxycycline users against women prescribed macrolides, the class of antibiotics that includes azithromycin (or "Z-Pak"). Again, the doxycycline users saw a higher risk — 39% and 36% higher, respectively.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Among the patients treated for acne, doxycycline users had a 49% higher risk of pregnancy loss in one database than those given the antibiotic clindamycin. In the second database, though, the difference wasn't statistically significant. Winterstein said that may be because there were fewer patients included in that analysis.

Overall, doxycycline was associated with seven to 11 additional pregnancy losses per 100 pregnancies, compared with the other antibiotic options assessed, the researchers reported.

The researchers examined the risk associated with taking various antibiotics in the first 12 weeks of pregnancy.

It is not yet clear how the drug might contribute to pregnancy loss. Because the study was observational, it cannot prove that the antibiotic itself caused those losses, which included miscarriages and stillbirths. (Miscarriage is pregnancy loss before 20 weeks of pregnancy, whereas stillbirth refers to pregnancy loss after the 20th week.)

Animal studies hint that doxycycline could interfere with early placental development, potentially making it harder for the placenta to support a growing pregnancy, Luke Grzeskowiak, an associate professor and clinical pharmacist at Flinders University in Australia who was not involved in the study, said in an email.

The study authors also noted in their report that the drug may have direct effects on the developing embryo. But these explanations remain hypothetical; the researchers have not established that either mechanism occurs in humans.

"Pregnancy loss affects around one in four pregnancies and can happen for many reasons," Grzeskowiak noted. Although doxycycline exposure may add to that risk, taking the antibiotic does not necessarily mean pregnancy loss will occur. The available data suggests that it is just one risk factor among many.

Because doxycycline may be prescribed before a pregnancy is recognized, doctors should consider the possibility of pregnancy when prescribing this drug to women of reproductive age, particularly those who are sexually active, Grzeskowiak suggested. That does not mean doctors should avoid prescribing the antibiotic to these women, he emphasized; rather, clinicians should consider pregnancy plans and medical history when choosing a treatment.

In some cases, doxycycline may still be the best option for a severe infection, Winterstein told Live Science, and that infection could itself put a pregnancy at risk. But for less-serious infections, safer alternatives may be available, she said.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Winterstein, A. G., Chen, H., Thai, T., Wang, Y., Smolinski, N. E., Wen, W., Ewig, C. L., Gilboa, S. M., Meaney-Delman, D., Maro, J. C., & Rasmussen, S. A. (2026). Doxycycline and risk for pregnancy loss: A multi-database, multi-indication cohort study. Annals of Internal Medicine. https://doi.org/10.7326/annals-26-01647

Isha Ishtiaq is a freelance health journalist based in Pakistan who covers health, medicine and biomedical research. Her work has appeared in Live Science, Science News, and Medscape, among other outlets. She holds a B.S. (Hons) in biotechnology from the University of Gujrat and an M.S. in biological sciences from the University of Sialkot, where her research focused on the use of deep learning models for disease detection.

#6245. Democrats flip House as Republicans confront ‘blue tsunami’

Democrats seized control of the House on Tuesday by safeguarding vulnerable incumbents and flipping districts in both battleground and deep-red terrain, delivering a sweeping repudiation of Donald Trump and Republicans that threatens to stall the president’s remaining agenda.

The Associated Press call came at 1:26 a.m. Eastern time Wednesday, hours after Democrats were projected to win a majority in the Senate, with a string of victories in deeply conservative states.

“The American people have spoken and made clear they've had enough of the extremism, enough of the corruption,’’ House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is poised to become the first Black speaker, told cheering supporters in Washington. “They want a Congress that's going to deliver for the American people, and that is exactly what House Democrats will do.”

Recent polls had forecast a strong Democratic showing amid rising discontent with the president's policies and economic anxiety driven by rising prices and the Iran war. But the magnitude of the Democratic majority surprised even the most optimistic Democratic partisans.

The “blue tsunami” marked an extraordinary turnaround for a party that suffered withering losses in 2024, when Trump returned to the White House and Republicans won a governing trifecta in Washington.

Republicans had hoped that a mid-decade redistricting push driven by Trump would help them keep their majority by flipping House seats in Texas, North Carolina, Florida and Ohio, among other states. Instead, many of those districts remained in Democrats’ hands.

Trump put himself front and center of the midterm campaign, imploring voters to “pretend that I’m on the ballot.” On Tuesday, he posted on social media that he “wasn’t on the ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!”

But in a later interview with CBS News, Trump congratulated Democrats on their rout. “My message is, congratulations to the Democrats, and I look forward to working with you for the good of our country," he said.

Among the night’s Democratic pickups were seats in rural and Republican-leaning districts. Farmer Jamie Ager defeated Republican state Rep. Jennifer Balkcom to flip a Western North Carolina seat that was left open after Republican Chuck Edwards announced his retirement after facing allegations of sexual harassment.

In Kentucky’s 6th District, Democrat Zach Dembo, a Navy veteran and former federal prosecutor, defeated former state Sen. Ralph Alvarado for an open seat anchored in Lexington.

Democrats also swept perennial battleground districts, flipping seats in states such as New Jersey, Colorado and Wisconsin. And in Pennsylvania, Democrats were projected to flip all four seats they were targeting, including the Philadelphia-area district of GOP Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick.

Anger over Trump’s tariff policy drove discontent in farm country, with Democrats ousting Republican Reps. Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks in Iowa and flipping the seat of Senate hopeful Ashley Hinson, who lost her bid to succeed retiring Sen. Joni Ernst.

Meanwhile, Latino voters, who were credited with helping propel Trump back into the White House in 2024, bolstered Democratic successes in Texas, scuttling GOP hopes of making good on the party’s mid-decade redistricting gambit.

Texas Republicans believed Latino voters would stick with the party this year when they redrew the state's congressional map to create up to five pickup opportunities. But anger over the president’s immigration policies, coupled with economic anxiety, has driven Trump’s approval numbers among Latinos to historic lows.

In South Texas, a pair of Democratic incumbents — Reps. Vicente Gonzalez and Henry Cuellar — easily held on to their redrawn seats, while former Bexar County sheriff's deputy Johnny Garcia prevailed over Air Force veteran Carlos De La Cruz in a district newly redrawn to elect a Republican. Democratic attorney and educator Katy Padilla Stout flipped the open 23rd District, which stretches across the state’s border with Mexico, and Tejano singer Bobby Pulido routed GOP Rep. Monica De La Cruz in another South Texas race.

The strength of the Democrats’ performance was evident in several under-the-radar races the party won in traditionally red districts, including Missouri’s 2nd District, where Republican Rep. Ann Wagner was ousted, and Indiana’s 5th, where Rep. Victoria Spartz lost reelection.

Speaker Mike Johnson, who crisscrossed the country to boost Republican candidates in the final weeks of the campaign, noted Tuesday night that history wasn’t on the GOP side: The president’s party almost always loses seats in a midterm election.

"From the first day of this election, we knew that to keep the House and sustain our majority we would have to defy more than a century of midterm history," Johnson said in Shreveport, La. "It looks like history will be kept tonight."

The new Democratic majority is expected to dedicate resources to investigating the activities of the Trump administration as well as the president.

The likely new Democratic chairman of the House Judiciary Committee is Maryland’s Jamie Raskin, while the Oversight and Government Reform panel is likely to be led by California Rep. Robert Garcia. Raskin and Garcia have already been busy making oversight requests of the administration.

For instance, the two lawmakers joined on a letter last week calling for the retention of conversations between the president and AI chatbots on matters of policy.

"The President and his advisors’ use of AI exposes the country to malign influence from unknown and unaccountable third parties. We already have ample evidence that AI chatbots can be manipulated to suit the commercial, political, or personal agendas of their designers​," Raskin and Garcia wrote.

Beyond the oversight, Jeffries outlined last month some of his legislative priorities for the next Congress.

"I think we need to put money in the pockets of everyday Americans by doing things like expanding the Child Tax Credit, as well as the Earned Income Tax Credit​," Jeffries told News12. "And, of course, we also need to end this war because the war has dramatically increased gas prices, fertilizer prices and diesel costs.​"

That was a reference to the military campaign against Iran, which appears likely to ratchet back up after the midterms.

I​n a pre-election interview with CNN, Jeffries said priorities that unite the Democratic Caucus include action on stopping the president's sweeping application of tariffs, as well as on reversing cuts to Medicaid and extending Affordable Care Act tax credits.

#6244. Light is hard to block from every direction. This physicist found a way

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

By Mandana Tadayon, Anna Mattson and Emily Conover

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Physicist Stefano Martiniani has designed an entirely new class of materials that blurs the line between order and chaos. Called gyromorphs, these metamaterials rely on crystal-like geometric structure and liquidlike randomness to block light from penetrating at any angle.

Physicists thought, structurally speaking, that they could not create such hybrid materials. “But this is evidence that you can, under certain constraints,” says Martiniani, of New York University. He likens the gyromorphs’ disorderliness to a crowd of people. You could see through the crowd if individuals stood still in straight lines, but not if they are clustered together in random groups. But there’s order too: From anywhere you stand in a gyromorph crowd, you’ll see a ring of people at a given distance.

Gyromorphs are a type of metamaterial, a substance with a structure designed to give it properties not found in naturally occurring materials. Metamaterials can control light, sound or other waves, and are often used in smartphones, medical imaging and computers. Martiniani says gyromorphs could be used to make more energy-efficient optical computers, which use light to process and store data.

To design a gyromorph, Martiniani needed to find a way to achieve the perfect structural balance. He turned to FReSCo, a program his lab created that designs molecular structures to meet researchers’ specifications, for help. “We had an algorithm, we gave it an objective, and then it was able to solve that objective, finding a solution that we were not expecting,” he says. “That is the best kind of discovery.”

#6242. These members of Congress are heading to the governor’s mansion

The number of governors who once served in Congress is set to grow next year after several lawmakers won gubernatorial races across the country.

The incoming governors include members who’ve served in Congress for decades and some with relatively short stints in Congress. But several Republican lawmakers were unsuccessful in their attempts to become the top executives of their home states on what was largely a poor night for the GOP.

Here are the lawmakers who won their governor’s races on election night:

It was a blast from the (recent) past in Alabama, where Republican Sen. Tommy Tuberville was elected governor after defeating Democrat Doug Jones, his Senate predecessor whom he defeated in 2020.

Despite the defeat, Jones — who won a 2017 special election to become the first Democrat to win a Senate race in Alabama in more than two decades — lost by a closer-than-anticipated margin to Tuberville, a staunch ally of President Donald Trump and the former head football coach at Auburn. With 99 percent of votes counted, according to The Associated Press, Tuberville was leading Jones 52 percent to 48 percent — the narrowest gubernatorial race in the Yellowhammer State since 2002.

The governor’s mansion in the Sunshine State will remain in GOP hands, with Rep. Byron Donalds narrowly defeating former Rep. David Jolly to become Florida’s first Black governor.

Donalds, who was first elected to Congress in 2020, will succeed term-limited Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, himself a former congressman.

Jolly is a former Republican lawmaker who left the party during Trump’s first term and joined Democrats last year. He was vying to become the first Democratic elected governor in Florida since Lawton Chiles won reelection in 1994. Jolly’s running mate was also a onetime House colleague — former Rep. Gwen Graham, the daughter of former Florida Gov. and Sen. Bob Graham.

The Volunteer State also made history on election night, electing its first female governor in Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn. Despite Tennessee’s deep-red lean, Blackburn only scraped by Democrat Jerri Green, a Memphis City councilwoman, with a self-funding independent pulling in a portion of the conservative vote.

Before her election to the Senate in 2018, Blackburn served in the Tennessee Senate and nearly two decades in the House. She is expected to be able to pick her Senate successor after she is sworn in as governor.

Democratic-Farmer-Labor Sen. Amy Klobuchar was another history-maker in Minnesota, becoming the first female governor of the North Star State. She defeated Republican state House Speaker Lisa DeMuth in the race to succeed retiring Gov. Tim Walz, the 2024 Democratic vice presidential nominee.

Like Blackburn, Klobuchar was also the first woman to represent her state in the Senate, where she has served since 2007. She is also expected to appoint her successor in the chamber.

Unofficial returns from the U.S. Virgin Islands showed Democrat Stacey Plaskett prevailing in the open governor’s race with more than 50 percent of the vote to avoid a runoff and become the island territory’s first female governor.

Plaskett was first elected to Congress in 2014 as the Virgin Islands’ nonvoting delegate and served as a House impeachment manager during Trump’s second impeachment trial. She faced controversy last year over her correspondence with sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, but narrowly avoided being censured and stripped of her position on the House Intelligence Committee.

Two former members of Congress who later served in Joe Biden’s Cabinet are also heading for their states’ governor’s mansions.

In California, Democratic former Rep. Xavier Becerra easily defeated Republican Steve Hilton to succeed outgoing Gov. Gavin Newsom. Since leaving Congress in 2017, Becerra has served as California attorney general and as Biden’s secretary of Health and Human Services.

And in New Mexico, former Rep. Deb Haaland easily kept the governorship in Democratic hands with her win over Republican Gregg Hull, the former Rio Rancho mayor. She succeeds another former House member, term-limited Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham.

Not all members of Congress were successful in governor’s races this year. A trio of Republican congressmen lost gubernatorial bids: Wisconsin’s Tom Tiffany, Arizona’s Andy Biggs and Michigan’s John James.

They join Republican colleagues who lost gubernatorial primaries this year, including David Schweikert of Arizona, Randy Feenstra of Iowa, Dusty Johnson of South Dakota, John W. Rose of Tennessee and Nancy Mace and Ralph Norman of South Carolina.

Sen. Michael Bennet, a Democrat from Colorado, lost a gubernatorial primary in June to state Attorney General Phil Weiser, who was easily elected Tuesday. Bennet, however, will continue to serve in the Senate as he isn’t up for reelection until 2028.

Andrew Menezes, Daniela Altimari, Mary Ellen McIntire and Nick Eskow contributed to this report.

Scientists on China's Tiangong space station used a laser trap to cool a clump of atoms to just above absolute zero, setting a new record.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists have cooled atoms to the coldest temperature ever recorded, using a laser trap aboard China's Tiangong space station.

Tiangong included an experiment in which atoms were cooled to 10 picokelvins, which is barely above absolute zero, the coldest theoretical temperature possible in physics. Absolute zero is minus 459.67 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 273.15 degrees Celsius) and the threshold at which all particles in an object are believed to stop moving.

Scientists hit the mark using "optical tweezers," known more formally as an optical-dipole trap (ODT), which hold atoms in a laser beam," the scientists reported Nov. 5 in the journal Science.

The team placed 20,000 rubidium atoms in the trap in order to restrict their motion. This reduced motion, along with the weightlessness induced by the low-gravity environment aboard the space station, caused the cloud of atoms to cool to much lower temperatures than are possible on Earth.

The experiment's results could help improve future space-based research, the team said.

"This record-low temperature could stimulate a new generation of ODT-based experiments in quantum simulation and precision measurements in space," the researchers wrote in the paper.

Despite this achievement, it's doubtful that scientists could ever hit absolute zero. One interpretation of the third law of thermodynamics, which looks at how systems behave when they approach absolute zero, is that the particles would always have a bit of entropy (disorder) associated with them, making absolute zero unachievable.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"One version of the third law states that it would require an infinite number of steps to reach absolute zero, which means you will never get there," Saibal Mitra, a professor of physics at Missouri State University, told Live Science in a 2024 interview.

The second law of thermodynamics, which states that entropy always increases, would also be violated if scientists could reach absolute zero, he added. "If you had a heat sink at absolute zero, then you could build a machine that was 100% efficient," Mitra said.

That said, space makes it easier to get close to absolute zero because microgravity allows atoms to "float" and become more efficient at cooling, Science News reported. The researchers took their weightless collection of atoms and created a quantum state of matter known as a Bose-Einstein condensate, in which very cold atoms clump and create a "fifth state" of matter as they behave akin to a single atom.

Tiangong's very cold clump follows similar experiments on the International Space Station that reached 52 picokelvins and from a weightless fall induced by a drop from a tall tower, in which atoms hit 38 picokelvins, Science News added.

#6240. This magic mushroom can kill

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Hallucinogens and poisons have never been found in the same mushroom — until now

Meet the dark magic mushroom, Galerina indica. The tiny fungus makes both a hallucinogen and a deadly toxin.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

People who eat this tiny magic mushroom may hit a lethal low instead of getting high.

The fungus makes hallucinogenic psilocybin and deadly amatoxin, researchers report November 11 in Current Biology. Dubbed “dark magic mushrooms,” it is the first species of fungus discovered to make both types of compounds.

Chemist and fungal biologist Andrew Kunik found the dark magic mushroom in 2025 growing on a decaying moss-covered palm trunk in a central Florida wetland. Kunik, who was then doing post-baccalaureate research in the lab of fungal biologist Matthew Smith at the University of Florida in Gainesville, identified the mini mushroom as Galerina indica.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

That species had not been reported in Florida before, Kunik says. “It’s quite rare and unusual.” He also found two other new related species, tagged with the placeholder names Galerina species 1 and Galerina species 2.

Other researchers had previously described G. indica’s appearance and found DNA signatures that distinguish the fungus from related species. But no one had cataloged the mushroom’s complete chemical or genetic makeup.

Related Galerina species make amatoxins, deadly chemicals that can kill in even tiny amounts and are found in death cap mushrooms and other species. Kunik and colleagues looked for those toxins in G. indica and the two other new Galerina species. G. indica makes a previously undiscovered form of amatoxin the team is calling alpha-proamanitin, the chemical analysis revealed.

The small mushroom also had blue bruises, a clue that it might make psilocybin, a psychedelic chemical being tested as a treatment for mental health disorders. Fungi usually make either amatoxin or psilocybin. Not both. Galerina species 1 also makes psilocybin but doesn’t make amatoxin, and species 2 makes neither.

“This finding shows that there’s a lot more diversity in [fungal] chemistry and the ways that they’re combined than we had really thought about,” says Anne Pringle, a mycologist at the University of Wisconsin–Madison who was not involved in the work.

Discovering these dual compounds in one mushroom was both exciting and required further analysis to confirm, Kunik says. “Surprising discoveries require great depth of evidence,” he says.

A complete workup of the mushroom’s DNA revealed genes for producing both types of chemicals. Ancestors of these dark magic mushrooms probably picked up those genes by swapping DNA with other species. Such DNA swapping, called horizontal gene transfer, is one way that organisms can quickly evolve new traits, like when bacteria exchange antibiotic resistance genes with unrelated species.

Ancestors of G. indica and its relatives probably acquired amatoxin genes early on. Those toxins are made by many of G. indica’s cousins, which indicates that amatoxins are probably heirlooms passed down from common ancestors. Ancestors of species 1 and species 2 seem to have dropped the amatoxin genes at some point since they no longer make the compounds.

The two psilocybin-producing species may have independently obtained the psychedelic genes in separate DNA swap meets, or a common ancestor may have picked up the genes and then passed them down to G. indica and species 1. There’s not enough known about the fungi’s family tree to sort out which scenario is correct.

And there’s another unsolved evolutionary mystery, Pringle says. “We still don’t know why mushrooms are poisonous.” Many scientists think it is for defending against predators, but hard evidence is lacking, she says.

“Can I eat it?” is often the first question people ask when finding a new mushroom, Pringle says. “I’m always so uncomfortable with that question and that conversation. And this paper confirms that, in fact, you should be uncomfortable.” After all, eating these dark magic mushrooms could send people tripping into the grave.

#6239. Our Cities Are Shrinking. Does That Mean They’re Doomed to Be Unlivable?

Population decline could leave thousands of cities struggling to maintain aging pipes, roads, and buildings. An engineer says it’s not too late to make the choices that will revive urban life.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

Two billion individuals. That’s economist and demographer Dean Spears’ forecast for our human population in 300 years. The last time we belonged to that small of a group was 1927. Now there are eight billion of us, and in 2080, we’re expected to hit our peak—around ten billion people. Yet, for the first time in history, demographers estimate that the average dropping birth rate over the past several decades means our species will no longer be able to replenish our numbers.

Civil engineers say this will cause major instability worldwide, including to the man-made structures of our world—roadways, buildings, safe water pipelines, and more. All of them will likely deteriorate without city residents who can pay to maintain such structures.

But we don’t have to fully reimagine what our infrastructure would look like under extreme population collapse; we can look to a swath of the industrial Midwest, known as the Rust Belt, which saw immense population decline when the steel industry cratered in the 1970s and ’80s. The fallout meant shedding at least 75 percent of the 350,000 jobs lost nationally, and massive population decline in cities from St. Louis, Missouri to Buffalo, New York. For example, in Cleveland, Ohio, 46 percent of the residents exited between 1970 and 2000, a typical scenario.

Depopulation on this scale is an unprecedented situation, but also an inevitable one, explains civil and environmental engineer Sybil Derrible, PhD, a professor at the University of Illinois Chicago. He calls himself an urban engineer, because he focuses on studying how population loss will affect multiple urban infrastructure systems over the coming century. “As far as I know, there's no policies about how to deal with depopulating cities,” he says. “No one’s going to give you $2 million to shrink.”

The total mass of all infrastructure systems humans have built over the past 200 years is truly mind-boggling; it exceeds all living biomass, which is 545.8 gigatons, according to the World Economic Forum. “So when the population goes down, infrastructure will go from being a thing we really need to being a burden. And it's already happening in many cities where there was a lot of infrastructure investment,” says Derrible.

In the 1970s, a massive exodus began in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, when the steel industry collapsed. The city of nearly 700,000 residents shrunk to about half its size between 1970 and 2025, and today more than 20,000 housing units sit vacant.

The engine that keeps a city running is its infrastructure, a vast, interconnected network of housing construction, roadways, public transit, electrical grids, and safe drinking water. But multiple factors, including job loss and a higher cost of living, have been pushing people—including new migrants—out of thousands of American cities for decades, leaving the infrastructure with little financial support. The problem will only worsen as the population fails to replace itself, Derrible believes.

Right now, about 40 percent of the nearly 30,000 U.S. cities are losing their people. In a century, it will be more like 50 percent. The larger ones, like New York City or Chicago, are likely to weather changes in population in the long run. It’s the smaller ones, home to about 10,000 to 20,000 people, that will truly suffer, Derrible says. About 12,000 cities, many of them in the Midwest, are facing infrastructure problems, but at least another 3,000 will be experiencing them by 2100, according to Derrible and his team’s 2024 paper in Nature. While the overall U.S. population is increasing due to immigration, people coming to this country don’t usually move to “small, rural cities,” he says. Instead, they settle in the suburbs.

Yet, policies designed to help people living with weakened infrastructure don’t yet exist, Derrible says. “Those people are completely being neglected. So I'm worried about that. I really want to make sure that we have some policies to be able to help them.”

But Derrible believes the solutions will come. Policymakers, engineers, scientists, city planners, and residents need to put their heads together and do the work, he says.

Here are three core parts of city infrastructure that are already being hit the hardest.

The most dire consequence of a shrinking population is the inability to maintain massive but increasingly derelict water distribution systems, Derrible says. If you don’t have money for upkeep, the result can be crises like Flint, Michigan’s untreated toxic water disaster, which happened after the cash-poor city switched its municipal water source from Detroit’s system to the Flint River to cut costs in 2014. The city has seen a mass departure of people since the 1980s, when the U.S. auto industry closed many plants and downsized operations. By 2010, four years before the water crisis, Flint’s population had dropped to nearly half its former peak.

“[The water problem] is especially overlooked because people don’t think about it too much,” Derrible says. Figuring out solutions to the lurking water crises in cities has to happen now, he says, but no easy solutions exist. Questions about how to deal with water contamination or shortages are many, though: “Do you go back to wells? Are there aquifers?” Derrible asks. And if you need to cut off a totally depopulated part of a city, how do you even do that?

According to industry organization Empowering Pumps and Equipment, aging water infrastructure is the biggest enemy of water, wastewater, and stormwater professionals who maintain and run these systems. The group cites the 2017 American Society of Civil Engineers (ASCE) Infrastructure Report Card, which says that pipes leak 6 billion gallons of treated drinking water each year, and that about 240,000 water main breaks happen annually. Upgrades and replacements require greater investment—to the tune of $670 billion, the ASCE’s 2025 infrastructure report says—but funding doesn’t come close to meeting need. With two million miles of drinking water pipes across the country, many of which were laid in the early- to mid‐20th century and are now technically at the end of their lifespan, it will take an estimated 200 years to replace the entire system at the current replacement rate of 0.5 percent of pipes per year, according to the 2017 report.

Underutilized roads are cracking and becoming harder to drive on, but also harder to fix in cities with far fewer people. A 2021 paper by Derrible and his team in the journal Environmental Research: Infrastructure and Sustainability reported that driving on rough roads in New Orleans cost about $685 per person each year. The city has lost half its population since Hurricane Katrina.

Instead of stretching thinning budgets to maintain underutilized roads, cities could consider current and future traffic patterns and potentially abandon some roadways. They could even rip out surfaces and turn them back into dirt roads, Derrible says. Each city must look at its individual needs and create its own solution.

Japan is implementing a similar kind of solution, where denser patches of houses and services keep their maintained roads and public transit areas, but in areas with few residents, the mostly unused streets are closed or repurposed.

Several cities in the U.S. have been choosing to remove the interstate highway sections that slice up their cities, most of which entered urban areas in the 1950s and destroyed and divided neighborhoods. One such city is Detroit, Michigan, which plans to replace the wide gray strips with roomy, walkable neighborhoods, in hopes of reconnecting residential areas.

Because fewer people means less tax revenue, cities that are being abandoned have less money to deal with aging or empty infrastructure like buildings. The other side of the coin is that new businesses don’t want to occupy old buildings. “New Costco? They’ll want new land to build it,” Derrible says. “At the same time we have all those abandoned buildings that we're not doing anything with, because it's just cheaper to build on new land than to retrofit an existing building.”

The picture of abandoned buildings doesn’t have to look like a post-apocalyptic nightmare of neglect. Existing buildings that are still in good shape could meet housing needs or become community spaces. For example, urban malls could be turned into apartments that are already conveniently located.

“At the very least, what I think we could be doing when a building is being abandoned is remove all the hazardous equipment, material, appliances, all of that,” Derrible says. Similar to the cleanup after a natural disaster, all furnaces and power and electrical hardware must come out to prevent fires and toxic materials.

Then you could either bulldoze the building and remove the debris, or you could strip the structure for useful parts, such as wood, metal, pipes, and electrical wire. Even skyscrapers could become rich sources of material that the civil engineering industry could mine. “Instead of going to quarries and getting new material, we could go to old skyscrapers or old concrete buildings. We crush them, so we have the aggregates to build new buildings,” Derrible says. The wood could also be reused, or it could become a source of fuel when burned. Derrible foresees abandoned city infrastructure as a potential source of new jobs that mine and process material for reuse. “Isn't that like the core of the American system, to turn any challenge into an opportunity, right?”

#6238. 9 Chefs on the Meals They're Traveling For in 2027—From Korean Soups to Peruvian Ceviche

Any professional chef can confirm that while menu development, staffing, interior design, and operations are all part of running a restaurant or kitchen, finding the time to travel in search of different flavors often feels like a rare luxury. But spending time in a different city or region is key to staying inspired. Even a quick weekend getaway can lead to incorporating new ingredients in familiar dishes, serve as an opportunity to learn a new culinary technique, help forge a connection with one’s own heritage, or connect with peers who are pushing the industry forward.

As the end of the calendar year draws near, we spoke with some of our favorite women chefs about where they’re most excited to visit in 2027—from a sushi counter in Tokyo to the oldest restaurant in Beirut—and what they’re hoping to eat and learn from those travels.

A table at ARREA!, Almuerzo Otoño's restaurant in Álava, Spain

I’ve been wanting to go back and really do it right ever since. At the top of my list of spots is Arrea!, Edorta Lamo’s restaurant in Kanpezu, a small village in the mountains of Álava. I’ve heard such wonderful things about it. What excites me is that it’s not the Basque Country most people think of first—as in, San Sebastián with its coastline and all of its pintxo bars. The seafood platter at the new Casa Juani in Boulder

Casa Juani's Spain-inspired sea urchin dish

“I am most looking forward to traveling to Boulder to visit my friends Kelly Jeun and Eduardo Vallelobo at their restaurant Casa Juani. Both are accomplished chefs who are experts in Italian and Spanish cuisines, and they recently made Bon Appétit's Best New Restaurants list. I am most excited to try everything on their menu, which is entirely Spanish. Eduardo is very proud of—and from!—Madrid, and the menu celebrates Spanish cuisine and culture.” —Melissa Rodriguez, Chef & Partner at Crane Club & Bar CC in New York City

For cookbook author Rebekah Peppler, edomae-style sushi is a must-eat in 2027.

“[Sushi Meino], a six-seat counter in Tokyo’s Azabujuban neighborhood by Chef Mei Kougo, one of only a few female sushi masters in Japan, has been high on my list since it opened in 2023 and I haven’t yet had the luck of securing a very-difficult-to-get reservation. I'm heading back to Tokyo in the spring and hoping 2027 will be my year! If I don’t get in, I’ll still be heading to Makimaki, her takeout-only hosomaki shop that opened nearby earlier this year.” — Rebekah Peppler, recipe developer and author

Baekyangsa Temple, where Buddhist nun and chef Jeong Kwan hosts meals

Freshly foraged ingredients, including mushrooms, herbs, and greens, used by chef Jeong Kwan

“Eating at venerable Jeong Kwan’s table has been high on my list for years, and I was devastated to be out of town when she and Chef Esu Lee were cooking together at his excellent restaurant Orson in Paris recently. It lit a fire in me to finally prioritize booking a trip to Baekyangsa Temple [where she cooks] to attend one of her demonstrations in 2027.” — R.P.

Street bread Ka'ak is the reason chef Mary Attea will be headed to Lebanon in 2027.

“I'm dying to try manakish and shawarma straight from the source. Plus ka'ak, the ring-shaped street bread with sesame, along with all the spreads from the market. And [I want to pay a] visit to El Soussi, one of Beirut's oldest restaurants, famous for its Lebanese breakfast, especially msabbaha, the warm mashed chickpeas with lemon and tahini. I'd be sure to get an order of beid ghanam as well, which is lambs testicles cooked in lemon and olive oil, served with fattet hummus. Growing up in the US with Lebanese heritage, we often ate many Lebanese meals as a family. But the dishes we prepared and enjoyed were such a small sliver of everything Lebanon has to offer. I've been wanting to go for such a long time so I could experience the vastness of this incredible cuisine and the country's beauty. I was meant to travel there this past March, which was postponed, so it's top of my list for 2027!” —Chef Mary Attea, executive chef of Musket Room and Raf’s in New York City

A ceviche dish at Lima restaurant Al Toke Pez

“I’m especially excited to explore Nikkei cuisine and experience Peruvian ceviche firsthand. In Mexico, we make wonderful ceviches, but I believe Peruvians have truly mastered the art of preparing this dish. I want to experience their approach to seafood, acidity, and flavor in its place of origin, while exploring the broader culinary traditions of Peru. I believe there are many shared histories and points of connection between Latin American cultures that we don’t always recognize, and I want to explore those connections through food. I’m also drawn to the opportunity to experience traditional Mesoamérican markets that are still operating throughout Peru, not only in Lima but in other regions as well. Markets reveal so much about a place: its ingredients, its people, its traditions, and the ways food connects communities. I’d also love to experience Inca culture firsthand and better understand the country’s rich cultural and culinary heritage.” —Norma Listman, chef and co-founder, Masala y Maíz in Mexico City

Traditional Assamese food items on sale at the annual Bhogali Bihu Festival in Assam

“I’m particularly interested in Assam’s distinctive use of black sesame and wild greens. During a trip to Mumbai, I had the opportunity to taste Assamese food prepared by two sisters who cook and preserve traditional Assamese foodways. Their food completely blew my mind. I would love to travel to Assam to learn more about the region’s culinary traditions and experience its food culture firsthand. As a chef who cooks both Indian and Mexican cuisine, I feel a responsibility to keep learning and exploring the vastness and richness of India’s food traditions. India is incredibly diverse, and there is still so much for me to discover. Now, as the mother of a mixed child with Indian heritage, I feel an even greater responsibility to expose him to his culture. Traveling to Assam would be an opportunity to continue learning for myself while creating a meaningful connection between my son and his cultural roots.” — N.L.

“I hosted a pop-up at ADI last year, and was able to witness firsthand the ways in which chef Kanchan [Adhikari] is doing the most incredibly inventive things with food within the South Asian diaspora while also marrying it with a Japanese omakase-style sentiment. One of my favorite restaurants of the past year and I am counting down the days until I can eat a meal in that gorgeous dining room again!"” —Samah Dada, chef and creator of recipe platform DADA Eats

A bowl of pollock soup, a dish local to Inje in South Korea

“Inje is the smallest county in South Korea and is most famous for hwangtae guk (dried pollock) soup. You can find many restaurants clustered together there that serve this regional specialty, but my absolute favorite is a place called Song-yi Sikdang. The brief menu basically comes down to the hwangtae jungsik—a set that includes pollock soup, a whole grilled pollock, an assortment of 12 perfectly seasoned namul banchans, and a warm bowl of rice. Inje is located in the Taebaek mountains alongside rivers and basins, so when you get there, you’re surrounded by stunning landscape and flora, which is absolutely gorgeous year round—ranging from verdant mountains, to golden and crimson foliage, to snowy tree tops. Inje is a short and tranquil two-hour drive from Seoul and feels similar to that of driving upstate on the Taconic from Manhattan. The geography and climate makes it the perfect environment for preparing dried pollock and also foraging for diverse wild greens and herbs (namuls), rare ones that you can only find there and are seasonally available at local farmers markets. —Clara Lee, co-author of Korean Soups and co-founder of food company Queens

I have been wanting to travel to Italy for many years, and Puglia has been top of mind. It feels like a place where food is still very much connected to the culture and deeply rooted in the abundance of the land. Since the provenance of things is our ethos, this feels particularly aligned for me. Anytime I travel (but specifically Europe). “I am really drawn to the simplicity of the cuisine. A beautiful local grilled fish with olive oil, handmade pasta, regional cheeses—these are all things that truly excite me as a chef because their beauty is in how uncomplicated they are. Local, fresh bounty, cooked well: to me this is what makes food memorable.” —Abigail Dahan-Kramer, pastry chef at Provenance in Philadelphia

#6237. I’m a Neurosurgeon. My Near-Death Experience Showed Me ‘Universal Consciousness’ for the First Time.

By comparison, it makes our material world feel “murky.”

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

When I earned my medical degree at Duke University, I was taught that consciousness is created out of chemical reactions occurring within the brain, a foundational assumption of scientific materialism, or physicalism—the notion that only the physical exists. After eleven years of rigorous training, I practiced as a neurosurgeon for more than two decades, including 15 years teaching and operating at Harvard Medical School.

I performed surgical procedures that took patients from extreme discomfort to full relief by releasing a nerve blockage or removing a tumor. I could stimulate the brain in conscious patients and affect their mental experience, which initially seemed to support my physicalist worldview. At the same time, patients deeply comatose from brain maladies would sometimes become fully alert right before dying. I couldn’t explain these phenomena, and so I dismissed them. That is, until November 2008, when a severe case of bacterial meningitis caused me to spend seven days in deep coma—and later reshaped my view of the universe.

Over three hours, I went from back pain and headache to epileptic fits and coma, as E. coli bacteria devoured my neocortex, or the outer surface of the brain, the part that is most responsible for human mentation. Healthcare professionals use the Glasgow Coma Scale to measure decreases in consciousness, with scores less than 9 indicating deep coma. A corpse would score a 3, the lowest grade on the scale, and my scores were 6 to 7 during most of that week—the doctor was out! Lumbar puncture revealed my cerebrospinal fluid to be filled with pus under pressure, and the glucose level in that fluid was only 1 mg/dl (normally 80-90, with severe bacterial meningitis occasionally as low as 20). CT and MRI scans revealed my entire neocortex was involved, meaning there was no physical functioning brain left to produce a dream or hallucination.

By the tenets of modern neuroscience, my awareness should have been zero. Without a functioning neocortex, my brain was incapable of producing a simple thought or image—and yet, I lived through a vivid, richly-detailed, hyper-real event, by comparison making this material world appear murky and dreamlike. I was unbound by space and time, immersed in universal consciousness, and wrapped in unconditional love. I had visions revealing structure to the non-physical realm that fully relates to and intertwines with our lives here on earth.

Back in the hospital, my prospects for survival were down to 2 percent when, on day seven, I startled everyone as I began to awaken. My doctors were even more surprised when I fully recovered over about two months. As my medical knowledge returned, I reviewed my records and scans, and discussed them with my doctors, trying to make sense of it all. I searched for a physicalist explanation, yet the case was unyielding—no conventional explanation could suffice. I was forced to acknowledge that an expansive model of reality was required to explain my experience.

In 2018, when my case records were peer-reviewed before publication in the Journal of Nervous and Mental Disease, the editors asked the authors to explain my unprecedented recovery. They replied that my miraculous recovery occurred because of my spiritual journey, knowing of similar extraordinary recoveries in the near-death literature. Due to techniques of cardiac resuscitation developed in the 1960s, millions of others have escaped the shackles of the physical brain and body, and reported similar near-death experiences (NDEs) of connection with a non-physical realm. Those descriptions have been categorized and evaluated using Greyson’s NDE Scale (developed by UVA psychiatrist Bruce Greyson), which quantifies the cognitive, affective, paranormal, and transcendental aspects of the experiences.

The vast evidence from these unusual experiences has convinced many former physicalists that their model is outdated. A more sufficient explanation is that the brain serves as a transceiver or antenna for tuning in to a larger, collective consciousness. Renowned Harvard psychologist William James, French philosopher Henri Bergson, and English writer Aldous Huxley, all postulated this “reducing valve” role for the brain in the early 20th century, noting that a shift in the primary physicalist assumption was required to explain these phenomena.

With a growing abundance of data, it is clearer that consciousness is fundamental and influences physical matter from the top down, rather than the bottom-up model of physicalism, where consciousness arises from the brain. Spontaneous remissions and the placebo effect confirm the power of the mind over matter and validate the observer effect seen in quantum mechanics experiments.

The “hard problem of consciousness” remains unsolved because its underlying premise is false.

I believe merging first-person subjective inquiry with rigorous empirical science will take us farther in knowing the true nature of our consensus reality.

To that point, humanity will thrive when science finally acknowledges that we are interconnected through love and part of one larger consciousness, with free will to become the best version of ourselves, both as individuals and collectively. The golden rule is woven directly into the fabric of the universe, providing a moral compass that shows that, ultimately, what matters most is how we treat each other.

Over 300 Live Science readers responded to a recent poll about whether they'd train themselves to lucid dream if they could.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Lucid dreaming describes when you realize you're in a dream as it's unfolding. Sometimes, people can control the content of their dreams from this state of awareness.

Recently, researchers claimed that they found a way to "train" people to lucid dream by having them meditate and complete virtual-reality-augmented exercises while they were awake. Following the release of that study, Live Science asked its readers whether they would learn to lucid dream if they could.

Over 300 readers weighed in, with 77% saying "Yes, I'd want to try to control my dreams." Additionally, 17% of respondents said "No, I already lucid dream enough without training," 3% said "No, I don't see the point," and the final 3% said they weren't sure.

In the comments, one reader shared that they'd once experimented with hypnagogic napping, a technique famously used by Thomas Edison and Salvador Dalí in which the famous luminaries would wake themselves up just as they were drifting to sleep. Edison claimed that this helped him access a creative sweet spot at the edge of sleep and wakefulness.

"When I was experimenting with the hypnagogic state (using the Edison method) I started having spontaneous lucid dreams," the reader wrote. "I can confidently say, that there were some of the most profound experiences of my life, so the answer is definitely yes."

Another reader reported having lucid dreams "about once or twice a year," adding that they typically wake up shortly after realizing it's a dream. "My most recent one was of my recently deceased wife. I became very sad when I realized she wasn't supposed to be there," the reader wrote. "I hugged her and told her I don't want to be without her. She replied that I could live a long life if I took care of myself (This was a very typical response from her...lol). I feel very blessed to have had that dream."

Other readers chimed in on Facebook. "Already have it [lucid dreaming], but if I didn't I would certainly practice to do so," one wrote. "Hell yes," another said, in response to the idea of training themselves to lucid dream.

Other readers noted that they already lucid dream quite often or that they can consistently control their dreams, with one even saying that all of their dreams are lucid. Another said, "Some nights I interrupt it [my dream] like Monty Python — 'Too silly!' and start over."

But while one person compared lucid dreaming to "writing and directing your own movie," another noted that "lucid dreams can be boring, repetitive, annoying." So while many people would practice lucid dreaming if they could, not everyone sees the appeal.

Nicoletta Lanese is the health channel editor at Live Science and was previously a news editor and staff writer at the site. She is a recipient of the 2026 AHCJ International Health Study Fellowship, with a project focused on antibiotic stewardship practices in Japan and the U.S. They hold a graduate certificate in science communication from UC Santa Cruz and degrees in neuroscience and dance from the University of Florida. Beyond Live Science, Lanese's work has appeared in The Scientist, Science News, the Mercury News, Mongabay and Stanford Medicine Magazine, among other outlets. Based in NYC, she also remains involved in dance and performs in local choreographers' work.

#6235. Mike Johnson won’t seek top GOP spot as House flips

Speaker Mike Johnson will not seek to serve as House minority leader in the next Congress.

A source familiar with the speaker’s decision confirmed that the Louisiana Republican would not seek the post after Tuesday’s midterm elections saw Republicans lose their narrow majority in a Democratic tsunami.

Other candidates were already lining up. Fellow Louisiana Republican Steve Scalise, the current majority leader, is expected to launch a bid for minority leader Wednesday, according to a person familiar with his plans who described him as a “proven and tested leader.” And House Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan of Ohio is also throwing in his hat, according to multiple reports.

The Republican conference is set to hold its leadership elections next week.

Johnson held an election night event in Shreveport, La., after crisscrossing the country trying to protect the GOP majority, arguing throughout the campaign that polling favoring Democrats would not be accurate.

“While the outcome of this midterm is not what we’d hoped and fought for, a new battle is just beginning. This Democrat House majority will be led by the most radical and extreme leftists in American history,” Johnson said in a statement after Democrats claimed the majority. “However, Republicans will never stop fighting to defend the Constitution and protect the foundations that have made America the greatest nation in the history of the world.”

The blame game had already begun Wednesday morning, as Republicans reeled from losses that cut deeper than expected.

“The polls were not wrong. You were,” Rep. Greg Steube, R-Fla., wrote on social media, referring to his party’s leaders in the House and Senate. “Please do us all a favor and step aside so new leadership can take a truly conservative direction.”

Mary Ellen McIntire contributed to this report.
